A: The Quran's most frequent divine names are 'the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful' (Quran 59:22), recited by Muslims before nearly every daily act. Justice is equally real — deeds are recompensed — but Islamic teaching, like Exodus 34:6-7, places mercy first.

Q: Why does Islam reject calling God 'Father'?
A: The Quran avoids parent-child language for God because, in its view, such language historically slid into literal sonship and division within God. It states that God 'neither begets nor is born' (Quran 112:3). God's tenderness is expressed instead through names like the Entirely Merciful, the Subtle, the Acquainted.

Q: Can anyone see God, according to these scriptures?
A: The Quran says 'Vision perceives Him not, but He perceives [all] vision' (Quran 6:103) — God cannot be seen in this life, though Muslims believe the people of Paradise will see Him in the hereafter. The Bible teaches that 'God is spirit' (John 4:24), while mainstream Christianity holds that God made Himself visible in Jesus — one of the key points where the two faiths differ.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The works below are offered as general further reading for readers who want to go deeper. They are listed as starting points, not as sources for specific claims in this article; every scriptural quotation above comes directly from the cited translations (Saheeh International via api.alquran.cloud, and the World English Bible via bible-api.com).

Al-Ghazali — The Ninety-Nine Beautiful Names of God (al-Maqsad al-Asna): a classical Muslim exploration of the divine names quoted in Quran 7:180 and 59:22-24.

Tim Winter (ed.) — The Cambridge Companion to Classical Islamic Theology: accessible academic essays on how Muslim scholars understood God's oneness and attributes.

Alister E. McGrath — Christian Theology: An Introduction: a standard, widely used textbook presenting the Trinity and incarnation as mainstream Christian scholarship understands them.

Karen Armstrong — A History of God: a readable comparative history of how Jews, Christians, and Muslims have understood the one God.

Gai Eaton — Islam and the Destiny of Man: a reflective introduction to the Islamic vision of God and humanity, written for Western readers.

title: How Was the Quran Preserved?
subtitle: Memorization, manuscripts, and mass transmission: how the recitation of seventh-century Arabia became the book on your shelf
summary: The Quran was preserved through two simultaneous channels: mass memorization by the Prophet Muhammad's companions and written records made by his scribes during his lifetime. A verified complete collection was assembled under Abu Bakr within about two years of the Prophet's death, and the third caliph, Uthman, distributed standardized copies about two decades later. Since then, unbroken chains of memorizers and manuscripts have carried the text in numbers Muslim scholars call mutawatir — too many independent transmitters for coordinated error. This article walks through that history, the Quran's own preservation promise, and an honest explanation of the canonical reading traditions (qira'at).

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body: The Quran was preserved through two channels working at once: living memorization and writing. During the Prophet Muhammad's lifetime his companions memorized the revelation as it came down while his scribes wrote it out; within about two years of his death the written records were gathered into one verified collection, and roughly two decades later the third caliph, Uthman, sent standardized copies to the major Muslim cities. Every generation since has passed the text on through both memory and manuscript in numbers Muslim scholars call mutawatir — too many independent carriers for coordinated error. The Quran frames this as a divine promise: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Ask an honest question of any scripture and you are really asking two questions at once. First: what did the original message say? Second: can I trust that the text in my hands today still says it? For the Quran, Muslims give an unusually confident answer to that second question, and this article explains why in plain language.

We will look at three things: the history of how the Quran was memorized, written, collected, and standardized; the Quran's own words about its preservation; and the qira'at — the canonical reading traditions — explained honestly, because a fair account should address them rather than hide them.

Two terms before we begin. A hafiz (plural: huffaz) is a person who has memorized the entire Quran word for word. Tawatur means mass transmission: a report carried independently by so many people in every generation that they could not all have agreed on a lie or made the same mistake.

sections.title: The Question We Are Answering
sections.body:
The precise question is this: by what mechanism did the words recited by the Prophet Muhammad in seventh-century Arabia reach the printed copy on a shelf today, and how strong is the evidence that nothing was lost or changed along the way?

Notice what the question is not. It is not whether the Quran is true or divine — those are separate questions with their own articles. It is a question about transmission: the pipeline between the original recitation and the modern page. The Quran's pipeline has an unusual structure: two independent channels — mass memorization and writing — running side by side from the first generation, each checking the other.

sections.title: From Recitation to Standard Copies: The History
sections.body:
The Quran was revealed piecemeal over about twenty-three years, from roughly 610 CE until the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE. It did not arrive as a bound book but as a recitation — the word Quran itself means "recitation" — and from the beginning the community received it by hearing and repeating it.

Seventh-century Arabia had a powerful memorization culture, and the Quran entered it as its most treasured text. The Prophet's companions memorized the revelation as it came, and because Muslims recite the Quran aloud in daily congregational prayers, the text was continuously performed in public — a slip before listeners who know it by heart is corrected on the spot. Hadith collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari also relate that the Prophet reviewed the revelation with the angel Gabriel every Ramadan, and twice in his final year.

Memory was not the only channel. The Prophet appointed scribes — Zayd ibn Thabit is the best known — who wrote each passage down as it was revealed, on parchment, palm stalks, flat stones, and shoulder bones, with the Prophet directing where each passage belonged within its surah (chapter). So by 632 CE the entire Quran existed twice over: in the memories of the huffaz and in written records.

The first gathering into a single collection came almost immediately. According to the account preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, after the Battle of Yamama killed a number of memorizers, Umar ibn al-Khattab urged the first caliph, Abu Bakr, to have the written records collected. Abu Bakr commissioned Zayd ibn Thabit, who verified each verse against both the written records and the testimony of those who had learned it directly from the Prophet. The collection passed from Abu Bakr to Umar and then to Umar's daughter Hafsa, a widow of the Prophet.

The final step came under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, around two decades after the Prophet's death. As Islam spread beyond Arabia, disputes arose over styles of recitation. Uthman had authoritative copies made from the collection kept with Hafsa, sent one to each major city, and ordered divergent private copies destroyed — a public policy to unify recitation, reported openly in Muslim sources, which also record that the companions broadly supported it. The standardized text is called the Uthmanic mushaf (a mushaf is a physical copy of the Quran), and its consonantal skeleton underlies every Quran printed today.

Physical evidence from that first century survives. Among the earliest is a set of parchment folios in the Mingana Collection at the University of Birmingham, containing parts of surahs 18, 19, and 20 in the early Arabic script known as Hijazi. According to the university, radiocarbon testing at Oxford dated the parchment to between 568 and 645 CE with 95.4 percent probability — a range overlapping the Prophet's own lifetime. Anyone can set those passages beside a modern copy and compare.

sections.title: The Quran's Own Promise of Preservation
sections.body:
Muslims read this history through a promise the Quran makes about itself. In Surah al-Hijr, God declares:

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا ٱلذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَحَٰفِظُونَ

"Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9)

The claim is striking: the Quran does not ask its community to preserve it as a duty they might fail; it announces that God Himself has taken responsibility for guarding it. Muslims understand the whole history above — memorizers, scribes, early collection, standardized copies — as the means by which that promise was carried out.

The same theme appears at the very moment of revelation. Surah al-Qiyamah addresses the Prophet as he received the words, moving his tongue hurriedly for fear of losing them:

إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُۥ وَقُرْءَانَهُۥ

"Indeed, upon Us is its collection [in your heart] and [to make possible] its recitation." (Quran 75:17)

فَإِذَا قَرَأْنَٰهُ فَٱتَّبِعْ قُرْءَانَهُۥ

"So when We have recited it [through Gabriel], then follow its recitation." (Quran 75:18)

From the first, then, retention was declared God's responsibility rather than a human hope.

Two further passages describe the Quran's guarded status. In Surah al-Waqi'ah:

إِنَّهُۥ لَقُرْءَانٌۭ كَرِيمٌۭ

"Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" (Quran 56:77)

فِى كِتَٰبٍۢ مَّكْنُونٍۢ

"In a Register well-protected;" (Quran 56:78)

And in Surah al-Buruj:

بَلْ هُوَ قُرْءَانٌۭ مَّجِيدٌۭ

"But this is an honored Qur'an" (Quran 85:21)

فِى لَوْحٍۢ مَّحْفُوظٍۭ

"[Inscribed] in a Preserved Slate." (Quran 85:22)

Muslim commentators have generally understood the "Register well-protected" and the "Preserved Slate" (in Arabic, al-lawh al-mahfuz) as the heavenly original kept with God: the Quran's source is guarded above, and its earthly text is guarded below.

A scripture's claim about itself cannot, by itself, prove that claim — a skeptic may fairly say so. That is why this article began with history rather than theology. The Muslim case is that the promise and the record fit together: the Quran announced it would be guarded, and the transmission history is what that guarding looked like in practice.

sections.title: What Are the Qira'at? The Reading Traditions Explained Honestly
sections.body:
Anyone who researches the Quran online will quickly meet the word qira'at, sometimes presented as a hidden problem. It is not hidden, and understanding it honestly is part of understanding preservation. (Because no Bible passages are required for this topic, this section stands in place of the usual biblical-perspective section.)

A qira'ah (plural: qira'at) is a canonical reading tradition — a complete, documented way of reciting the text, transmitted from the Prophet through his companions and the named master reciters of the early generations. Ten readings are recognized as canonical, each named after a master reciter and carried by his students. The most widespread today is the reading of Asim of Kufa as transmitted by Hafs; the reading of Nafi of Medina as transmitted by Warsh is common in North and West Africa. A printed Quran follows one of these readings and identifies which.

Most differences between readings are matters of pronunciation: vowel length, articulation, dialectal features of early Arabic. A smaller number involve a different grammatical form or word — transmitted as complementary, not contradictory. The best-known example is the fourth verse of the opening chapter. In the reading of Hafs it is:

مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ

"Sovereign of the Day of Recompense." (Quran 1:4)

Other canonical readings recite the first word as malik, "King," rather than the long maalik, "Master" or "Owner." King of the Day of Judgment and Master of the Day of Judgment are two true descriptions of the same God — a difference in emphasis, not doctrine. This example is typical: no article of Islamic belief or practice differs between canonical readings.

Hadith collections relate that the Quran was revealed in several modes (ahruf) to ease recitation for tribes with different dialects. Scholars have long discussed how exactly the ahruf relate to the qira'at, but the practical criteria are agreed: a reading is canonical only if it has an authentic, unbroken chain to the Prophet, conforms to the Uthmanic written skeleton, and is sound Arabic. Readings that failed these tests were set aside by Muslim scholars themselves, openly.

The honest summary: the qira'at are not textual corruption uncovered by critics. They are a documented canon of recitation, preserved with the same chains and rigor as the text itself, and written about openly since Islam's earliest centuries.

sections.title: How This Compares with Other Ancient Texts
sections.body:
Most works from the ancient world survive through one channel only: manuscript copying. Scribes copied manuscripts, later scribes copied the copies, and scholars today reconstruct the earliest recoverable wording by comparing surviving copies — a discipline called textual criticism. That is not an insult to any tradition; it is simply how texts without a living memorization institution travel through time.

The New Testament, for example, is described by Christian textual scholars themselves as a manuscript tradition: the original autographs have not survived, thousands of later Greek manuscripts exist with variations among them, and modern critical editions are careful reconstructions of the earliest attainable text. Mainstream Christian scholarship states this plainly and regards most variants as minor; the companion article on how the Bible was transmitted tells that story fairly.

The Quran's transmission has a different structure. It has two channels rather than one — complete memorization and writing, each correcting the other from the first generation. Standardization happened within about two decades of the source rather than emerging from centuries of copying. And the oral channel is institutional and continuous: every generation has produced huffaz in large numbers, certified in unbroken teacher-to-student chains, with the text performed daily in public worship where errors are caught immediately.

None of this, by itself, settles which scripture is true. What it establishes is narrower and important: the claim that the Quran read today is the Quran of the seventh century rests on an unusually strong transmission mechanism, and readers can weigh that evidence for themselves.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A few misunderstandings come up so often that they deserve direct answers.

"Uthman created his own version of the Quran and burned the evidence." Uthman did not compose or edit a text; he had copies made from the collection compiled under Abu Bakr — assembled by the Prophet's own scribe under strict verification — and distributed them. The destruction of divergent private copies was a public, announced policy to end recitation disputes, supported by the companions and reported openly in Muslim sources — which is not how cover-ups behave.

"The qira'at prove there are many different Qurans." The qira'at are canonical reading traditions with documented chains, differing mostly in pronunciation, with no difference in doctrine. Muslim scholars catalogued them centuries ago; they are a studied feature of the tradition, not a leak.

"The Quran was only written down centuries after Muhammad." Writing began during the Prophet's lifetime; a complete verified collection existed within about two years of his death; standard copies circulated within about two decades. The Birmingham folios described earlier were radiocarbon dated, per the University of Birmingham, to a range overlapping the Prophet's lifetime.

"Early Qurans had no dots or vowel marks, so the text must have changed when marks were added." Early Arabic script recorded a consonantal skeleton (the rasm), and readers supplied pronunciation from the oral tradition — the primary channel all along. The dots and vowel signs added later did not create a new text; they encoded in ink the recitation the community already carried by heart.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
Put the pieces side by side. A promise: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9). A mechanism: memorization and writing in parallel from the first generation, a verified collection within about two years of the Prophet's death, standardized copies within about two decades, and unbroken teacher-to-student chains ever since. And a result anyone can test: a hafiz from Indonesia and a hafiz from Senegal who learned the same canonical reading will recite the entire book identically.

For Muslims this is not a fortunate accident; it is what a fulfilled divine promise looks like. The Quran describes itself as "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" "In a Register well-protected;" (Quran 56:77-78) — guarded at its source with God and, Muslims hold, guarded in its earthly text among people.

So here is an invitation rather than a demand. If you are weighing Islam's claims, start where the evidence is most concrete and checkable. Read the text, listen to a memorizer recite it, and compare a seventh-century folio with a modern page. A serious search for God deserves a text you can trust — and the Quran's case for that trust is open for inspection.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: What does hafiz mean, and how many huffaz are there today?
A: A hafiz is a person who has memorized the entire Quran word for word. There is no official global census, but memorization schools operate on every continent and complete memorizers are commonly numbered in the millions. The text has never depended on a few individuals.

Q: What is tawatur?
A: Mass transmission: a report carried independently by so many people in every generation that coordinated fabrication or shared error is practically impossible. Muslim scholars hold that the Quran's text is mutawatir, transmitted this way both orally and in writing.

Q: Are the qira'at different Qurans?
A: No. They are canonical reading traditions transmitted with documented chains, differing mostly in pronunciation and occasionally in complementary word forms. No Islamic belief or practice differs between canonical readings.

Q: What is the Birmingham Quran manuscript?
A: Parchment folios at the University of Birmingham containing parts of surahs 18, 19, and 20 in early Hijazi script. Per the university, radiocarbon testing dated the parchment to 568-645 CE with 95.4 percent probability — a range overlapping the Prophet's lifetime.

Q: Did Uthman change the Quran?
A: No. He commissioned copies of the collection already compiled under Abu Bakr by the Prophet's scribe Zayd ibn Thabit and sent them to the major cities to end disputes over recitation. Muslim sources report the episode openly and record broad support from the companions.

Q: Does the Quran itself claim it will be preserved?
A: Yes. Quran 15:9 states: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." Muslims understand the memorizers, manuscripts, and unbroken chains of history as the fulfillment of that promise.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Muhammad Mustafa al-Azami's The History of the Qur'anic Text is a detailed scholarly study of the Quran's collection and transmission. Ingrid Mattson's The Story of the Qur'an is an accessible academic overview of how the Quran was revealed, compiled, and lived with. Ahmad von Denffer's Ulum al-Qur'an is a beginner-friendly manual of the classical Quranic sciences, including the qira'at. Michael Sells's Approaching the Qur'an introduces the sound of the recited Quran to readers with no Arabic.

For the manuscript evidence discussed above, the University of Birmingham's Cadbury Research Library publishes information about its Quran folios, including the radiocarbon dating, on its official website.

title: How Was the Bible Transmitted?
subtitle: From spoken word to Greek manuscripts to modern translations — the journey of the Christian scriptures, told honestly
summary: The Bible reached today's readers through a long historical journey: oral teaching, composition in Greek, hand copying for many centuries, gradual agreement on the canon, and chains of translation. This article presents that history as mainstream Christian scholarship itself describes it, using Luke's own prologue as a window into how the Gospels were composed. It then offers the Islamic perspective: the Quran affirms the original Gospel of Jesus as guidance and light, while warning that scripture can be altered by human hands. The aim is an honest, respectful account that helps seekers compare the two transmission stories fairly.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body:
The Bible did not arrive as a single finished book. It grew over centuries: Jesus taught orally, authors later wrote accounts in Greek, scribes copied those writings by hand for well over a thousand years, and church leaders gradually agreed on which books belonged.

Almost everything in this article comes from Christian scholarship itself — the discipline called textual criticism, built largely by devout Christians. Islam, for its part, honors the original Gospel given to Jesus as true revelation from God. Knowing how the Bible reached us helps Christians and Muslims discuss scripture honestly, without caricature on either side.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Every scripture has a history — a real, human journey from the moment of revelation to the printed page in your hands. This article traces that journey for the Bible, especially the New Testament.

A word about method. Nothing here relies on polemics. The account below is the standard picture taught in Christian seminaries. The discipline that studies it, textual criticism, was developed overwhelmingly by Christian scholars who loved the Bible and wanted to recover its earliest wording. When modern Christian Bibles carry footnotes noting that some ancient manuscripts lack a verse, that honesty is the fruit of their work.

Islam enters this conversation with respect. The Quran speaks of the Injil — the Gospel given to Jesus — as genuine revelation, "guidance and light." The Islamic question is not whether God spoke through Jesus; Muslims affirm that He did. The question is what happened to that message afterward.

sections.title: The Question We Are Asking
sections.body:
What happened between Jesus teaching in Galilee and the Bible on a bookshelf today?

Break it into stages. First, an oral stage: Jesus wrote no book, and his teaching circulated by word of mouth. Second, a writing stage: letters and Gospel accounts were composed in Greek in the decades after his ministry. Third, a copying stage: before printing, every copy was made by hand. Fourth, a canon stage: communities gradually agreed on which writings counted as scripture. Fifth, a translation stage: the text passed through Greek and Latin into thousands of languages.

Each stage is described by Christian historians themselves.

sections.title: From Spoken Word to Printed Page
sections.body:
Begin with language. Historians broadly agree that Jesus taught in Aramaic, the everyday tongue of first-century Jewish Galilee, yet the New Testament was written in Greek. Apart from a few preserved Aramaic phrases, the recorded words of Jesus therefore already stand in translation — a point made routinely in Christian introductions to the New Testament.

The earliest Christian writings are generally held to be the letters of Paul; the four Gospels came later in the first century, according to mainstream dating, drawing on oral tradition and earlier written material. None of the original documents — the autographs — survives for any book of the Bible. What survives are copies of copies.

Hand copying introduces variation. The surviving Greek manuscripts of the New Testament number in the thousands, from small early papyrus fragments — the earliest commonly dated to the second century — to complete codices such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, generally dated to the fourth century. Comparing them reveals many textual variants. Mainstream textual critics, most of them Christians, describe the great majority as trivial: spelling, word order, slips of the pen. A smaller number are significant, and modern Christian Bibles mark them openly — well-known examples include the longer ending of Mark and the story of the woman caught in adultery in John, both flagged in standard translations as absent from the earliest manuscripts.

The canon — the official list of biblical books — took shape gradually. Early communities used differing collections, and the earliest surviving list matching exactly today's twenty-seven New Testament books appears in a letter of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in the later fourth century. Even now the Old Testament canon differs among Christians: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books, called deuterocanonical, that Protestant Bibles omit.

Finally, translation. The Hebrew scriptures were rendered into Greek — the Septuagint — before Jesus's time, and New Testament authors often quote that version. Jerome's Latin Vulgate later served the Western church for roughly a thousand years. Modern translations work from critical editions: scholarly reconstructions assembled by comparing manuscripts. All of this is the mainstream account, told by Christian scholarship with admirable honesty.

sections.title: What the Quran Says About the Gospel
sections.body:
The Quran's starting point is reverence for what God gave Jesus. In Surah al-Ma'idah, God says:

وَقَفَّيْنَا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم بِعِيسَى ٱبْنِ مَرْيَمَ مُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ ۖ وَءَاتَيْنَٰهُ ٱلْإِنجِيلَ فِيهِ هُدًۭى وَنُورٌۭ وَمُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ وَهُدًۭى وَمَوْعِظَةًۭ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ

"And We sent, following in their footsteps, Jesus, the son of Mary, confirming that which came before him in the Torah; and We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light and confirming that which preceded it of the Torah as guidance and instruction for the righteous." (Quran 5:46)

The Injil — the Gospel given to Jesus — is described as genuine revelation: guidance and light, confirming the Torah before it. Islam affirms the message of Jesus as coming from the same God who sent the Quran.

The very next verse addresses Christians directly:

وَلْيَحْكُمْ أَهْلُ ٱلْإِنجِيلِ بِمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ فِيهِ ۚ وَمَن لَّمْ يَحْكُم بِمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْفَٰسِقُونَ

"And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient." (Quran 5:47)

Christians are called the People of the Gospel and urged to judge by what God revealed in it — the Gospel's original content is treated as authoritative divine guidance.

At the same time, the Quran warns that revelation can be interfered with by human hands:

فَوَيْلٌۭ لِّلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ بِأَيْدِيهِمْ ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ هَٰذَا مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ لِيَشْتَرُوا۟ بِهِۦ ثَمَنًۭا قَلِيلًۭا ۖ فَوَيْلٌۭ لَّهُم مِّمَّا كَتَبَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَوَيْلٌۭ لَّهُم مِّمَّا يَكْسِبُونَ

"So woe to those who write the "scripture" with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," in order to exchange it for a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written and woe to them for what they earn." (Quran 2:79)

This is the concept Muslims call tahrif: distortion of scripture. Two nuances matter. First, classical Muslim scholars differed over its extent — some emphasized alteration of the text, others alteration of meaning while much true text remained. Second, the verse condemns those who wrote material and falsely attributed it to God; it is not a blanket charge against every scribe or every Christian.

So the Islamic frame is neither "the Bible is worthless" nor "the Bible is exactly the original revelation." God truly gave Jesus a Gospel of guidance and light, and today's texts reach us through a long human history — carrying truth, alongside the marks of human hands.

sections.title: What the Bible Says About Itself
sections.body:
The New Testament gives us candid windows into its own composition. The clearest is the opening of Luke's Gospel, where the author explains his method:

"Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed." (Luke 1:1-4)

Read that slowly. Luke says many others had already written accounts. He says the material was "delivered" — handed down — from eyewitnesses to people like himself, who was not one. He describes tracing everything "accurately from the first": the language of careful investigation. This is an author describing historical research in his own words; many Christians would say God's inspiration worked precisely through such human effort.

John's Gospel closes with a similar candor about selection:

"There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written." (John 21:25)

The Gospels, by their own testimony, are selections from a much larger body of things Jesus did and said — chosen and arranged by authors writing for particular audiences.

The classic Christian statement about scripture's nature comes from a letter to Timothy:

"Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness," (2 Timothy 3:16)

This verse anchors the Christian doctrine of inspiration: scripture is "God-breathed." It is also fair to note, as many Christian commentators themselves do, that when this letter was written the "Scripture" its first readers knew was above all the Hebrew scriptures — the New Testament as a collection did not yet exist — and that the verse describes scripture's character without listing which books belong.

By the Bible's own account, then, its composition involved prior sources, handed-down testimony, human investigation, and selection. That is where any honest account of transmission must begin.

sections.title: Two Transmission Stories, Side by Side
sections.body:
Set the two transmission stories side by side — each as its own scholarship tells it — and structural differences emerge.

Language: the Quran is preserved and recited in its original Arabic, while the words of Jesus were spoken in Aramaic but preserved in Greek — with few exceptions, not available in his own tongue.

Timescale: Muslim tradition and the early manuscript record describe a complete text standardized within a generation of the Prophet Muhammad's death, while the New Testament canon took shape over centuries.

Mechanism: the Quran's transmission ran on two parallel tracks — mass memorization alongside written copies — each checking the other; the Bible's ran on hand copying alone, which is why variants accumulated and textual criticism became necessary.

Self-description: Luke's prologue describes research and compilation of handed-down reports; the Quran presents itself throughout as the direct speech of God to one messenger.

Two cautions keep this honest. None of these differences impugns anyone's sincerity: generations of Christian scribes labored devotedly, and Christian scholars' candor about variants is a mark of integrity. And the Quran's own history — standardization under the caliph Uthman, early manuscripts, modes of recitation — deserves the same scrutiny, and receives it elsewhere in this library. The narrow point here is that the two scriptures traveled very different roads to reach us.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A few misunderstandings cloud this topic on both sides.

"Muslims believe the Bible is worthless." Not so. The Quran calls the original Torah and Gospel guidance and light and calls Christians the People of the Gospel. The Islamic claim concerns transmission, not a denial that God spoke through Jesus.

"Textual variants mean nobody knows what the Bible says." Also not so. Mainstream textual critics hold that the vast majority of variants are minor and the general shape of the text is well established. The serious questions concern specific passages and wording — significant, but not a free-for-all.

"The books of the Bible were chosen at the Council of Nicaea." This story circulates in novels and internet memes, but historians of Christianity describe canon formation as a gradual process reflected in usage, debate, and later lists and councils. Repeating the Nicaea legend weakens any argument built on it.

"Since 2 Timothy says scripture is God-breathed, the transmission question is settled." The verse states a doctrine of inspiration; it does not list the canon's contents, and it could not certify copies and translations made centuries later. Inspiration and transmission are two different questions, and this article is about the second.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion: Continuity and Criterion
sections.body:
Islam's answer to all this is continuity. God did not speak once and fall silent: He sent the Torah to Moses, the Gospel to Jesus, and finally — Muslims believe — the Quran. The Quran describes its own role in that sequence:

وَأَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ بِٱلْحَقِّ مُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ ۖ فَٱحْكُم بَيْنَهُم بِمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ ۖ وَلَا تَتَّبِعْ أَهْوَآءَهُمْ عَمَّا جَآءَكَ مِنَ ٱلْحَقِّ ۚ لِكُلٍّۢ جَعَلْنَا مِنكُمْ شِرْعَةًۭ وَمِنْهَاجًۭا ۚ وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَجَعَلَكُمْ أُمَّةًۭ وَٰحِدَةًۭ وَلَٰكِن لِّيَبْلُوَكُمْ فِى مَآ ءَاتَىٰكُمْ ۖ فَٱسْتَبِقُوا۟ ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ ۚ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ جَمِيعًۭا فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ

"And We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], the Book in truth, confirming that which preceded it of the Scripture and as a criterion over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their inclinations away from what has come to you of the truth. To each of you We prescribed a law and a method. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation [united in religion], but [He intended] to test you in what He has given you; so race to [all that is] good. To Allah is your return all together, and He will [then] inform you concerning that over which you used to differ." (Quran 5:48)

The Quran calls itself a confirmation of earlier scripture and a criterion over it — in Arabic, muhaymin, a guardian and standard. Whatever survives of the earlier revelation is confirmed where it agrees with the Quran, and the Quran serves as the measure where the records differ.

Notice the posture this creates. A Muslim has no need to mock the Bible's history — it is simply what Christian scholarship reports — nor to deny the light that remains in it, which the Quran affirms by name. The invitation is gentler than polemic: if you love the message of Jesus, look at the book that confirms him, honors his mother, and preserves the heart of what he taught — the call to worship the one God alone.

For the Christian reader, this history need not be threatening; your own scholars uncovered it. The open question is where God's guidance is available today in a form whose transmission can be traced with confidence. Islam's answer is the Quran — a claim to be tested against evidence in the companion articles.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Did Jesus write any part of the Bible?
A: No. Mainstream Christian scholarship agrees that Jesus left no writings. The Gospels were written about him, in Greek, in the decades after his ministry — a process Luke describes in his prologue.

Q: Do Muslims believe the Bible is completely corrupted?
A: No. The Quran affirms the original Torah and Gospel as guidance and light, and classical scholars differed over whether the distortion it warns of affected mainly the text or its interpretation. Today's Bible is seen as containing truth alongside material shaped by long human transmission.

Q: What language did Jesus speak, and why does it matter?
A: Historians broadly agree Jesus taught in Aramaic, while the New Testament was composed in Greek. With few exceptions, his words reach us in translation — a fact acknowledged in standard Christian scholarship.

Q: Who decided which books belong in the Bible?
A: No single meeting decided it. Books circulated and were debated for generations; the earliest surviving exact list of today's twenty-seven New Testament books comes from Athanasius in the later fourth century, and Christian communions still differ over the Old Testament canon.

Q: Is textual criticism an attack on Christianity?
A: No. It is a discipline built largely by Christian scholars seeking the earliest recoverable wording of the Bible. The manuscript footnotes in modern Christian Bibles are the fruit of that work.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The following works are offered as further reading; listing them does not imply agreement with every conclusion.

Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman — The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration. The standard scholarly introduction to New Testament textual criticism.

Bruce M. Metzger — The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance. A detailed history of how the twenty-seven-book New Testament canon took shape.

F. F. Bruce — The Canon of Scripture. An evangelical Christian scholar's account of canon formation for both Testaments.

Bart D. Ehrman — Misquoting Jesus: The Story Behind Who Changed the Bible and Why. A popular-level introduction to manuscripts and variants; its conclusions are debated among scholars.

Muhammad Mustafa al-Azami — The History of the Qur'anic Text from Revelation to Compilation: A Comparative Study with the Old and New Testaments. A Muslim scholar's comparative study of Quranic and biblical transmission.

A note on sources: Quran quotations were fetched from api.alquran.cloud (Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation) and Bible quotations from bible-api.com (World English Bible), reproduced verbatim. Historical statements are kept to widely established findings, phrased in general terms rather than precise dates.

title: What Is Tawhid?
subtitle: The Oneness of God: Islam's Foundational Doctrine and the Message of Every Prophet
summary: Tawhid is the Islamic doctrine of the oneness of God: He alone is Lord, He alone deserves worship, and nothing is like Him. Muslims believe it was the message of every prophet, from Noah and Abraham to Moses and Jesus. This article defines Tawhid and its opposite, shirk, in plain language for beginners. It then quotes the Quran and the Bible side by side, including the Shema of Moses and the words of Jesus in the Gospel of Mark.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
Tawhid (pronounced taw-HEED) is the Arabic word for the oneness of God, and it is the single most important teaching in Islam. It means that there is only one God, that He alone has the right to be worshipped, that He alone is the Lord and Sustainer of everything, and that nothing in creation is like Him.

Muslims believe Tawhid was not invented in the seventh century. They believe it was the one message carried by every prophet God ever sent, from Noah and Abraham to Moses, Jesus, and finally Muhammad, peace be upon them all.

This article explains what Tawhid means in plain language, introduces its opposite, called shirk, and then lets the texts speak for themselves: first the Quran, and then the Bible, where the same theme of God's exclusive oneness appears in the words of Moses, Isaiah, and Jesus himself.

sections.title: Introduction: The Center of Islam
sections.body:
Every religion has a center of gravity. In Islam, that center is not a ritual, a place, or even a prophet. It is a statement about God: la ilaha illa Allah, "there is no deity worthy of worship except God." The doctrine behind that statement is called Tawhid, from an Arabic root meaning "to make one" or "to affirm as one."

Muslim scholars have traditionally unpacked Tawhid into three connected aspects, and learning them makes everything else in Islam easier to understand. The first is the oneness of God's lordship (in Arabic, tawhid al-rububiyyah): God alone creates, sustains, gives life, and governs the universe, with no helper, rival, or committee. The second is the oneness of worship (tawhid al-uluhiyyah): because God alone is Lord, He alone deserves prayer, devotion, sacrifice, and ultimate love. Worship, in other words, is God's exclusive right. The third is the oneness of His names and attributes (tawhid al-asma wa-l-sifat): God is described by the most beautiful names, such as the Most Merciful and the All-Knowing, and His perfection is His alone; nothing in creation resembles Him.

These three aspects are teaching categories, not three separate doctrines. In the Quran they are woven together into a single, seamless picture of one God who made you, who sustains you, and who asks for your heart undivided.

sections.title: The Question: What Does "One God" Really Mean?
sections.body:
The question this article answers is simple to ask and profound to think through: what exactly does Islam mean when it says God is one, and was that oneness the original message of all the prophets, including Moses and Jesus?

"One" here is not merely a number, as if the only issue were counting. Tawhid means God is one in an exclusive and absolute sense: no partners who share His power, no intermediaries who receive a portion of worship, no offspring who inherit His nature, and no image or likeness that captures Him. It is oneness of being, oneness of authority, and oneness of the right to be worshipped, all at once.

Tawhid also has an opposite, and the Quran treats it with the utmost seriousness. It is called shirk, which means associating partners with God: directing any act of worship to something other than Him, believing that anything shares His lordship, or giving His unique attributes to a created being. Shirk can be as obvious as bowing to a statue or as subtle as making wealth, power, or one's own desires the true object of devotion. In Islam it is the gravest of all sins, because it gives away the one thing that belongs to God alone.

sections.title: One Message, Many Prophets
sections.body:
The Quran does not present Islam as a new religion founded in seventh-century Arabia. It presents Islam as the restoration of the original faith of humanity: surrender to the one God. In the Quran's telling, history is a long chain of prophets, each sent to his own people, each carrying the same core message of Tawhid, and each followed, in time, by communities that drifted from it.

The Hebrew Bible preserves that same core message in some of its most famous lines. The declaration known as the Shema, from the Book of Deuteronomy, is the closest thing Judaism has to a creed; observant Jews have recited it in daily prayer for many centuries, and it declares in a single breath that God is one. The Ten Commandments open not with a rule about honesty or family, but with God's exclusive claim to worship. The prophet Isaiah repeats the theme with striking force: there is no god besides the one God.

The Gospels then record something remarkable for this discussion. When Jesus was asked which commandment is the greatest of all, he did not announce a new doctrine of God. He recited the Shema of Moses. Centuries after Jesus, church councils formulated the doctrine of the Trinity, the teaching that the one God exists as three persons; Christians regard this as the correct interpretation of their scriptures. Islam, arriving after those debates, called people back to what it presents as the older, simpler creed: the unqualified oneness proclaimed by every prophet. The sections below quote the texts on which that claim rests.

sections.title: Tawhid in the Quran
sections.body:
The Quran's most concentrated statement of Tawhid is its 112th chapter, Surah al-Ikhlas, "Purity of Faith." It is only four verses long, and Muslim tradition holds that it summarizes the Quran's entire teaching about who God is. Its first verse reads (the Arabic below opens with the basmala, "In the name of God, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful," the phrase with which the chapter begins):

بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ

"Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One," (Quran 112:1)

ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ

"Allah, the Eternal Refuge." (Quran 112:2)

The word translated "Eternal Refuge" is al-Samad: the One on whom all creation depends, while He depends on nothing and no one. Then come two verses that draw the boundary lines of Tawhid with complete precision:

لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ

"He neither begets nor is born," (Quran 112:3)

وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌۢ

"Nor is there to Him any equivalent."" (Quran 112:4)

God has no parents and no offspring, no origin and no heirs, and nothing anywhere is comparable to Him. In four short verses, the chapter rules out idolatry, polytheism, and any doctrine that gives God a son or an equal.

Is this oneness unique to the Quran's own message? The Quran says no. It insists that Tawhid was the message of every messenger God ever sent:

وَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا مِن قَبْلِكَ مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا نُوحِىٓ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُۥ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعْبُدُونِ

"And We sent not before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that, "There is no deity except Me, so worship Me."" (Quran 21:25)

وَلَقَدْ بَعَثْنَا فِى كُلِّ أُمَّةٍۢ رَّسُولًا أَنِ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَٱجْتَنِبُوا۟ ٱلطَّٰغُوتَ ۖ فَمِنْهُم مَّنْ هَدَى ٱللَّهُ وَمِنْهُم مَّنْ حَقَّتْ عَلَيْهِ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةُ ۚ فَسِيرُوا۟ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَٱنظُرُوا۟ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلْمُكَذِّبِينَ

"And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid Taghut." And among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was [deservedly] decreed. So proceed through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers." (Quran 16:36)

The word Taghut in this verse means false objects of worship: anything served or deified in place of God. According to these verses, no nation on earth was left without a messenger, and every messenger preached the same two-part call that defines Tawhid: worship God, and renounce whatever is worshipped besides Him.

The Quran is equally careful about how we may describe God. He is utterly unlike His creation, yet He is not an abstraction; He hears and sees:

فَاطِرُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۚ جَعَلَ لَكُم مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَٰجًۭا وَمِنَ ٱلْأَنْعَٰمِ أَزْوَٰجًۭا ۖ يَذْرَؤُكُمْ فِيهِ ۚ لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِۦ شَىْءٌۭ ۖ وَهُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْبَصِيرُ

"[He is] Creator of the heavens and the earth. He has made for you from yourselves, mates, and among the cattle, mates; He multiplies you thereby. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing." (Quran 42:11)

That single verse contains the balance Muslim theology strives to keep: nothing is like God, and yet He is genuinely knowable through the names and attributes He reveals about Himself. The Quran calls these the most beautiful names:

ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۖ لَهُ ٱلْأَسْمَآءُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ

"Allah - there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names." (Quran 20:8)

One passage near the end of Surah al-Hashr gathers many of these names into a crescendo that Muslims often recite:

هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِى لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۖ عَٰلِمُ ٱلْغَيْبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ ۖ هُوَ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

"He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful." (Quran 59:22)

هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِى لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱلْقُدُّوسُ ٱلسَّلَٰمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُ ٱلْمُهَيْمِنُ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْجَبَّارُ ٱلْمُتَكَبِّرُ ۚ سُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ

"He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior. Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him." (Quran 59:23)

هُوَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْخَٰلِقُ ٱلْبَارِئُ ٱلْمُصَوِّرُ ۖ لَهُ ٱلْأَسْمَآءُ ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ ۚ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ وَهُوَ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ

"He is Allah, the Creator, the Inventor, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth is exalting Him. And He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise." (Quran 59:24)

Notice what these verses accomplish together. They keep God transcendent, exalted above whatever is associated with Him, and at the same time intimately describable: merciful, sovereign, pure, creating, fashioning, wise. Tawhid is not the worship of a distant force; it is a personal relationship with the one Lord who has told us who He is.

Finally, the Quran states the seriousness of Tawhid's opposite in the plainest possible terms:

إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَغْفِرُ أَن يُشْرَكَ بِهِۦ وَيَغْفِرُ مَا دُونَ ذَٰلِكَ لِمَن يَشَآءُ ۚ وَمَن يُشْرِكْ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدِ ٱفْتَرَىٰٓ إِثْمًا عَظِيمًا

"Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And he who associates others with Allah has certainly fabricated a tremendous sin." (Quran 4:48)

Shirk, the association of partners with God, is the one sin the Quran singles out this way, because it violates the very purpose for which, in Islam, human beings exist. The door of repentance remains open in this life to anyone who turns back to God; the warning concerns those who die still insisting on it.

sections.title: The Oneness of God in the Bible
sections.body:
A reader who opens the Bible looking for the theme of God's oneness does not have to search long. The Torah, the Prophets, and the Gospels each contain declarations that Muslims immediately recognize as the language of Tawhid. All quotations below are from the World English Bible translation.

The most famous is the Shema, the verse at the heart of Jewish faith and prayer: "Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one." (Deuteronomy 6:4). One God, stated without qualification or elaboration. This is the creed Moses delivered to Israel.

The Ten Commandments begin the same way, with God's exclusive claim on worship: "“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. “You shall have no other gods before me." (Exodus 20:2-3). Before any command about human conduct comes the command that defines all the others: no other gods. Worship belongs to God alone, which is precisely the second aspect of Tawhid described earlier.

The prophet Isaiah presses the point to its logical end, ruling out not just the worship of other gods but their very existence: "I am Yahweh, and there is no one else. Besides me, there is no God. I will strengthen you, though you have not known me;" (Isaiah 45:5).

Then comes the passage that matters most for a conversation between Muslims and Christians. In the Gospel of Mark, a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is the greatest of all. Mark records: "Jesus answered, “The greatest is, ‘Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one:" (Mark 12:29). The verse continues into the command to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength. Asked to name the very core of faith, Jesus answered with the Shema of Moses: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.

Christians, of course, hold all of these verses sacred and read them in harmony with the doctrine of the Trinity, which they understand as monotheism: one God in three persons, not three gods. That reading deserves to be stated fairly, and it is examined on its own terms elsewhere in this library. The observation made here is more modest: the verses themselves, as they stand, proclaim God's oneness in simple, exclusive, unqualified terms, and that is exactly what Islam means by Tawhid.

sections.title: Side by Side: Tawhid and the Trinity
sections.body:
It helps to state each position honestly and side by side.

Islam holds that God is one in an absolute and undifferentiated sense: one divine being, with no distinction of persons within Him, no incarnation in human flesh, and no partner, offspring, or equal. Worship of anyone or anything besides Him, including any prophet or saint, is shirk. On this view, Jesus was a mighty messenger of God who taught the same creed as Moses, and devotion belongs to the God Jesus worshipped.

Mainstream Christianity holds that God is one being in three co-equal, co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Christians insist, and have always insisted, that this is monotheism, not the worship of three gods; the Trinity is presented as a deeper description of the one God's inner life, with the Son becoming incarnate in Jesus.

The texts quoted in this article say: "Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one"; "You shall have no other gods before me"; "I am Yahweh, and there is no one else"; and, from the lips of Jesus, "the Lord our God, the Lord is one." On the Quran's side: "He is Allah, [who is] One"; "He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent"; "There is no deity except Me, so worship Me."

The Islamic argument is straightforward. Read on their own, these texts express oneness that needs no further doctrinal machinery: no persons to distinguish, no natures to unite, no councils required to settle the definition. A Muslim can affirm every word of the Shema, the first commandment, Isaiah's declaration, and Jesus's answer to the scribe, exactly as written. Tawhid, Muslims argue, is not a rival to the message of the Bible's prophets; it is that message, preserved in its original simplicity.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A few misunderstandings come up so often that they deserve direct answers.

First: "Allah is a different god from the God of the Bible." Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, related to the Hebrew Elohim and the Aramaic Alaha. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use the word Allah for God in their own prayers and Bibles. When Muslims say Allah, they mean the God of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

Second: "A God so transcendent must be cold and distant." The same Quran that says nothing is like God also names Him the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful, the Hearing, the Seeing. Tawhid removes intermediaries precisely so that every person can turn to God directly, with no priesthood or broker in between.

Third: "Muslims accuse Christians of worshipping three gods." That is not the careful Islamic position, and this library does not argue that way. Christian doctrine explicitly affirms one God, and honesty requires saying so. The Islamic critique is different: that the Trinity, however sincerely intended as monotheism, goes beyond the simple oneness that the quoted texts proclaim, and that the safer path is to stay with what Moses and Jesus actually said.

Fourth: "Shirk just means bowing to idols." Idolatry is its clearest form, but shirk includes any act of worship directed to other than God: praying to saints, seeking from the dead what only God can give, or making money, status, or desire one's functional god.

Fifth: "Muslims worship the Kaaba in Mecca." Muslims pray toward the Kaaba as a single direction that unites worshippers worldwide, the way the Bible describes prophets praying toward Jerusalem. No Muslim worships the building; worship is for God alone.

sections.title: Conclusion: One God, One Message
sections.body:
Tawhid is Islam's answer to the oldest and most important question a human being can ask: who deserves my worship? The answer is the One who made you, sustains you every second, and will one day call you back: God alone, without partner, without son, without equal.

What gives that answer its force is its consistency. The Quran proclaims it: there is no deity except Him. The Torah proclaims it: the Lord is one; you shall have no other gods. The prophets proclaim it: besides Me there is no God. And when Jesus himself was asked to name the greatest commandment, he reached for the same creed. Islam asks the reader to take that pattern seriously. Either the prophets shared one message, or they did not; the texts, quoted throughout this article, speak with one voice.

For the Muslim, Tawhid is not an abstract doctrine but a way of standing in the world: one God to please rather than a thousand masters to appease, one door to knock on, one judge whose verdict matters. It is, Muslims believe, the faith of Abraham in its purest form, open to anyone willing to say with conviction that there is no deity worthy of worship except God. The invitation of this entire library begins here, because in Islam everything else follows from this.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: What does the word Tawhid literally mean?
A: Tawhid comes from an Arabic root meaning "to make one" or "to affirm as one." As a doctrine, it means affirming that God is one in His lordship, one in His exclusive right to worship, and unique in His names and attributes.

Q: Is Allah the same God that Jews and Christians worship?
A: Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians use it themselves. Muslims understand Allah to be the God of Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. The three faiths describe God differently in doctrine, but the reference is to the Creator worshipped by the biblical prophets.

Q: What is shirk, and why is it so serious in Islam?
A: Shirk means associating partners with God: giving worship, ultimate devotion, or God's unique attributes to anything created. The Quran calls it the one sin God does not forgive for a person who dies upon it without repenting, because it gives away the sole right for which humans were created. Sincere repentance in this life wipes it away.

Q: Did Jesus teach the oneness of God?
A: According to the Gospel of Mark, when Jesus was asked which commandment is the greatest, he recited the Shema: "Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one." Muslims see in this the same creed of Tawhid taught by Moses and every prophet, while Christians read it in harmony with later Trinitarian doctrine.

Q: Do Muslims believe Christians worship three gods?
A: No. Christian doctrine explicitly teaches one God in three persons, and fairness requires representing it that way. The Islamic critique is not that Christians intend polytheism, but that the Trinity adds distinctions to God's oneness that the plain declarations of the Torah, the Prophets, and Jesus do not contain.

Q: What are the three categories of Tawhid?
A: Scholars traditionally teach Tawhid in three aspects: oneness of lordship (God alone creates and sustains), oneness of worship (God alone deserves devotion), and oneness of names and attributes (God's perfection is unique and incomparable). They are three angles on a single truth, not three separate doctrines.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The following well-known works are offered as further reading for readers who want to go deeper. They are listed for orientation, not as sources for specific claims made in this article.

Abu Ameenah Bilal Philips — The Fundamentals of Tawheed: a widely read English-language introduction to the categories of Tawhid and the forms of shirk.

Imam Abu Ja'far al-Tahawi — The Creed of Imam al-Tahawi (al-Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah): a classical summary of Muslim beliefs about God, accepted across the major Sunni schools.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab — Kitab al-Tawhid: a classical thematic collection on the oneness of worship and warnings against shirk.

Hamza Andreas Tzortzis — The Divine Reality: a contemporary case for God's existence and oneness addressed to modern readers, including atheists and agnostics.

title: What Is the Trinity?
subtitle: The doctrine as Christian theology defines it, how it was formalized at Nicaea and Constantinople, and the Quran's response
summary: The Trinity is mainstream Christianity's central doctrine: one God existing eternally as three co-equal, co-eternal persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — sharing one essence. This article presents the doctrine as Christian theology itself defines it and traces its formal definition at the Councils of Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE). It then reads the Bible passages Christians cite alongside passages that complicate the doctrine, and presents the Quran's response of absolute divine oneness (tawhid). Written for beginners, with every verse quoted from published translations.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body:
Most Christian churches teach that God is a Trinity: one God who exists eternally as three distinct, co-equal, co-eternal persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit — sharing one divine essence. This article explains that doctrine exactly as mainstream Christian theology states it, and traces how it was formally defined at the Councils of Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE).

It then reads the Bible passages Christians cite alongside passages that complicate the doctrine, and presents the Quran's response: God is absolutely one, without persons, partners, or a son. No prior knowledge of either faith is assumed.

sections.title: Introduction: Defining the Doctrine Fairly
sections.body:
The Trinity is the central doctrine of mainstream Christianity, shared by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and most Protestant churches. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy summarizes it like this: “A Trinity doctrine is commonly expressed as the statement that the one God exists as or in three equally divine ‘Persons’, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

Three technical terms will help. A “person” (Greek: hypostasis) here does not mean a separate god, but a real, distinct “who” within the one God. “Essence” or “substance” (Greek: ousia) means what God is — the one divine being itself. And homoousios, meaning “of the same essence,” is the word the Council of Nicaea used to declare that the Son is fully God in exactly the same sense that the Father is God: co-equal and co-eternal, not a lesser or later being.

Just as important is what the doctrine does not claim. It does not teach three gods — that idea, called tritheism, has always been condemned as heresy. Nor does it teach that one divine person merely plays three roles — that idea, called modalism, was rejected too. The doctrine holds, as a mystery beyond full human comprehension, that there is exactly one God, and that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each fully that one God while remaining really distinct. Any fair comparison with Islam must start from that definition, not from a caricature.

sections.title: The Main Question
sections.body:
The question of this article is simple to state: what exactly does the doctrine of the Trinity claim, where did the formal doctrine come from, and how does it fare when tested against the scriptures that Christians and Muslims each hold up?

For a Christian reader, the live question is whether the Bible itself teaches one God in three co-equal persons, or whether that formula emerged later, in vocabulary the biblical authors never used. For a Muslim reader, it is how to describe Christian belief accurately while presenting the Quran's uncompromising monotheism. For a seeker between the two, it is the oldest question there is: who, exactly, is God?

The method follows the rest of this library: present each side from its own sources, quote scripture exactly as published translations render it, then compare.

sections.title: How the Doctrine Was Defined: Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381)
sections.body:
The word “Trinity” does not appear anywhere in the Bible. The New Testament speaks constantly of God the Father, of Jesus the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but nowhere states a formula of “one God in three co-equal persons.” Christian scholarship itself acknowledges that the formal doctrine took shape gradually across the first four centuries.

The turning point was a fourth-century dispute. Arius, a church elder in Alexandria, taught that the Son was God's first and most exalted creature — supremely honored, but not eternal and not equal to the Father. The dispute spread so widely that the Roman emperor Constantine convened a council of bishops at Nicaea in the year 325 CE. According to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's historical survey, the council met in mid-325 with perhaps 220 bishops; it condemned Arius's teaching and issued a creed declaring the Son homoousios — one in essence — with the Father. Arius and a few supporters refused to sign and were exiled.

Nicaea did not end the argument. Debate over the creed's wording and the status of the Holy Spirit continued for decades. Around the Council of Constantinople in 381 CE, the trinitarian belief that ultimately prevailed, in the Stanford Encyclopedia's words, “began to gel into a recognizable form,” now backed by imperial authority; views that subordinated the Son were progressively suppressed. The expanded creed associated with this era — recited today as the Nicene Creed — confesses Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as together the one God.

Two readings of this history will matter later. Christian theologians describe the councils as clarifying what was implicit in scripture all along. Muslims read the same history as evidence that a philosophical doctrine, in Greek terms the prophets never used, gradually replaced the simple monotheism Jesus himself taught. The dates themselves — 325 and 381, roughly three centuries after Jesus — are not in dispute.

sections.title: The Quranic Perspective
sections.body:
The Quran addresses Christians directly, respectfully — as “People of the Scripture” — and with a clear correction. The fullest statement is Quran 4:171:

يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَكَلِمَتُهُۥٓ أَلْقَىٰهَآ إِلَىٰ مَرْيَمَ وَرُوحٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ فَـَٔامِنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۖ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ ثَلَٰثَةٌ ۚ ٱنتَهُوا۟ خَيْرًۭا لَّكُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱللَّهُ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۖ سُبْحَٰنَهُۥٓ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ۘ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ وَكِيلًۭا

“O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist - it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.” (Quran 4:171, Saheeh International)

Notice what the verse affirms before what it denies. Jesus is called the Messiah, a messenger of God, God's word directed to Mary, and a soul created at His command — titles of immense honor. Then comes the boundary: “do not say, ‘Three.’” The Quran's objection is not to Jesus but to elevating him, or anyone, into the Godhead.

A second verse addresses the three-fold confession directly. Quran 5:73:

لَّقَدْ كَفَرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ثَالِثُ ثَلَٰثَةٍۢ ۘ وَمَا مِنْ إِلَٰهٍ إِلَّآ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۚ وَإِن لَّمْ يَنتَهُوا۟ عَمَّا يَقُولُونَ لَيَمَسَّنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ

“They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Allah is the third of three." And there is no god except one God. And if they do not desist from what they are saying, there will surely afflict the disbelievers among them a painful punishment.” (Quran 5:73, Saheeh International)

The Quran does not engage the church's technical vocabulary of essence and persons; it addresses the confession as ordinary believers voice it — God spoken of as one of three — and rules out every formula in which the one God's divinity is shared: “there is no god except one God.”

A third passage stages a scene from the Day of Judgment. Quran 5:116:

وَإِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ءَأَنتَ قُلْتَ لِلنَّاسِ ٱتَّخِذُونِى وَأُمِّىَ إِلَٰهَيْنِ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ قَالَ سُبْحَٰنَكَ مَا يَكُونُ لِىٓ أَنْ أَقُولَ مَا لَيْسَ لِى بِحَقٍّ ۚ إِن كُنتُ قُلْتُهُۥ فَقَدْ عَلِمْتَهُۥ ۚ تَعْلَمُ مَا فِى نَفْسِى وَلَآ أَعْلَمُ مَا فِى نَفْسِكَ ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ عَلَّٰمُ ٱلْغُيُوبِ

“And [beware the Day] when Allah will say, "O Jesus, Son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?'" He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, it is You who is Knower of the unseen.” (Quran 5:116, Saheeh International)

Here Jesus himself disowns every claim to be worshiped: he does not even claim to know what is in God's self. The verse asks a question about worship as practiced — including veneration of his mother Mary — rather than quoting a church creed; the misconceptions section returns to this point.

Finally, Surah Al-Ikhlas (chapter 112), the Quran's most concentrated statement of who God is, answers the trinitarian formula line by line:

بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ

“Say, "He is Allah, [who is] One,” (Quran 112:1, Saheeh International)

ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.” (Quran 112:2, Saheeh International)

لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ

“He neither begets nor is born,” (Quran 112:3, Saheeh International)

وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌۢ

“Nor is there to Him any equivalent."” (Quran 112:4, Saheeh International)

“He neither begets nor is born” meets the creed's language of an eternally begotten Son head-on, and “nor is there to Him any equivalent” excludes any co-equal person. In four short verses the Quran states tawhid: God's absolute, indivisible oneness.

sections.title: The Biblical Texts: For and Against
sections.body:
Fairness requires hearing the passages Christians actually cite, in their own scripture. The most famous triadic text is the baptismal command at the end of Matthew's Gospel: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” (Matthew 28:19, World English Bible). Christians point out that one “name” — singular — is shared by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Paul closes a letter with a similar three-fold blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen.” (2 Corinthians 13:14, World English Bible). Texts like these show that placing the three side by side is genuinely early, not a later invention.

The Gospel of John supplies the strongest material. Its opening line runs: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” (John 1:1, World English Bible), and a few verses later: “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14, World English Bible) — the foundation of the doctrine of the incarnation, that the eternal Word became the man Jesus. And in a dispute with his opponents Jesus says: “I and the Father are one.” (John 10:30, World English Bible).

Yet the same scriptures contain passages that complicate the doctrine. In the same Gospel of John, Jesus tells his disciples: “You heard how I told you, ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I.” (John 14:28, World English Bible). And in Mark, speaking of the final hour, he says: “But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” (Mark 13:32, World English Bible). A Son who calls the Father greater, and who does not know what the Father knows, sits uneasily beside co-equality.

Mainstream Christian theology answers by distinguishing Jesus's two natures: as God he is equal and all-knowing; as man, lesser and limited. Interpreters likewise debate whether the oneness of John 10:30 is a oneness of essence or of will and purpose. These are serious answers, offered in good faith. Whether they are the most natural reading of the texts is the question the next section takes up.

sections.title: Weighing the Two Positions
sections.body:
Begin with common ground. Christianity and Islam both confess one God — the disagreement is not monotheism versus polytheism, and it is unfair to call the Trinity belief in three gods. The question is whether the one God's inner life contains three co-equal persons, or whether God is one in an absolute, undifferentiated sense — tawhid.

Now test each claim against the texts quoted above. The triadic passages — Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14 — genuinely name the three together, but naming three together is not the doctrine; neither verse states that the three are one being, co-equal and co-eternal. Those further claims required the councils' vocabulary — ousia, hypostasis, homoousios — which appears nowhere in the Bible. John's Gospel brings the reader closest: “the Word was God.” Yet the same Gospel has Jesus say “the Father is greater than I,” and Mark has the Son not knowing the day or the hour. The two-natures explanation can absorb these verses, but only by adding another layer of post-biblical doctrine.

The Quranic position requires no such machinery. God is one; Jesus is His honored messenger, word, and servant. On that reading, “the Father is greater than I” and “only the Father” knows the hour mean exactly what they say. Every verse quoted in this article — from either scripture — is consistent with the sentence “Indeed, Allah is but one God” (Quran 4:171). The trinitarian must explain the subordination texts; the affirmer of God's oneness need only explain honorific language about a uniquely honored prophet — language the Quran itself uses of Jesus.

That asymmetry — which side needs the more elaborate auxiliary doctrine — is, in the Islamic argument, decisive.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
Misconception one: “Christians worship three gods.” They do not, and Muslims who say so misdescribe their neighbors. Every mainstream church condemns tritheism as heresy. The Islamic critique is that the formula “one God in three persons” compromises God's oneness in a way no prophet taught, however sincerely its holders affirm monotheism.

Misconception two: “The Quran misunderstands the Trinity as Father, Jesus, and Mary” — an objection usually aimed at Quran 5:116. Read the verse again: it is a question posed to Jesus on the Day of Judgment about worship offered to him and his mother, not a definition of the church's creed. The Quran's concern is worship as practiced — devotion directed to anyone besides God — and devotion to Mary was, and in some traditions remains, a live feature of Christian piety. Where the Quran addresses the three-fold confession, in 4:171 and 5:73, it says “do not say, ‘Three’” and “third of three,” without naming Mary at all.

Misconception three: “The Trinity is stated plainly in the Bible.” The word never appears, and the developed formula was defined at Nicaea and Constantinople, as the historical section showed. One verse that once seemed to state the doctrine outright — the “three heavenly witnesses” wording found at 1 John 5:7 in some older translations — is regarded by modern textual scholars across confessional lines as a later addition, and modern Bibles omit it or flag it in a footnote.

Misconception four: “Muslims reject the Trinity because they dishonor Jesus.” The opposite is true: no Muslim's faith is valid without belief in Jesus as the Messiah, God's messenger, born of a virgin. The Quran denies him nothing except divinity — and reports him denying that himself.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
The Islamic conclusion can be stated gently. The Quran does not ask Christians to abandon Jesus; it asks them to return to him — to the prayerful, dependent, obedient servant of God the Gospels themselves portray, who calls the Father greater, confesses that only God knows the hour, and directs all worship to the One who sent him.

Islam's claim is that the simple creed — “Say, ‘He is Allah, [who is] One’” (Quran 112:1) — is the original message of every prophet, Jesus included. On the Islamic reading, the Trinity is a sincere but mistaken development, assembled from real scriptural honor for Jesus and Greek philosophical categories, formalized by councils in 325 and 381 — not in the preaching of Jesus.

The invitation of Quran 4:171 is therefore precise: “do not commit excess in your religion.” Honor the Messiah as much as truth allows — messenger, word from God, spirit from Him — and stop exactly at the line he himself never crossed: “Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son.” For the seeker weighing both faiths, the question to carry away is this: which description of God do the words of Jesus, taken at face value, actually fit?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Christians believe in three gods?
A: No. Mainstream Christianity condemns tritheism as heresy. The doctrine of the Trinity claims one God in three co-equal persons — and the Islamic critique addresses that actual claim, not a caricature.

Q: Does the word “Trinity” appear in the Bible?
A: No. The New Testament names the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together in verses like Matthew 28:19, but the word “Trinity” and the formula “one essence, three persons” come from later centuries of theology.

Q: What do the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople have to do with it?
A: Nicaea (325 CE) declared the Son homoousios — one in essence — with the Father, against Arius, who taught the Son was a created being. Around Constantinople (381 CE) the full trinitarian position, including the Holy Spirit, became mainstream Christianity's established doctrine.

Q: Does the Quran say the Trinity is Father, Jesus, and Mary?
A: No. Quran 5:116 records a Judgment-Day question to Jesus about people worshiping him and his mother; it is about misdirected worship, not a definition of the creed. Where the Quran addresses the three-fold confession (4:171, 5:73) it simply says: do not say “Three.”

Q: If Muslims honor Jesus, why reject the Trinity?
