sections.title: A Standard Christians Recognize Too
sections.body:
This article needs no Bible quotations, but the instinct to verify is one Christians recognize from their own scripture. Paul instructs the church in Thessalonica:

'Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.' (1 Thessalonians 5:21, World English Bible)

We quote it as an invitation: test this library by its own standard. Every Bible verse here is drawn verbatim from the World English Bible, a modern public-domain translation — never paraphrased from memory, never trimmed to change its sense, never marked Verified until checked against that named edition. If a Christian reader ever finds their scripture misquoted here, the error-report link exists precisely for them.

sections.title: One Standard for Both Religions
sections.body:
A trust system is only trustworthy if it is symmetrical, so the labels apply identically to Islamic and Christian material. A Quran verse and a Bible verse pass through the same pipeline; a claim about early church history meets the same evidentiary bar as one about early Islamic history; an untraceable quotation is removed whether it comes from a Christian scholar or a Muslim one.

The same symmetry governs descriptions: before any comparison is drawn, each religion's position is presented the way its own mainstream scholarship states it. An article that summarized the Trinity in words no informed Christian would accept could not survive review, any more than one misstating Tawhid (the Islamic doctrine of God's absolute oneness).

This is not neutrality about truth — this library argues openly for Islam. But a true position gains nothing from weakened opposition: Islam's case is strongest when the Christian case is presented at full strength and every quotation on both sides is exact.

sections.title: What the Labels Do Not Mean
sections.body:
'Draft means the article is wrong.' No — it means checking has not finished, so the label does not yet ask for your trust.

'Verified means the library endorses the source.' No — Verified is a claim about accurate quotation, not agreement. A Bible verse marked Verified matches the World English Bible exactly; it does not mean we accept every doctrine built on it.

'Published means final.' No — a confirmed error can send a published article back to Under Review. The labels are a live status, not an unbreakable seal.

'The labels are just branding.' That claim is testable: pick any quotation in a published article and check it against the named source; if the words are not there, the error report works.

sections.title: Verification as an Act of Faith
sections.body:
For Muslims, careful sourcing is not merely good editorial practice; it is obedience. The Quran commands believers to 'investigate' information before acting on it (Quran 49:6) and warns that a person 'will be questioned' about what they repeat (Quran 17:36). A library built to present Islam's case is therefore bound, by Islam itself, to the strictest accuracy — especially when quoting the scriptures of others.

There is a quiet argument inside the system too: a position that fears checking hides its sources, while a position confident of the truth invites scrutiny.

So read published articles knowing every citation has been verified, treat Draft and Source Pending with the caution they ask for, and if you find an error, report it. Correcting us is not an attack; it is a service to the truth we are all accountable for.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: What is the difference between Draft and Under Review?
A: Draft means checking has not finished and the article is not shown to general readers; Under Review means checking is actively underway.

Q: What does Verified mean for a scripture quotation?
A: It was compared word-for-word against a named edition — a claim about accurate quotation, not endorsement of any interpretation.

Q: Can a Published article lose its status?
A: Yes. A confirmed error rolls it back to Under Review until fixed.

Q: How do I report an error?
A: Use the error-report link on any published article; describe the problem and, if you can, point to the correct source.

Q: Why does one unverified citation hold up a whole article?
A: Because a single false quotation can mislead a seeker, and the Quran commands verification before information is acted on (Quran 49:6).

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body: The verification instinct behind these labels has deep roots in both traditions. These works introduce how Muslim scholars authenticated reports about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and how Christian scholars study the Bible's transmission. None is quoted in this article; they are starting points for the larger story.

title: Did Jesus Claim to Be God?
subtitle: What the Gospels record, what the Quran declares, and how to weigh Jesus’s own words
summary: Whether Jesus himself ever claimed to be God is the pivotal question between Islam and Christianity. This article presents the Gospel passages Christians cite for his divinity, with their mainstream Christian interpretation, alongside the many sayings in which Jesus distinguishes himself from God. It notes honestly that no Gospel records Jesus saying “I am God” or “worship me,” and that the most exalted language appears in the latest Gospel. The Quran’s verdict is then given in Jesus’s own voice: worship God, “my Lord and your Lord.”

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body: Did Jesus ever say, in his own words, “I am God — worship me”? This is perhaps the single most important question separating Islam and Christianity, because so much else — the Trinity, the meaning of the crucifixion, the nature of salvation — depends on the answer. This article examines the Gospel passages Christians cite as claims to divinity, the passages in which Jesus plainly distinguishes himself from God, and the Quran’s account of what Jesus actually taught. The Islamic position is that Jesus, peace be upon him, was the Messiah and a mighty messenger who called people to worship the one God alone — and that his own recorded words, read as a whole, support exactly that.

sections.title: Two Faiths, One Question
sections.body:
Muslims and Christians agree on a remarkable amount about Jesus of Nazareth. Both honour him as the Messiah, born miraculously of the Virgin Mary, a worker of wonders by God’s permission, and a teacher of profound righteousness. The Quran names Jesus in dozens of verses and devotes an entire chapter to his mother, Maryam (Mary). No one can be a Muslim without loving and believing in Jesus.

The disagreement begins at one precise point: is Jesus God? Christianity, as defined by its historic creeds, answers yes — Jesus is God the Son, the second person of the Trinity, fully divine and fully human. Islam answers no — Jesus is a beloved prophet and messenger, honoured above almost all of humanity, but a servant of God like every other created being.

Because the stakes could not be higher, the question deserves a careful answer from the sources themselves — beginning with the words of Jesus, as each tradition records them.

sections.title: What Exactly Is Being Asked?
sections.body:
It is important to be precise about what is being asked. The question is not whether the New Testament contains exalted language about Jesus; it does. Nor is it whether later church councils declared him divine; they did. The question is narrower and more decisive: did Jesus himself, in his own recorded words, ever clearly claim to be God and instruct people to worship him?

Here a simple textual fact should be stated plainly, because careful readers on both sides acknowledge it: nowhere in the four Gospels does Jesus utter the sentence “I am God,” and nowhere does he command “worship me.” Mainstream Christian scholarship does not generally dispute this. Instead, it argues that Jesus claimed divinity indirectly — through titles he accepted, actions such as forgiving sins, and statements whose implications his hearers understood. Muslims respond that for a doctrine on which, in Christian teaching, eternal salvation depends, God would not leave humanity to rely on inference — and that the indirect statements read very differently beside everything else Jesus said.

Both readings are laid out below, each in its strongest form.

sections.title: How and When the Gospels Were Written
sections.body:
To weigh the Gospel evidence fairly, a few background facts accepted by mainstream historical scholarship are needed.

Jesus taught in Aramaic in first-century Palestine, but the four Gospels were written in Greek, decades after his ministry, by authors drawing on earlier oral and written tradition. Scholars broadly agree on their relative order: Mark is generally regarded as the earliest Gospel, commonly dated to around 70–75 CE; Matthew and Luke followed over roughly the next two decades; and John is usually dated to around 95 CE or slightly later, making it the latest of the four.

That order matters, because the Gospels do not all speak about Jesus in the same register. In Mark, the earliest account, Jesus prays to God, says that no one knows the Hour but the Father, and deflects even the compliment “good.” The most elevated divine-sounding sayings — “before Abraham came into existence, I AM,” “I and the Father are one,” “he who has seen me has seen the Father” — appear only in John, the latest Gospel. Critical scholars of the New Testament widely note this trajectory: the highest christology (the understanding of Christ’s status) appears in the latest source. Christian scholars respond that John preserves genuine early tradition, and some argue devotion to Jesus arose very early; that debate is ongoing, but where the strongest sayings sit in the timeline is not in dispute.

Finally, the formal doctrine that Jesus is fully God was defined at the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE, roughly three centuries after Jesus — amid serious disagreement among Christians themselves, since the priest Arius and his many followers held that the Son was a created being.

sections.title: The Quran: Jesus in His Own Words
sections.body:
The Quran does not treat the message of Jesus as a mystery to be reconstructed. It states that message directly, and it places it on Jesus’s own lips. Announcing his mission to the Children of Israel, Jesus says:

إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ فَٱعْبُدُوهُ ۗ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ

“Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. That is the straight path."” (Quran 3:51)

The same declaration is recorded in Surah Az-Zukhruf, where the Quran summarises both his credentials and his call:

وَلَمَّا جَآءَ عِيسَىٰ بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ قَالَ قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِٱلْحِكْمَةِ وَلِأُبَيِّنَ لَكُم بَعْضَ ٱلَّذِى تَخْتَلِفُونَ فِيهِ ۖ فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ

“And when Jesus brought clear proofs, he said, "I have come to you with wisdom and to make clear to you some of that over which you differ, so fear Allah and obey me.” (Quran 43:63)

إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ رَبِّى وَرَبُّكُمْ فَٱعْبُدُوهُ ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ

“Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path."” (Quran 43:64)

Notice what the Quranic Jesus asks for: obedience to himself as God’s messenger, and worship directed to God alone. The two are never confused. On that basis the Quran issues one of its most solemn warnings — grounded, again, in Jesus’s own words:

لَقَدْ كَفَرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ هُوَ ٱلْمَسِيحُ ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ ۖ وَقَالَ ٱلْمَسِيحُ يَٰبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبَّكُمْ ۖ إِنَّهُۥ مَن يُشْرِكْ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدْ حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ ٱلْجَنَّةَ وَمَأْوَىٰهُ ٱلنَّارُ ۖ وَمَا لِلظَّٰلِمِينَ مِنْ أَنصَارٍۢ

“They have certainly disbelieved who say, "Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary" while the Messiah has said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." Indeed, he who associates others with Allah - Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And there are not for the wrongdoers any helpers.” (Quran 5:72)

The Quran then looks forward to the Day of Judgment, when God will question Jesus before humanity about what was done in his name:

وَإِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ءَأَنتَ قُلْتَ لِلنَّاسِ ٱتَّخِذُونِى وَأُمِّىَ إِلَٰهَيْنِ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ قَالَ سُبْحَٰنَكَ مَا يَكُونُ لِىٓ أَنْ أَقُولَ مَا لَيْسَ لِى بِحَقٍّ ۚ إِن كُنتُ قُلْتُهُۥ فَقَدْ عَلِمْتَهُۥ ۚ تَعْلَمُ مَا فِى نَفْسِى وَلَآ أَعْلَمُ مَا فِى نَفْسِكَ ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ عَلَّٰمُ ٱلْغُيُوبِ

“And [beware the Day] when Allah will say, "O Jesus, Son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as deities besides Allah?'" He will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for me to say that to which I have no right. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, it is You who is Knower of the unseen.” (Quran 5:116)

And Jesus’s answer, in the Quran, is a complete summary of his ministry:

مَا قُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِلَّا مَآ أَمَرْتَنِى بِهِۦٓ أَنِ ٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ رَبِّى وَرَبَّكُمْ ۚ وَكُنتُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا مَّا دُمْتُ فِيهِمْ ۖ فَلَمَّا تَوَفَّيْتَنِى كُنتَ أَنتَ ٱلرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ وَأَنتَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ شَهِيدٌ

“I said not to them except what You commanded me - to worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Observer over them, and You are, over all things, Witness.” (Quran 5:117)

In the Quran’s telling, then, Jesus never claimed divinity, never sought worship, and will himself disown any such claim before God. His message was the message of every prophet: worship the one God, “my Lord and your Lord.”

sections.title: The Gospels: Both Sets of Sayings
sections.body:
Christians who affirm the divinity of Jesus point above all to the Gospel of John, and three passages carry most of the weight.

The first is John 8:58: “Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM.”” In mainstream Christian interpretation, “I AM” deliberately echoes God’s self-identification to Moses at the burning bush in the book of Exodus, so Jesus is claiming the divine name — and the crowd’s attempt to stone him shows they understood it that way.

The second is John 10:30–33: “I and the Father are one.” Therefore Jews took up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?” The Jews answered him, “We don’t stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy: because you, being a man, make yourself God.”” Here, Christians note, the audience itself accuses Jesus of making himself God — and he does not simply say, “you have misunderstood me.”

The third is John 14:9: “Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father?’” On the Christian reading, Jesus is the perfect visible revelation of the invisible Father.

These interpretations deserve to be stated fairly, and they have been. But alongside them stand other sayings of Jesus — spread across the Gospels, including John itself — that point in a different direction. In Mark 10:18, when a man addresses him as “good teacher,” Jesus replies: “Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.” In John 14:28 he tells his disciples: “You heard how I told you, ‘I go away, and I come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I said ‘I am going to my Father;’ for the Father is greater than I.” In Mark 13:32, speaking of the Last Day, he says: “But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” — a plain statement that the Son’s knowledge is limited. After the events of Easter morning, in John 20:17, he says: “Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers, and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’”” And in John 17:3, praying to the Father, he defines salvation itself: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.”

Christian theology harmonises these sayings through later doctrinal categories: the Father is “greater” in role but not in nature; the Son’s ignorance of the Hour belongs to his human nature. These harmonisations are coherent once the doctrine of the two natures is assumed. The Muslim observation is that the doctrine must be assumed first — the plain sense of the words describes a servant of God who prays, obeys, depends, and worships.

sections.title: Weighing the Totality of Jesus’s Words
sections.body:
Set the two portraits side by side and something striking emerges: the Jesus of the Quran and the Jesus of the earliest Gospel material sound remarkably alike.

In Mark, Jesus deflects the word “good” toward God, confesses that only the Father knows the Hour, and prays to God in his hardest moments. In the Quran, Jesus says, “Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.” The registers match. The explicit claims of divinity that Christians cite come overwhelmingly from John, written around six decades after Jesus’s ministry — and even John preserves “the Father is greater than I,” “the only true God,” and “my God and your God.”

That last phrase deserves a pause. In John 20:17 Jesus speaks of “my Father and your Father… my God and your God.” In Quran 3:51 and 43:64 he speaks of “my Lord and your Lord.” In these passages the two scriptures attribute to Jesus the very same self-understanding: he stands with humanity on the worshipping side of the line between Creator and creature.

The Islamic argument, then, is not built on ignoring the Bible. It is built on the totality of Jesus’s recorded words: a man who prayed to God, called God “my God,” disclaimed unlimited knowledge and goodness, and defined eternal life as knowing “the only true God” — and the one whom that God sent.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A few recurring misunderstandings deserve direct answers.

First: “Muslims deny Jesus.” They do not. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and one of the greatest of all messengers is an article of faith in Islam. What Muslims deny is that he is God — which, Muslims argue, is also what he himself denied.

Second: “‘I and the Father are one’ can only mean identity of essence.” Yet in the same Gospel, Jesus prays for his disciples “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me. The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one;” (John 17:21–22). Whatever oneness Jesus shares with the Father in John’s language, he asks the same oneness for his followers — which fits unity of purpose and will far more naturally than unity of divine essence.

Third: “the Quran misunderstands the Trinity, because in 5:116 it speaks of Jesus and Mary.” The verse does not claim to define the church’s creed. It is a question God puts to Jesus about what people actually did — taking him and his mother as objects of devotion “besides Allah.” The Quran addresses worship as practised, and the exaltation of Mary in popular devotion was and is a real phenomenon; the verse condemns directing worship to anyone other than God, however it is theologised.

Fourth: “Jesus is called the Son of God, so he must be divine.” In biblical idiom, “son of God” was an honorific applied to kings, to the righteous, and to Israel collectively; Jewish hearers did not take it as a claim to be the Creator. The Quran rejects the title precisely because, in later usage, it came to mean something no prophet taught.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
Islam’s verdict on this question is not an attack on Jesus; it is a defence of him. The Quran insists that Jesus said nothing more and nothing less than what God sent him to say: “I said not to them except what You commanded me - to worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord” (Quran 5:117).

On the Islamic reading, the evidence lines up. No Gospel records Jesus saying “I am God” or “worship me.” The earliest Gospel presents a praying, dependent servant of God. The loftiest language appears in the latest Gospel, and even there Jesus calls the Father “the only true God” and “my God.” The formal doctrine of his deity was settled by councils centuries later. The Quran cuts through that development and restores the original voice: “Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path.” (Quran 43:64)

For the sincere seeker, the invitation of Islam is simple and, Muslims would say, deeply loyal to Jesus: worship the God Jesus worshipped, pray to the God Jesus prayed to, and follow him as he asked to be followed — as the Messiah and messenger of the one God. That, in the Quran’s words, is the straight path.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe in Jesus?
A: Yes. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and one of God’s greatest messengers is required of every Muslim. The Quran affirms his virgin birth and his miracles by God’s permission.

Q: Does Jesus ever say “I am God” anywhere in the Bible?
A: No. The sentence appears nowhere in the four Gospels, and Jesus never commands anyone to worship him. Christian scholars argue his divinity is claimed indirectly; Muslims argue the indirect passages are outweighed by his plain statements of dependence on God.

Q: What about “before Abraham came into existence, I AM” (John 8:58)?
A: Christians read it as invoking the divine name from Exodus. Muslims note it is an ambiguous phrase found only in the latest Gospel, which also records Jesus calling the Father “the only true God” (John 17:3) and “my God” (John 20:17).

Q: Why does Jesus sound so exalted in the Gospel of John?
A: Mainstream critical scholarship dates John latest of the four Gospels, around 95 CE or after, and observes that the most elevated language about Jesus appears there rather than in the earlier accounts. Muslims see in this the gradual exaltation of a prophet by later generations.

Q: What did Jesus ask people to do, according to the Quran?
A: To worship God alone: “Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. That is the straight path.” (Quran 3:51)

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The following works, from Christian, critical-historical, and Muslim perspectives, allow the reader to go deeper into how the understanding of Jesus developed and what his own words show.

Bart D. Ehrman — How Jesus Became God traces, from a critical-historical standpoint, how a Jewish preacher came to be regarded as divine, including the rising christology across the Gospels. Larry W. Hurtado — Lord Jesus Christ: Devotion to Jesus in Earliest Christianity presents the strongest scholarly case that devotion to Jesus arose early, and is included here for balance. Raymond E. Brown — An Introduction to New Testament Christology is a careful treatment by a leading Catholic scholar, candid about what the texts do and do not say. Geza Vermes — Jesus the Jew reads Jesus within his first-century Jewish context. James D. G. Dunn — Christology in the Making examines how the doctrine of the incarnation developed within the New Testament period. Muhammad ‘Ata ur-Rahim — Jesus: Prophet of Islam presents the Muslim understanding of Jesus’s mission and of how it was transformed after him.

title: Jesus as the Messiah
subtitle: One shared title, two understandings — what al-Masih means in Islam and what “Christ” means in Christianity
summary: Islam and Christianity both call Jesus “the Messiah” — a title the Quran itself gives him through the angels before his birth. The word means “anointed one” and originally described human kings and priests chosen by God, which is how Jewish tradition has always understood the awaited Messiah. Christianity came to fill the title with belief in Jesus’s divinity and atoning death, while Islam holds that it means what it originally meant: God’s anointed prophet and servant sent to Israel. This article traces the title’s history and compares the two understandings verse by verse.

sections.title: In Brief: A Title Both Faiths Share
sections.body:
Muslims and Christians share something remarkable: both call Jesus “the Messiah.” The Quran itself gives Jesus this title — al-Masih — announcing it through the angels before his birth. But the two faiths fill the shared title with different content. Christians understand “Christ” to mean the divine Son of God who died for humanity’s sins and rose again; Islam understands al-Masih as the anointed prophet and servant of God, sent to the Children of Israel with the Gospel.

This article explains where the title came from, what each tradition means by it, and why Islam sees its own understanding as the original one — reading the key verses of the Quran and the Bible in full along the way.

sections.title: Introduction: Christ Is a Title, Not a Name
sections.body:
Few words carry as much weight between Islam and Christianity as “Messiah.” In English Bibles it usually appears in its Greek-derived form, “Christ” — so often that many readers assume Christ is part of Jesus’s name. It is not a name but a title, from the Hebrew mashiach, meaning “anointed one,” rendered in Greek as christos and in Arabic as al-Masih.

Remarkably, the Quran itself uses this title for Jesus — freely, repeatedly, and with honor, bestowing it through an angelic announcement before he is even born. This is genuine common ground, and this library tries to be honest about common ground wherever it exists.

But shared words can carry different meanings. When a Christian confesses “Jesus is the Christ” and a Muslim says “Isa al-Masih,” the same title is being understood in importantly different ways. This article walks through what the title meant in its original setting, what Christians came to mean by it, and what the Quran means by it.

sections.title: The Main Question: Same Title, Same Meaning?
sections.body:
The question is easy to state: when the Quran calls Jesus al-Masih and the New Testament calls him the Christ, are the two faiths saying the same thing?

Three positions need distinguishing. Jewish tradition, which produced the term, expected the Messiah to be a human being — a divinely chosen king and deliverer, never God Himself. Christianity confesses Jesus as the Messiah and, over time, bound that confession to belief in his divinity, so that “Christ” came to mean the divine Son who died for sins and rose again. Islam affirms Jesus as the Messiah in a sense much closer to the original: the anointed human servant of God, a prophet sent to the Children of Israel.

So the real question is not whether Jesus is the Messiah — Muslims and Christians agree he is — but what being the Messiah means.

sections.title: Historical Context: Anointing in Ancient Israel
sections.body:
In ancient Israel, oil was poured over the head of a person set apart for sacred office. Kings were anointed this way, and so were high priests. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly calls the king of Israel God’s “anointed” — the mashiach. The word thus began its life as a title for human beings chosen and commissioned by God. The Hebrew Bible even applies it to a foreign ruler: in the book of Isaiah, the Persian king Cyrus, who allowed the Jewish exiles to return home, is described as God’s anointed. Whatever else the word meant, it meant a human being appointed by the divine — not a divine being.

After the line of David’s kings fell and the Jewish people came under foreign empires, a hope grew that God would one day raise up a final anointed king from David’s descendants — a righteous ruler who would restore justice and gather the scattered people. By the time of Jesus, under Roman rule, this hope was very much alive and took different forms — a royal deliverer, a priestly figure, a prophet like Moses — but it consistently centered on a human agent of God.

When Jesus’s contemporaries asked whether he was the Messiah, this is what they were asking. And Jewish tradition, from that day to this, has continued to expect a human servant of God — not God become man.

sections.title: The Quranic Perspective: Al-Masih, Servant of God
sections.body:
The Quran’s use of the title begins before Jesus’s birth. When the angels bring Mary the news of the son she will bear, the title Messiah is part of the announcement itself:

إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍۢ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًۭا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ

“[And mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].” (Quran 3:45)

Notice what this verse does. It gives Jesus the title al-Masih as an honor conferred by God, calls him “a word from Him” — brought into being by God’s creative command — and declares him distinguished in this world and the Hereafter. No other prophet in the Quran bears this title. In Arabic, al-Masih comes from the root m-s-h, to wipe or anoint — the same Semitic root family as the Hebrew mashiach. Muslim commentators have traditionally explained it along these lines: Jesus was anointed — blessed, purified, and set apart by God — and some connected it to the way he passed his hand over the sick, who were healed by God’s permission.

Yet the Quran is equally careful to state what the title does not mean. Its most direct passage on the subject addresses Christians — the “People of the Scripture” — by name:

يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلْحَقَّ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولُ ٱللَّهِ وَكَلِمَتُهُۥٓ أَلْقَىٰهَآ إِلَىٰ مَرْيَمَ وَرُوحٌۭ مِّنْهُ ۖ فَـَٔامِنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۖ وَلَا تَقُولُوا۟ ثَلَٰثَةٌ ۚ ٱنتَهُوا۟ خَيْرًۭا لَّكُمْ ۚ إِنَّمَا ٱللَّهُ إِلَٰهٌۭ وَٰحِدٌۭ ۖ سُبْحَٰنَهُۥٓ أَن يَكُونَ لَهُۥ وَلَدٌۭ ۘ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ وَكِيلًۭا

“O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion or say about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, was but a messenger of Allah and His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers. And do not say, "Three"; desist - it is better for you. Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs.” (Quran 4:171)

Here the Quran affirms the exalted titles — the Messiah, a messenger of God, His word, a soul from Him — and in the same breath draws the boundary: do not commit excess in religion; do not say “Three”; God is one, exalted above having a son. The very next verse explains why servanthood is no insult to the Messiah:

لَّن يَسْتَنكِفَ ٱلْمَسِيحُ أَن يَكُونَ عَبْدًۭا لِّلَّهِ وَلَا ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ ٱلْمُقَرَّبُونَ ۚ وَمَن يَسْتَنكِفْ عَنْ عِبَادَتِهِۦ وَيَسْتَكْبِرْ فَسَيَحْشُرُهُمْ إِلَيْهِ جَمِيعًۭا

“Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them to Himself all together.” (Quran 4:172)

To be a servant of God is, in the Quran’s vision, the highest station a creature can hold. The Messiah does not disdain it — he embodies it.

Finally, the Quran points to something disarmingly simple about Jesus and his mother:

مَّا ٱلْمَسِيحُ ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌۭ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُۥ صِدِّيقَةٌۭ ۖ كَانَا يَأْكُلَانِ ٱلطَّعَامَ ۗ ٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ نُبَيِّنُ لَهُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرْ أَنَّىٰ يُؤْفَكُونَ

“The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded.” (Quran 5:75)

The Messiah and his truthful mother “both used to eat food.” Whoever eats depends on nourishment, and whoever depends on anything is a creature, not the self-sufficient Creator. For the Quran, Jesus’s messiahship and his full humanity sit together without tension.

sections.title: The Biblical Perspective: The Christ in the Gospels
sections.body:
The New Testament was written in Greek, and it translates the Hebrew title mashiach with the Greek word christos. One of its own verses shows the equivalence explicitly. When Andrew meets Jesus and runs to tell his brother, the Gospel of John pauses to explain the Hebrew title for its Greek-speaking readers:

“He first found his own brother, Simon, and said to him, “We have found the Messiah!” (which is, being interpreted, Christ).” (John 1:41, World English Bible)

“Messiah” and “Christ” are one word in two languages. The most famous confession of the title comes from Peter. When Jesus asks his disciples who they say he is, Peter answers:

“Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”” (Matthew 16:16)

Christians have historically read “the Son of the living God” as a confession of Jesus’s divinity, joining the two halves of Peter’s sentence into one: the Messiah is the divine Son. Readers should know, however, that scholars of early Judaism note that “son of God” in a first-century Jewish setting was also a familiar way of speaking about the anointed king — a title of appointment rather than of shared divine essence. Which reading is correct is taken up in this library’s article on whether Jesus claimed to be God.

Jesus himself, in the Gospels, accepts the title of Messiah plainly. To a Samaritan woman who says she knows the Messiah is coming, he replies directly:

“The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”” (John 4:25-26)

And in the synagogue at Nazareth, the Gospel of Luke records Jesus defining his own anointing by reading aloud from the scroll of the prophet Isaiah:

““The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” He closed the book, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fastened on him. He began to tell them, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”” (Luke 4:18-21)

This passage repays attention. Jesus says the Spirit of the Lord is on him because God “has anointed” him — to preach good news, to heal, to proclaim release. The anointing is something done to Jesus by God, for a mission of preaching and mercy. For Christians, this scene opens a messiahship that culminates in the cross and resurrection: mainstream Christian teaching holds that Jesus fulfilled and transformed the messianic hope by dying for humanity’s sins and rising again, and “Christ” carries all of that within it.

sections.title: Comparing the Two Understandings
sections.body:
Set side by side, the agreement is real — and so is the difference.

Both faiths agree that Jesus is the Messiah, the anointed one promised to Israel; that the title was announced from God’s side, not seized as human ambition; and that it sets Jesus apart with unique honor. A Muslim can read Peter’s “You are the Christ” and Andrew’s “We have found the Messiah!” and affirm those confessions as far as the words themselves go.

The difference lies in what each tradition pours into the title. In Christian understanding, “Christ” came to mean the eternal Son of God made flesh, whose anointed mission was to die an atoning death and rise again. In Islamic understanding, al-Masih means what the word itself says: one anointed by God — chosen, purified, and commissioned as His servant and messenger to the Children of Israel.

Islam’s case is straightforward. The very grammar of the title implies servanthood: an anointed one is, by definition, anointed by someone above him. That is exactly what the synagogue scene in Luke shows — “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor.” The Anointer is God; the anointed is His servant. The Quran’s declaration that “Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of Allah” (Quran 4:172) is, on this reading, not a demotion of Jesus but a return to the title’s plain sense.

Honesty requires naming where the disagreement runs deepest. Christian scholarship holds that Jesus redefined the messianic hope around his death and resurrection, and historians of antiquity — religious and secular alike — overwhelmingly accept that Jesus was crucified. The Quran denies that the crucifixion befell Jesus, and Muslims accept this on the authority of revelation rather than by claiming the historical sources say otherwise; that question is examined honestly in this library’s article on the crucifixion. But Islam’s position on the meaning of “Messiah” does not depend on that dispute: the title, in its origin and on Jesus’s own lips at Nazareth, describes a human being anointed by God — precisely what the Quran affirms.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A first misconception: “Muslims deny that Jesus is the Messiah.” The opposite is true. The Quran names him al-Masih again and again, conferring the title through the angels before his birth (Quran 3:45). Denying it would contradict the Quran itself.

A second: “Messiah means a divine being, so calling Jesus the Messiah is calling him God.” Linguistically and historically, that is not what the word means. “Anointed one” was a title of Israel’s human kings and priests, and the Hebrew Bible applies it even to the Persian king Cyrus. Divinity entered the meaning of “Christ” through later Christian doctrine about Jesus — not through the word itself.

A third: “The Quran uses al-Masih as an empty borrowed name.” In fact the Quran deploys the title deliberately: it bestows it at the annunciation (3:45), joins it to Jesus’s role as God’s messenger and word (4:171), and reaches for it precisely where servanthood is affirmed (4:172) — as if to say that the anointed one, of all people, is God’s servant.

A fourth: “Accepting Jesus as the Messiah logically requires accepting the Trinity.” The title functioned for centuries in a strictly monotheistic Jewish setting where the anointed one was expected to be human. The Quran confesses Jesus as Messiah, messenger, and word of God, and immediately adds, “Indeed, Allah is but one God. Exalted is He above having a son” (Quran 4:171).

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
Islam’s conclusion begins with agreement. Yes — Jesus, son of Mary, is the Messiah. The Quran says so in the voice of the angels. He is God’s word cast to Mary, honored in this world and the next, strengthened with miracles, sent to the Children of Israel with the Gospel. A Muslim who did not honor the Messiah would not be a Muslim.

But Islam invites Christians and seekers alike to ask what the title meant before later councils defined it. An anointed one is anointed by Another. The kings of Israel were anointed servants of God; the awaited deliverer was expected to be the same; and Jesus at Nazareth read aloud the words “he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor” — a mission received, not a deity disclosed. The Quran’s teaching that “Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of Allah” (Quran 4:172) asks to be heard not as a denial of Jesus’s greatness but as its truest description.

To the sincere seeker, Islam offers the shared title with what it holds to be its original content: Jesus the Messiah — the anointed prophet sent to Israel, born of a virgin as a sign to the worlds, who ate food, prayed, and worshipped the One who anointed him. On this understanding, honoring the Messiah and worshipping God alone are the same act of faithfulness that Jesus himself modeled.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus is the Messiah?
A: Yes. The Quran itself names him al-Masih — the Messiah — and no other figure in the Quran bears this title. Affirming it is part of mainstream Islamic belief.

Q: Does the word “Messiah” itself mean “God”?
A: No. It means “anointed one” and was used in the Hebrew Bible for human kings and priests set apart by God. The belief that the Messiah is divine is a later theological claim about Jesus, not the meaning of the word.

Q: Why does the Quran call Jesus “a word from Him”?
A: Muslims understand this as pointing to Jesus’s miraculous origin — created by God’s direct command, without a father. The same verse insists that God is one (Quran 4:171), so “word” is an honor, not a claim that Jesus is an eternal divine person.

Q: Is the “false messiah” in Islamic teaching related to this title?
A: Linguistically, yes. Narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim describe an end-times deceiver called al-Masih ad-Dajjal, “the false messiah,” whom Jesus will confront after his return. That Arabic can attach masih even to a deceiver shows the word is a title, not a statement of divinity.

Q: Do Muslims believe the Messiah will return?
A: Yes. Mainstream Islamic teaching, drawing on the Quran’s allusions and well-known narrations in the major hadith collections, holds that Jesus will return before the end of history. See this library’s article on the second coming of Jesus.

Q: Can someone accept Jesus as the Messiah without accepting the Trinity?
A: Islam answers yes — that is precisely the Muslim position, and it mirrors the original Jewish expectation of a human, divinely appointed Messiah.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
For readers who want to go deeper, the following books are widely available. Tarif Khalidi’s The Muslim Jesus gathers the sayings and stories about Jesus preserved in classical Islamic literature and shows the reverence Muslim civilization has held for him. Mustafa Akyol’s The Islamic Jesus is an accessible modern account of how Jesus is understood in Islam. Geza Vermes’s Jesus the Jew is a classic historical study that places Jesus and his titles — including “Messiah” and “son of God” — within first-century Judaism. The Study Quran, edited by Seyyed Hossein Nasr, provides a full translation with commentary on the verses discussed in this article. For a concise statement of how Christian scholarship reads Jesus, Richard Bauckham’s Jesus: A Very Short Introduction is a helpful starting point.

As always in this library, we encourage readers to read both sides carefully and to weigh the evidence for themselves.

title: The Crucifixion Question
subtitle: What happened to Jesus at the end? The Christian account, the historians' verdict, and the Quran's answer
summary: Did Jesus die on the cross? This is the sharpest single disagreement between Christianity and Islam. Christianity places the crucifixion and resurrection at the very center of its faith, and mainstream historians widely accept that the crucifixion happened. The Quran declares that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, but that it was made to appear so, and that God raised him to Himself. This article presents all three positions fairly and explains what is really at stake: whether God's forgiveness requires a blood sacrifice, or whether He forgives directly out of His mercy.

sections.title: The Short Answer
sections.body:
Did Jesus die on the cross? On almost no other question do Christianity and Islam disagree so sharply. Christianity teaches that Jesus was crucified, died for humanity's sins, and rose from the dead — and makes this event the center of the faith. The Quran teaches that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, but that it was made to appear so, and that God raised him to Himself.

Between the two stands a third voice: historians without religious commitments generally accept that the crucifixion happened. An honest comparison cannot ignore this, and this article does not.

What follows presents each position as its own scholars state it, then explains why Muslims hold theirs with confidence — and what is at stake: whether forgiveness requires the blood of an innocent, or flows directly from God's mercy.

sections.title: Introduction: Where Two Faiths Part Ways
sections.body:
Islam and Christianity agree about Jesus to a surprising degree. Both affirm his virgin birth, his miracles, his title of Messiah, and his return before the end of history. A Muslim cannot be a Muslim without honoring Jesus.

Yet the two faiths tell different stories about how his earthly mission ended. For Christians the crucifixion is the heart of everything: it stands at the center of worship and of the doctrine of salvation. For Muslims, the Quran's declaration that Jesus was not killed and not crucified is equally non-negotiable, because it comes as the direct speech of God.

The subject deserves gentleness. For Christians the cross carries their deepest experience of grace; for Muslims, God's rescue of His messenger expresses His justice and power. This article will not mock either conviction. It states each position from its own sources, admits honestly where historical scholarship stands, and then makes the Islamic case openly rather than pretending the disagreement is smaller than it is.

sections.title: What Exactly Is Being Asked?
sections.body:
The crucifixion question is really three questions folded into one.

First, a textual question: what do the scriptures claim? The New Testament: Jesus was crucified, died, was buried, and was raised. The Quran: his enemies neither killed nor crucified him, it was made to appear otherwise, and God raised him to Himself. Neither text is vague about its own claim.

Second, a historical question: what can historians, using ordinary methods of evidence and probability, conclude about what happened outside Jerusalem in the first century? That question has a mainstream answer, stated plainly below.

Third — and here lie the deepest stakes — a theological question: how are human beings forgiven? Christianity's answer runs through the cross, an atoning sacrifice. Islam's answer runs directly from the sinner to God: repentance met by mercy, no blood required. The crucifixion question is finally a question about the character of salvation.

sections.title: The Historical Setting and the Historians' Verdict
sections.body:
Jesus lived in the first century in Galilee and Judea, then governed as part of the Roman Empire. Crucifixion was a Roman method of public execution — slow, deliberately degrading, used especially against slaves and those accused of rebellion. Its purpose was not only to kill but to warn.

The Gospels devote long narratives to Jesus' arrest, his condemnation under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, and his crucifixion. The letters of Paul, generally regarded as the earliest surviving Christian documents, already preach the crucifixion and resurrection as settled proclamation, and references to Jesus' execution appear in later non-Christian sources as well.

Here honesty requires a plain statement. In mainstream historical-critical scholarship — including scholars who are neither Christian nor Muslim — the crucifixion is regarded as among the most widely accepted facts about Jesus' life. Historians reason that early Christians were unlikely to invent a shameful execution for the man they proclaimed Messiah, and that multiple early sources report it.

The same honesty requires a second statement. That method treats the resurrection not as an establishable fact but as a faith claim, because the historian's tools weigh probabilities of ordinary events and cannot certify miracles. What the method affirms, and what it cannot see, will both matter when we weigh the Quranic account.

sections.title: What the Quran Says
sections.body:
The Quran addresses the crucifixion directly in Surah An-Nisaa, rebuking those who boasted of having killed Jesus. Quran 4:157 reads:

وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا

"And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain." (Quran 4:157, Saheeh International)

Notice what the verse does and does not deny. It does not deny that an event took place or that onlookers believed they had crucified Jesus. It denies that they killed him and that they crucified him, explaining the gap in one phrase: shubbiha lahum — it was made to appear so to them. It even asserts that those involved were confused: those who differ over it, it says, are in doubt about it.

The next verse states what actually happened. Quran 4:158:

بَل رَّفَعَهُ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًۭا

"Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise." (Quran 4:158, Saheeh International)

How was it made to appear so? The Quran does not say, and beginners should know that everything beyond this point is interpretation, not scripture. Many classical commentators understood shubbiha lahum as substitution: another person, made to resemble Jesus, was crucified in his place. Others placed the weight on appearance itself: the crowd, the chaos, and God's intervention left observers certain of something that had not happened. The identities proposed for a substitute come from commentary literature of varying reliability, not from the Quran, and no version is required belief.

A related verse, Quran 3:55, records God's promise to Jesus:

إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَىٰٓ إِنِّى مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَجَاعِلُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوكَ فَوْقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ

"[Mention] when Allah said, "O Jesus, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve and make those who follow you [in submission to Allah alone] superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ." (Quran 3:55, Saheeh International)

The phrase rendered "I will take you" (mutawaffika) has been read in more than one way: the classical majority held that God took Jesus up alive, his death deferred until his return, while a minority read it as a peaceful death before the raising. On either reading, the decisive point stands — Jesus did not die on a cross at his enemies' hands.

Finally, Quran 4:159 points forward:

وَإِن مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا لَيُؤْمِنَنَّ بِهِۦ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِۦ ۖ وَيَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ يَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا

"And there is none from the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in Jesus before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness." (Quran 4:159, Saheeh International)

Most commentators connect this to Jesus' return at the end of history, and narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim describe Jesus, son of Mary, descending near the end of time — a hope Muslims share, in their own form, with Christians.

sections.title: What the New Testament Says
sections.body:
Fairness requires letting Christianity speak in its strongest voice, and that voice is Paul's. Writing to the church in Corinth, he summarizes the message he says he received:

"For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures," (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, World English Bible)

This compact formula — died for our sins, buried, raised — is widely regarded by Christian scholars as one of the earliest summaries of Christian preaching. In the same chapter Paul argues that if Christ was not raised, the faith itself is emptied. The crucifixion and resurrection are not one doctrine among many; they are the load-bearing wall of the whole structure.

The Gospels narrate the event with stark brevity:

"It was the third hour, and they crucified him." (Mark 15:25, World English Bible)

Readers have long noticed that John's Gospel appears to place the final sentencing at a later hour, a detail Christian interpreters and critical scholars discuss in different ways; but all four Gospels treat the crucifixion as the climax of the story.

Two sayings from these narratives deserve special attention. The first is the cry from the cross:

"About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”" (Matthew 27:46, World English Bible)

Christian interpreters note that these words open Psalm 22 and read the cry as Jesus bearing the weight of human sin while trusting the psalm's arc toward vindication. Muslim readers ask a different question: how could one who is himself God cry out that God has forsaken him? To Muslims the cry fits a beloved prophet in extremity far more naturally than an incarnate deity.

The second comes from Gethsemane, the night before:

"He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.”" (Mark 14:36, World English Bible)

Christian theology reads this as the human will of Jesus submitting perfectly to the divine plan. Muslims read it as something simpler: a righteous prophet, in anguish, begging his Lord — for whom all things are possible — to be spared. And the Quran's answer in 4:158, Muslims note, is that this prayer was heard: God raised him to Himself.

sections.title: Three Positions, Weighed Honestly
sections.body:
Set the three positions side by side. Christianity: Jesus was crucified, died for sins, and rose — the center of the faith. Historical scholarship: the crucifixion is the most securely attested event of Jesus' life, but the resurrection lies beyond what the method can affirm. Islam: Jesus was neither killed nor crucified; it was made to appear so; God raised him alive.

Each position rests on a different authority: apostolic testimony, probabilistic reasoning over sources, and the Quran received as God's direct speech. That is why the debate cannot be settled simply by announcing the historians' verdict.

Consider what historical method can see. Its conclusion follows from weighing sources under a working rule that excludes miracles from explanation. But the Quranic claim is precisely a claim of divine intervention in what observers perceived. A miracle of appearance is, by definition, invisible to a method that assumes appearances were normal — and every chain of testimony runs back through the very eyewitnesses the Quran says were deceived and confused. A Muslim can grant everything the method genuinely shows — an execution event, communities convinced Jesus had died — while denying the one link it cannot secure: that the man on the cross was Jesus.

Honesty requires admitting the argument cuts both ways. The Muslim accepts a miracle on the authority of revelation, which the secular historian will not. But the Christian does the same at the decisive point, since the resurrection — the actual center of the faith — is likewise held on revelation and testimony, not neutral history. At the moment that matters most, both faiths ask for trust in a revelation; the real question is which revelation deserves it, which is why the transmission of the Quran and of the Bible are examined elsewhere in this library. And beneath the historical question lies the theological one: if Jesus did not die for sins, forgiveness must come — as Islam says it does — from God's own direct mercy.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
First: the Quran does not deny that Jesus existed or that a dramatic public event took place. It denies that Jesus was the one killed and crucified, and states that observers were made to perceive otherwise. The position is not that nothing happened, but that what happened is not what they thought.

Second: it is often said that Muslims believe Judas was crucified instead. No name appears in the Quran. Proposed identities for a substitute come from later commentary of uneven reliability, and none is an article of faith. The Quran leaves the mechanism with God.

Third: the denial is not hostility toward Christianity. The Quran affirms Jesus' virgin birth, miracles, messiahship, and return. Muslims understand the denial of the crucifixion as God's vindication of Jesus — a rescue, not a rejection.

Fourth, a misconception in the other direction: that Christians believe God simply died on the cross. Mainstream Christian theology is more careful: it holds that the divine nature cannot die, and that Christ died in his human nature. Muslims find the two-natures framework untenable — that critique belongs to the article on the Trinity — but fairness requires stating the doctrine as Christians hold it.

Fifth: some academic writers compare Quran 4:157 to early sects called docetists, who taught that Christ only seemed to suffer because he was too divine to have a real body. The comparison fails at the crucial point: the Quran insists Jesus was fully human — born of a mother, eating food, praying. Its claim is not that Jesus had no real body, but that God protected His human messenger from that death. Muslims receive the verse as revelation correcting the record, not as an echo of anyone's speculation.

sections.title: The Islamic Case: Rescue, Not Sacrifice
sections.body:
The Islamic position is not an evasion of history; it is a claim about God, resting on three convictions.

The first is God's justice. Guilt is not transferable: no innocent can justly be punished so that the guilty go free. The Quran states the principle in Surah Faatir:

وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌۭ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۚ وَإِن تَدْعُ مُثْقَلَةٌ إِلَىٰ حِمْلِهَا لَا يُحْمَلْ مِنْهُ شَىْءٌۭ وَلَوْ كَانَ ذَا قُرْبَىٰٓ ۗ إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَيْبِ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ ۚ وَمَن تَزَكَّىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِۦ ۚ وَإِلَى ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمَصِيرُ

"And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to [carry some of] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and have established prayer. And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his soul. And to Allah is the [final] destination." (Quran 35:18, Saheeh International)

If no soul bears another's burden, salvation cannot run through the execution of an innocent man, even a willing one. It must run through each soul's own turning to God.

The second is God's mercy. Christianity reasons that sin against an infinite God demands an infinite payment that only the cross could supply. Islam replies that forgiveness is not a debt to be settled but a gift to be granted: the Lord who commands His servants to forgive freely does not need blood before doing the same. The sinner repents, and God forgives directly — nothing stands between the servant and the Master. This is explored fully in the article on forgiveness in Islam and Christianity.

The third is God's faithfulness to His messengers. Across the Quran, God rescues His prophets as their enemies close in; read in that light, the ending of Jesus' story is the pattern's most glorious case. The prophet who prayed "all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me" was answered by the God for whom all things are possible: "Rather, Allah raised him to Himself. And ever is Allah Exalted in Might and Wise." (Quran 4:158). Where the cross would say God's beloved was forsaken, the Quran says he was honored and taken up — and, per Quran 4:159, his story is not finished.

A Muslim therefore faces this question without anxiety. The historical debate is real, and this article has stated it honestly. But where every party must finally trust a testimony, the Muslim trusts the speech of God, and finds in it a conclusion worthy of both God's justice and His mercy: no scapegoat, no forsaken prophet, no debt collected in blood — a rescue, a raising, and a door of forgiveness open to every soul that knocks.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus was crucified?
A: No. The Quran states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified but that it was made to appear so (4:157), and that God raised him to Himself (4:158). Muslims receive this as God's direct testimony.

Q: If it was not Jesus on the cross, who was it?
A: The Quran does not say. Many classical commentators spoke of a substitute made to resemble Jesus, but no identification is part of the Quranic text or required belief. Muslims are content to leave the mechanism with God.

Q: Don't historians agree the crucifixion happened?
A: Mainstream scholarship does regard it as among the best-attested facts of Jesus' life, and Muslims should acknowledge that honestly. But historical method excludes divine intervention by design, while the Quran's claim is precisely that God intervened in what observers perceived. The same method also declines to affirm the resurrection — so both faiths ultimately rest on revelation at the decisive point.

Q: Without the cross, how are sins forgiven in Islam?
A: Directly. The sinner repents sincerely and God forgives out of His mercy — no intermediary, no sacrifice, no transferred guilt, for no soul bears the burden of another (Quran 35:18).

Q: Is Jesus alive now, according to Islam?
A: The majority view is that God raised him alive and that he will return before the Day of Resurrection — a hope described in narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and connected by most commentators to Quran 4:159.

Q: Does denying the crucifixion dishonor Jesus?
A: The opposite. In the Islamic account the denial is God's rescue and vindication of a beloved messenger, whom Muslims may never mention except with reverence.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The works below cover the ground from several angles: a scholarly history of Muslim interpretation of Quran 4:157; comparative studies of Jesus in the Quran and in Christian doctrine; the image of Jesus in the wider Islamic tradition; and a reconstruction of Jesus' life by a prominent non-Christian historian, useful for seeing how the secular case is actually argued.

As with every article in this library, the list exists so you can check the claims for yourself. Read the strongest version of each position, and weigh them with the seriousness the question deserves.

title: The Miracles of Jesus
subtitle: What the Quran and the Gospels report — and what the miracles were meant to prove
summary: Islam and Christianity both affirm that Jesus (peace be upon him) performed real miracles: healing the blind and lepers, raising the dead, and feeding the faithful. The Quran adds distinctive wonders such as Jesus speaking as an infant in the cradle and giving life to a bird formed from clay. Strikingly, the Quran says each miracle happened 'by permission of Allah', while the New Testament itself describes them as works 'which God did by him'. This article catalogs the miracles in both scriptures and asks whether miracles prove Jesus's divinity — or his prophethood.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body:
Few things surprise new readers of the Quran more than how much it honors Jesus (peace be upon him) — and how vividly it affirms his miracles. The Quran states that Jesus healed the blind and the leper, raised the dead, and formed a bird from clay that came alive when he breathed into it. It adds wonders the Bible does not record, such as Jesus speaking from the cradle as a newborn to defend his mother's honor.

The Gospels report their own catalog: healings, the feeding of thousands from a few loaves, and the raising of Lazarus from the tomb. So both traditions agree that Jesus was a true worker of miracles.

Where they differ is on what the miracles mean. The Quran repeats, again and again, that Jesus did these things 'by permission of Allah'. The New Testament itself describes Jesus as a man through whom God worked wonders, and records Jesus saying he can do nothing by himself. This article lays out the evidence from both scriptures and examines the central question: do miracles prove that Jesus is God, or that God sent him?

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
This article belongs to a series on Jesus as the Quran and the Bible present him. Our method throughout is simple: let each scripture speak in its own words first, quote it exactly, and only then compare. Every verse below was retrieved directly from the source texts — the Quran in the Uthmani Arabic script with the Saheeh International translation, and the Bible in the World English Bible translation.

Miracles are a natural meeting point between the two faiths. A Christian reading the Quran for the first time discovers that Islam does not reduce Jesus to a mere teacher of ethics: the Quran presents him as one of the mightiest messengers God ever sent, marked out by signs no ordinary man could produce. A Muslim reading the Gospels finds accounts of healing and mercy that feel deeply familiar in spirit.

Precisely because both traditions affirm the miracles, they make an excellent test case for the deeper question that separates the two faiths: who was Jesus? A prophet empowered by God, as Islam teaches — or God incarnate, as the later Christian creeds defined him? The miracles themselves, as we will see, carry an answer within the very way both scriptures describe them.

sections.title: The Question: Do Miracles Prove Divinity?
sections.body:
The argument is often put like this: 'Only God can raise the dead. Jesus raised the dead. Therefore Jesus is God.' It sounds compelling. But it stands or falls on one point: did Jesus perform miracles by his own inherent power, or did God perform them through him?

Both scriptures address this directly. The Quran answers with a repeated, deliberate phrase — bi-idhnillah, 'by permission of Allah' — attached to each miracle. The New Testament, in the very first public sermon of Christianity recorded in the book of Acts, describes the miracles as works 'which God did by him'. And the Hebrew Bible describes earlier prophets — Moses, Elijah, Elisha — performing wonders of the same kind, including raising the dead, without anyone concluding that those prophets were divine.

So the real question is not whether the miracles happened; both faiths say they did. The question is what they were for: proof of Jesus's own deity, or God's public endorsement of His messenger.

sections.title: Historical Context
sections.body:
Jesus lived in the first century, in Galilee and Judea, when the region was under Roman rule. Historians of early Christianity — whatever their personal beliefs — broadly agree that Jesus was known among his contemporaries as a healer, and his reputation for extraordinary deeds is among the most widely accepted features of his public life. The written Gospels, composed in Greek in the decades after his ministry, preserve that reputation in narrative form.

In the Israelite tradition Jesus's audience knew, miracles had a well-understood job: they were credentials. Moses came to Pharaoh with signs. Elijah and Elisha healed the sick and even raised the dead. A prophet's wonders were read as God's endorsement of the man's message, not as evidence that the man himself was divine. Jesus's miracles landed in exactly this context, and the earliest recorded Christian preaching, as we will see below, describes them in exactly these terms.

The Quran was revealed in the seventh century in Arabia, and it addresses Jews and Christians directly and by name. On the subject of Jesus's miracles it does something remarkable: rather than disputing them, it affirms them emphatically — including wonders not found in the Bible — and then frames every one of them with a phrase that settles the question of whose power was at work.

sections.title: The Miracles in the Quran
sections.body:
The Quran's fullest single catalog of Jesus's miracles appears in Surah Aal-i-Imraan (the third chapter), where Jesus announces his mission to the Children of Israel. Quran 3:49 reads:

وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنِّى قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِـَٔايَةٍۢ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ ۖ أَنِّىٓ أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ وَأُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ ۖ وَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِى بُيُوتِكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَةًۭ لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ

'And [make him] a messenger to the Children of Israel, [who will say], 'Indeed I have come to you with a sign from your Lord in that I design for you from clay [that which is] like the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by permission of Allah. And I cure the blind and the leper, and I give life to the dead - by permission of Allah. And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.' (Quran 3:49, Saheeh International)

One verse gathers four wonders: giving life to a bird of clay, curing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, and announcing hidden knowledge. Twice in a single breath comes the refrain bi-idhnillah — 'by permission of Allah'. And notice what the verse says the miracles are: 'a sign for you, if you are believers.' A sign points beyond itself, to the One who sent it.

The fifth chapter returns to the same catalog, but this time the speaker is God Himself, addressing Jesus. Quran 5:110 reads:

إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱذْكُرْ نِعْمَتِى عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ وَٰلِدَتِكَ إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ تُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًۭا ۖ وَإِذْ عَلَّمْتُكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ ۖ وَإِذْ تَخْلُقُ مِنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ بِإِذْنِى فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا فَتَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِى ۖ وَتُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِى ۖ وَإِذْ تُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِى ۖ وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ فَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ

'[The Day] when Allah will say, "O Jesus, Son of Mary, remember My favor upon you and upon your mother when I supported you with the Pure Spirit and you spoke to the people in the cradle and in maturity; and [remember] when I taught you writing and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel; and when you designed from clay [what was] like the form of a bird with My permission, then you breathed into it, and it became a bird with My permission; and you healed the blind and the leper with My permission; and when you brought forth the dead with My permission; and when I restrained the Children of Israel from [killing] you when you came to them with clear proofs and those who disbelieved among them said, "This is not but obvious magic."' (Quran 5:110, Saheeh International)

Four times in this one verse: 'with My permission.' The repetition is not decoration; it is doctrine. Every miracle is affirmed in the same movement that attributes its power entirely to God.

The verse also mentions a miracle unique to the Quran: Jesus 'spoke to the people in the cradle'. Surah Maryam narrates the scene. When Mary, unmarried and accused, brought her newborn to her people, she simply pointed to the child. Quran 19:29 reads:

فَأَشَارَتْ إِلَيْهِ ۖ قَالُوا۟ كَيْفَ نُكَلِّمُ مَن كَانَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ صَبِيًّۭا

'So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?"' (Quran 19:29, Saheeh International)

Then the infant spoke — and his first recorded words in the Quran define his whole identity. Quran 19:30 reads:

قَالَ إِنِّى عَبْدُ ٱللَّهِ ءَاتَىٰنِىَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَجَعَلَنِى نَبِيًّۭا

'[Jesus] said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet.' (Quran 19:30, Saheeh International)

The miracle that saves Mary's honor is, at the same moment, a declaration: servant of Allah, prophet.

The Quran also records a table miracle. The fifth chapter is named Al-Maaida, 'The Table Spread', after it. The disciples ask for a meal sent down from heaven, and the exchange is telling. Quran 5:112 reads:

إِذْ قَالَ ٱلْحَوَارِيُّونَ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ رَبُّكَ أَن يُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْنَا مَآئِدَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ ۖ قَالَ ٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ

'[And remember] when the disciples said, "O Jesus, Son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven? [Jesus] said," Fear Allah, if you should be believers."' (Quran 5:112, Saheeh International)

The disciples explain their motive in Quran 5:113:

قَالُوا۟ نُرِيدُ أَن نَّأْكُلَ مِنْهَا وَتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُنَا وَنَعْلَمَ أَن قَدْ صَدَقْتَنَا وَنَكُونَ عَلَيْهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّٰهِدِينَ

'They said, "We wish to eat from it and let our hearts be reassured and know that you have been truthful to us and be among its witnesses."' (Quran 5:113, Saheeh International)

Notice what Jesus does next. He does not produce the meal himself; he prays. Quran 5:114 reads:

قَالَ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ ٱللَّهُمَّ رَبَّنَآ أَنزِلْ عَلَيْنَا مَآئِدَةًۭ مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ تَكُونُ لَنَا عِيدًۭا لِّأَوَّلِنَا وَءَاخِرِنَا وَءَايَةًۭ مِّنكَ ۖ وَٱرْزُقْنَا وَأَنتَ خَيْرُ ٱلرَّٰزِقِينَ

'Said Jesus, the son of Mary, "O Allah, our Lord, send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven to be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us and a sign from You. And provide for us, and You are the best of providers."' (Quran 5:114, Saheeh International)

And God answers in Quran 5:115:

قَالَ ٱللَّهُ إِنِّى مُنَزِّلُهَا عَلَيْكُمْ ۖ فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بَعْدُ مِنكُمْ فَإِنِّىٓ أُعَذِّبُهُۥ عَذَابًۭا لَّآ أُعَذِّبُهُۥٓ أَحَدًۭا مِّنَ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ

'Allah said, "Indeed, I will sent it down to you, but whoever disbelieves afterwards from among you - then indeed will I punish him with a punishment by which I have not punished anyone among the worlds."' (Quran 5:115, Saheeh International)

Many readers hear in this passage an echo of the Gospel table scenes — the blessed meals, the feeding miracles — retold with the lines of authority drawn sharply: the disciples ask, Jesus prays, God sends.

For the Quran, this is not a rule about Jesus alone but about every messenger. Quran 13:38 states the principle:

وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنَا رُسُلًۭا مِّن قَبْلِكَ وَجَعَلْنَا لَهُمْ أَزْوَٰجًۭا وَذُرِّيَّةًۭ ۚ وَمَا كَانَ لِرَسُولٍ أَن يَأْتِىَ بِـَٔايَةٍ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ ۗ لِكُلِّ أَجَلٍۢ كِتَابٌۭ

'And We have already sent messengers before you and assigned to them wives and descendants. And it was not for a messenger to come with a sign except by permission of Allah. For every term is a decree.' (Quran 13:38, Saheeh International)

And the Quran draws the conclusion explicitly, in a verse that names the miracles' limit. Quran 5:75 reads:

مَّا ٱلْمَسِيحُ ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌۭ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُۥ صِدِّيقَةٌۭ ۖ كَانَا يَأْكُلَانِ ٱلطَّعَامَ ۗ ٱنظُرْ كَيْفَ نُبَيِّنُ لَهُمُ ٱلْءَايَٰتِ ثُمَّ ٱنظُرْ أَنَّىٰ يُؤْفَكُونَ

'The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food. Look how We make clear to them the signs; then look how they are deluded.' (Quran 5:75, Saheeh International)

A man who eats depends on food; the One who sustains all things depends on nothing. The miracle worker was mighty — but he was a messenger, in a long line of messengers.

sections.title: The Miracles in the Bible
sections.body:
The Gospels present Jesus healing the blind and lepers, feeding great crowds, and raising the dead. The question for our purposes is how the New Testament itself frames these works — and its earliest summary is strikingly clear. In the book of Acts, Peter stands up at Pentecost and delivers the first public sermon of the new community. Acts 2:22 reads:

'Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know,' (Acts 2:22, World English Bible)

Three phrases carry the theology: Jesus is 'a man', he is 'approved by God', and the wonders are works 'which God did by him'. The miracles authenticate the messenger; the power belongs to God.

Jesus says the same of himself in the Gospel of John. John 5:30 reads:

'I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don't seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me.' (John 5:30, World English Bible)

The most dramatic miracle in John is the raising of Lazarus, and the narrative detail matters: before the dead man walks out, Jesus prays — aloud, deliberately, and he explains why. John 11:41-44 reads:

'So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, "Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me." When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Free him, and let him go."' (John 11:41-44, World English Bible)

Jesus states the miracle's purpose in his own prayer: 'that they may believe that you sent me.' Not 'that I am God' — 'that you sent me'.

The same posture appears in the feeding of the five thousand. Matthew 14:19-20 reads:

'He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes. They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.' (Matthew 14:19-20, World English Bible)

Before the bread multiplies, Jesus looks 'up to heaven' and blesses — the gesture of a servant receiving, not a source producing.

The Hebrew Bible supplies the precedent that Jesus's first audience already knew. Centuries earlier, the prophet Elisha raised a dead child. 2 Kings 4:32-35 reads:

'When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and lying on his bed. He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to Yahweh.
