He went up, and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the child's flesh grew warm. Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth; and went up, and stretched himself out on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.' (2 Kings 4:32-35, World English Bible)

Elisha prayed, and God raised the dead through him. No one, in either faith, concludes that Elisha was divine.

Jesus even extends the miracles beyond himself. John 14:12 reads:

'Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.' (John 14:12, World English Bible)

In fairness, Christian scholarship reads these same texts within a different frame. The Gospel of John calls the miracles 'signs' that reveal Jesus's glory and his unique relationship to the Father, and classical Christian theology understands statements like 'I can of myself do nothing' as the voluntary submission of the divine Son — an expression of his humanity or of his eternal relation to the Father, not a denial of his deity. Christians do not typically rest the case for Jesus's divinity on the miracles alone; they rest it on the resurrection and on the way John's Gospel speaks of Jesus's identity. That is the mainstream Christian position, and any honest comparison must engage it rather than a caricature.

sections.title: Reading the Two Accounts Side by Side
sections.body:
Set the two scriptures beside each other and a remarkable convergence appears. The Quran says Jesus gave life to the clay bird, cured the blind and the leper, and raised the dead 'by permission of Allah' (Quran 3:49) — 'with My permission', God says four times over (Quran 5:110). The New Testament's first sermon calls the miracles 'wonders and signs which God did by him' (Acts 2:22). Jesus himself says, 'I can of myself do nothing' (John 5:30), and before raising Lazarus he thanks the Father 'that you listened to me' (John 11:41). On the mechanics of the miracles — whose power was at work — the Quran and the earliest Christian preaching speak with one voice: the power was God's.

The two scriptures even agree on the purpose. The Quran calls the wonders 'a sign for you, if you are believers' (Quran 3:49). Jesus, in John, prays aloud 'that they may believe that you sent me' (John 11:42). In both texts the miracle is an argument for sent-ness — for prophethood — addressed to an audience deciding whether to trust the man who stands before them.

The precedent of earlier prophets seals the logical point. Elisha prayed and a dead child revived (2 Kings 4:32-35). Moses came to Pharaoh with signs. If raising the dead proved divinity, the proof would prove far too much: it would deify Elisha and Elijah, and — by Jesus's own words that believers 'will do greater works than these' (John 14:12) — his followers too. No Christian accepts those conclusions, which shows that the inference from miracle to divinity is not one the Bible itself teaches.

Where the traditions genuinely part ways is elsewhere. Christian theology reads Jesus's dependence on the Father as the internal life of the Trinity: the Son eternally receives from the Father, so dependence is compatible with deity. Islam replies that this reading arrives after the fact: taken plainly, a man who prays, receives permission, and credits God is showing us what a servant of God looks like — which is exactly what the infant Jesus of the Quran announces: 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah' (Quran 19:30). It is also worth saying honestly that the Christian case for Jesus's divinity does not mainly rest on the miracles; it rests on the resurrection and on the exalted language of John's Gospel. Those questions deserve their own careful treatment — see our articles on the crucifixion and on whether Jesus claimed to be God. But on the ground this article covers, the miracles themselves, the two scriptures point the same way.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
A first misconception: 'Muslims deny the miracles of Jesus.' The truth is the reverse. The Quran affirms every major category of miracle the Gospels report — healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, wondrous provision of food — and adds wonders of its own: the newborn Jesus speaking in the cradle (Quran 19:29-30) and the clay bird brought to life (Quran 3:49). Within Islam these are real events, affirmed by God's own word, not legends to be explained away.

A second misconception: 'If Jesus raised the dead, he must be God.' As we have seen, both scriptures block this inference. The Quran attaches 'by permission of Allah' to the miracles; Acts says God did them 'by him'; Jesus says he can do nothing of himself; and Elisha raised the dead centuries earlier without anyone worshiping him. A miracle demonstrates that God is acting; it does not identify the man through whom God acts as God Himself.

A third misconception, raised from the other direction: 'The Quran borrowed the clay-bird story from a Christian legend.' It is true, and should be said plainly, that a similar story of the child Jesus bringing clay birds to life appears in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, an early non-canonical Christian writing that circulated long before the Quran, and secular scholars often describe the Quran as engaging stories its first audience already knew. The Islamic response is twofold. First, the Quran presents itself as confirming and correcting earlier tradition; if the event truly happened, its survival in Christian memory — even outside the canonical Gospels — is precisely what one would expect, and retelling a true event is not borrowing a fiction. Second, the Quran's framing is pointedly its own: where a legend might display a boy wielding wondrous power, the Quran twice inserts 'by permission of Allah' into the telling (Quran 3:49), stripping the story of any suggestion of independent divine power. The Quran does not copy; it corrects.

A fourth misconception: 'Christians claim the miracles alone prove Jesus is God.' Thoughtful Christian theologians generally do not argue this — they know their own Bible describes prophets and apostles working wonders by God's power. The serious Christian arguments lie elsewhere, in the resurrection and in John's portrait of Jesus. Recognizing this keeps the conversation honest: the miracles are common ground between the two faiths, not a battleground.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
In Islamic theology a prophet's miracle is called a mu'jizah — literally, something that disables imitation — and its function is fixed: it is God's public endorsement of His messenger. By that measure the Quran gives Jesus extraordinary honor. He is one of the greatest of the resolute messengers, whose signs began at birth and ran through his whole mission: he spoke in the cradle, gave life to clay, opened blind eyes, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and was answered from heaven with a table spread before his disciples. Islam does not diminish the miracles of Jesus. It insists on them.

But Islam also insists on what the miracles meant, and here it appeals to the pattern both scriptures share: permission, prayer, dependence. 'It was not for a messenger to come with a sign except by permission of Allah' (Quran 13:38). 'Which God did by him' (Acts 2:22). The consistent witness of the texts is tawhid — the absolute oneness of God — with Jesus as God's servant and messenger, exactly as his first recorded words in the Quran declare: 'Indeed, I am the servant of Allah' (Quran 19:30).

For the sincere seeker, this is good news rather than a demotion. It means the wonder you feel reading about Lazarus walking out of the tomb, or the crowds fed from five loaves, needs no revision — only redirection. The miracles were always signposts. Islam's invitation is to follow them where they point: past the blessed hands of the messenger, to the God who healed and raised and provided through him — the God Jesus prayed to, and the God he called his Lord.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Does the Quran really affirm the miracles of Jesus?
A: Yes, emphatically. The Quran states that Jesus healed the blind and the leper, raised the dead, brought a clay bird to life, announced hidden knowledge, spoke as an infant in the cradle, and was answered with a table sent down from heaven (Quran 3:49, 5:110, 5:112-115, 19:29-30). Muslims accept all of these as real events.

Q: Do miracles prove that Jesus is God?
A: Not according to either scripture. The Quran says each miracle happened 'by permission of Allah', and the New Testament describes them as wonders 'which God did by him' (Acts 2:22), while Jesus says, 'I can of myself do nothing' (John 5:30). Earlier prophets such as Elisha also raised the dead (2 Kings 4:32-35), and no one concludes they were divine.

Q: Which miracles appear in the Quran but not in the Bible?
A: Two stand out: Jesus speaking from the cradle as a newborn to defend his mother (Quran 19:29-30), and the clay bird that came alive when he breathed into it (Quran 3:49). The table sent down from heaven (Quran 5:112-115) has no exact biblical parallel, though many readers hear echoes of the Gospel feeding narratives and the Last Supper.

Q: Why does the Quran keep repeating 'by permission of Allah'?
A: Because the phrase settles the very question this article examines. In one verse God says 'with My permission' four times (Quran 5:110). The repetition affirms the miracles fully while attributing their power entirely to God — honoring Jesus as a mighty messenger without deifying him.

Q: Didn't the Quran take the clay-bird story from a Christian legend?
A: A similar story appears in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a non-canonical Christian text older than the Quran, and scholars note the parallel. Muslims respond that the Quran confirms and corrects earlier tradition: if the event was real, its memory surviving among Christians is expected, and the Quran retells it with its own theological frame — 'by permission of Allah' — which the legend lacks.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The works below come from Muslim, Christian, and secular academic authors, so a reader can test this article's claims against several perspectives. Khalidi gathers the rich Islamic literary tradition about Jesus; Reynolds sets the Quran beside the Bible passage by passage; Akyol writes an accessible Muslim account of Jesus; Ehrman and Vermes represent critical historical scholarship on how Jesus was remembered and how claims about him developed.

As always on this site, we encourage readers to open the primary sources themselves: read Surah Aal-i-Imraan and Surah Al-Maaida alongside the Gospel accounts, and weigh what each text actually says about where the power behind the miracles came from.

title: The Miraculous Birth of Jesus
subtitle: The virgin birth in the Quran and the Gospels — one miracle, two conclusions
summary: Both the Quran and the New Testament teach that Jesus was born of the virgin Mary without a human father — a rare, deep agreement between Islam and Christianity. This article presents the Quranic annunciation to Maryam, the only woman named in the Quran and the namesake of its nineteenth chapter, alongside the Gospel accounts in Matthew and Luke. It then compares what each tradition concludes from the same miracle: Christianity reads it together with divine sonship and incarnation, while Islam reads it as a sign of God's creative power, comparing Jesus to Adam, who was created without father or mother. The aim is to give sincere seekers both readings fairly and to explain why Islam finds its conclusion the more consistent one.

sections.title: In Brief: A Miracle Both Faiths Affirm
sections.body:
Few things unite Islam and Christianity as clearly as this: both the Quran and the New Testament teach that Jesus was born of the virgin Mary, without a human father. That is a rare and deep point of agreement between the world's two largest religions.

This article walks through the annunciation — the moment an angel announced the coming child to Maryam (Mary) — as told in the Quran and in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, quoting each scripture in its own words. Along the way it shows how highly Islam honors Mary: she is the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran, and its nineteenth chapter, Surat Maryam, is named after her.

The two faiths part ways not over the miracle itself but over what it means. Christianity reads the virgin birth alongside its doctrine that Jesus is the divine Son of God. Islam affirms the same miracle as a sign of God's creative power — comparing Jesus to Adam, created without father or mother — while insisting that God has no son.

sections.title: A Rare Point of Deep Agreement
sections.body:
Discussions between Muslims and Christians often concentrate on the points of disagreement: the Trinity, the crucifixion, the nature of scripture. It is easy to forget that on one of the most astonishing claims in either scripture, the two faiths stand together. Both affirm that Jesus was conceived in the womb of a virgin, by the direct action of God, without any human father.

A quick definition helps at the start. "Virgin birth" — more precisely, virginal conception — means that Mary conceived Jesus while remaining a virgin: no man was involved at any point. This is not a fringe opinion in either religion. It is stated plainly in the Quran and in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, confessed in the historic Christian creeds, and affirmed by Muslim scholarship across all schools.

The Quran's regard for Mary goes further than many readers expect. She is the only woman referred to by her own name anywhere in the Quran — other women, such as the wife of Pharaoh or the mother of Moses, are identified by their relationships. An entire chapter, Surah 19, bears her name: Surat Maryam. In what follows we will read the two annunciation accounts side by side, notice how strikingly similar they are, and then ask the question that actually divides the two faiths: what does a miraculous birth prove?

sections.title: The Real Question: What Does the Miracle Mean?
sections.body:
The main question of this article is not whether the virgin birth happened. Both scriptures say it did, and both faith communities have always believed it. The question is what the miracle means.

For Christian tradition, the virgin birth belongs to a larger claim: that the child conceived in Mary was the eternal Son of God taking on human nature — the doctrine known as the incarnation. On this reading, the miraculous conception is the doorway through which God entered the world as a man.

Islam draws a different conclusion from the same event. In the Quran, the virgin birth is a sign — in Arabic, an ayah — of God's unlimited power to create. God created Adam with no father and no mother; He creates every other human being from two parents; and He created Jesus from a mother alone. When God decrees a thing, He says "Be," and it is. A miraculous origin, in this reading, makes Jesus a uniquely honored prophet and Messiah — not a divine son.

So the real dispute is a dispute about inference: does the miracle show that God became man, or that God needs no means at all to create a man? Keeping that question in view will make the comparison easier to follow.

sections.title: The Story in Its Historical Setting
sections.body:
The Gospel accounts place the story in a first-century Jewish setting. Luke locates the annunciation in Nazareth, a town in Galilee, where Mary is a young woman pledged in marriage to Joseph, a descendant of David. Matthew tells the story from Joseph's side and presents the conception as fulfilling words of the prophet Isaiah. In that Jewish world, betrothal was a binding commitment, which is why Matthew describes Joseph's distress when Mary was found to be pregnant.

Belief in the virgin birth entered Christianity's core confessions early. The ancient creeds recited in churches to this day — including the one commonly called the Apostles' Creed — confess that Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary. Roughly six centuries after Jesus, the Quran was revealed in Arabia, a region with Jewish and Christian communities in and around it. On this subject its position is distinctive: it affirms the virgin birth as firmly as any church creed, defends Mary's chastity against those who slandered her, and at the same time rejects the conclusion that the child was God's son.

Honesty requires one more note. Modern critical historians point out that, within the New Testament, only Matthew and Luke narrate the virginal conception, and that miracles by their nature lie beyond what historical method can verify; many secular scholars therefore treat the infancy narratives with reserve. Muslims and traditional Christians both accept the virgin birth on the authority of revelation, not because secular historians can prove it. That clarifies what kind of agreement this is: two scriptures, independently trusted by their communities, testifying to the same miracle.

sections.title: The Annunciation in the Quran
sections.body:
The Quran tells the story of Jesus's conception twice, in Surah 3 (Aal Imran) and Surah 19 (Maryam), with briefer references in Surahs 21 and 66. Before the annunciation itself, the Quran establishes Mary's standing:

وَإِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱصْطَفَىٰكِ وَطَهَّرَكِ وَٱصْطَفَىٰكِ عَلَىٰ نِسَآءِ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ

"And [mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds." — Quran 3:42 (Saheeh International)

"Chosen you above the women of the worlds" — this is the Quran's own description of Mary. Then comes the announcement:

إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلَٰٓئِكَةُ يَٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍۢ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ ٱلْمَسِيحُ عِيسَى ٱبْنُ مَرْيَمَ وَجِيهًۭا فِى ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ وَمِنَ ٱلْمُقَرَّبِينَ

"[And mention] when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah]." — Quran 3:45 (Saheeh International)

Notice the titles packed into one verse: Jesus is "a word from Him" — brought into being by God's command — and "the Messiah" (al-Masih), the anointed one awaited by Israel. The angels continue:

وَيُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًۭا وَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ

"He will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity and will be of the righteous."" — Quran 3:46 (Saheeh International)

Mary's response is the natural one, and the answer she receives sets the theological key for everything Islam says about this miracle:

قَالَتْ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى وَلَدٌۭ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِى بَشَرٌۭ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ ٱللَّهُ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُ ۚ إِذَا قَضَىٰٓ أَمْرًۭا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ

"She said, "My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me?" [The angel] said, "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is." — Quran 3:47 (Saheeh International)

Surah 19, the chapter named after Mary, narrates the scene itself. The verses read almost like a film sequence:

وَٱذْكُرْ فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مَرْيَمَ إِذِ ٱنتَبَذَتْ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا مَكَانًۭا شَرْقِيًّۭا

"And mention, [O Muhammad], in the Book [the story of] Mary, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east." — Quran 19:16 (Saheeh International)

فَٱتَّخَذَتْ مِن دُونِهِمْ حِجَابًۭا فَأَرْسَلْنَآ إِلَيْهَا رُوحَنَا فَتَمَثَّلَ لَهَا بَشَرًۭا سَوِيًّۭا

"And she took, in seclusion from them, a screen. Then We sent to her Our Angel, and he represented himself to her as a well-proportioned man." — Quran 19:17 (Saheeh International)

The "Spirit" sent to her, understood by Muslim commentators as the angel Gabriel, appears in the form of a man — and Mary's first reaction is to seek God's protection, a mark of her piety:

قَالَتْ إِنِّىٓ أَعُوذُ بِٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ مِنكَ إِن كُنتَ تَقِيًّۭا

"She said, "Indeed, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, [so leave me], if you should be fearing of Allah."" — Quran 19:18 (Saheeh International)

قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أَنَا۠ رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأَهَبَ لَكِ غُلَٰمًۭا زَكِيًّۭا

"He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you [news of] a pure boy."" — Quran 19:19 (Saheeh International)

قَالَتْ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِى غُلَٰمٌۭ وَلَمْ يَمْسَسْنِى بَشَرٌۭ وَلَمْ أَكُ بَغِيًّۭا

"She said, "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?"" — Quran 19:20 (Saheeh International)

قَالَ كَذَٰلِكِ قَالَ رَبُّكِ هُوَ عَلَىَّ هَيِّنٌۭ ۖ وَلِنَجْعَلَهُۥٓ ءَايَةًۭ لِّلنَّاسِ وَرَحْمَةًۭ مِّنَّا ۚ وَكَانَ أَمْرًۭا مَّقْضِيًّۭا

"He said, "Thus [it will be]; your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and We will make him a sign to the people and a mercy from Us. And it is a matter [already] decreed.' "" — Quran 19:21 (Saheeh International)

"A sign to the people and a mercy from Us" — that phrase is the Quran's summary of what the virgin birth is for. The same idea appears in Surah 21, where mother and son together are called a sign:

وَٱلَّتِىٓ أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا فَنَفَخْنَا فِيهَا مِن رُّوحِنَا وَجَعَلْنَٰهَا وَٱبْنَهَآ ءَايَةًۭ لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ

"And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her [garment] through Our angel [Gabriel], and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds." — Quran 21:91 (Saheeh International)

And Surah 66 holds Mary up as a model for all believers, singling out her chastity, her faith, and her devotion:

وَمَرْيَمَ ٱبْنَتَ عِمْرَٰنَ ٱلَّتِىٓ أَحْصَنَتْ فَرْجَهَا فَنَفَخْنَا فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِنَا وَصَدَّقَتْ بِكَلِمَٰتِ رَبِّهَا وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَكَانَتْ مِنَ ٱلْقَٰنِتِينَ

"And [the example of] Mary, the daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We blew into [her garment] through Our angel, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures and was of the devoutly obedient." — Quran 66:12 (Saheeh International)

Finally, the Quran itself draws the comparison that anchors the Islamic reading of the whole event:

إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ ءَادَمَ ۖ خَلَقَهُۥ مِن تُرَابٍۢ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ

"Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. He created Him from dust; then He said to him, "Be," and he was." — Quran 3:59 (Saheeh International)

Adam came into existence with no father and no mother, yet he was a created human being. Jesus's fatherless conception, the Quran argues, belongs to the same category: a direct act of the Creator, accomplished by the command "Be."

sections.title: The Annunciation in the Gospels
sections.body:
The New Testament narrates the virginal conception in two places: Luke tells it from Mary's perspective, Matthew from Joseph's. Here is Luke's annunciation scene in full, in the World English Bible translation:

"Now in the sixth month, the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee, named Nazareth, to a virgin pledged to be married to a man whose name was Joseph, of David’s house. The virgin’s name was Mary. Having come in, the angel said to her, “Rejoice, you highly favored one! The Lord is with you. Blessed are you among women!” But when she saw him, she was greatly troubled at the saying, and considered what kind of salutation this might be. The angel said to her, “Don’t be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb, and give birth to a son, and will call his name ‘Jesus.’ He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father, David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom.” Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?” The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of God." — Luke 1:26-35 (World English Bible)

A reader who has just come from Surah 19 will feel the resemblance immediately. An angel — named here as Gabriel — comes to a virgin. She is troubled. She is told she has found favor with God and will bear a son. She asks the same question Mary asks in the Quran: "How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?" And the answer, as in the Quran, appeals to the power of God, not to any human cause.

Matthew's account centers on Joseph:

"Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly. But when he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take to yourself Mary, your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. She shall give birth to a son. You shall call his name Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.” Now all this has happened, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel”; which is, being interpreted, “God with us.”" — Matthew 1:18-23 (World English Bible)

Matthew adds two things. First, the child's mission is stated in his name: Jesus, "for it is he who shall save his people from their sins." Second, Matthew presents the conception as fulfilling the prophet Isaiah's words about a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel. (Students of the Hebrew Bible note that the Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14, almah, means a young woman, and that Matthew quotes the ancient Greek translation, which uses a word meaning virgin; interpreters have discussed that wording for centuries. It matters for how Matthew uses Isaiah, not for whether Matthew teaches the virgin birth — he plainly does.)

What does mainstream Christianity conclude from these passages? Luke's angel says the child "will be called the Son of the Most High" and "the Son of God," and Christian theology came to read those words in the strongest possible sense: the child is the eternal Son taking human flesh in Mary's womb. It is worth stating that position precisely, because it is often misstated: classical Christian theology does not claim that God physically fathered Jesus, nor that Jesus became the Son at his conception — it holds that the Son existed eternally and was made man through the virgin. The virgin birth, for Christians, is the manner of the incarnation, not its cause. That precision will matter in the comparison below.

sections.title: One Miracle, Two Conclusions
sections.body:
Set side by side, the agreements between the two accounts are remarkable. Both scriptures describe an angelic annunciation to a virgin — Luke names the angel Gabriel, and Muslim commentators have long identified the "Spirit" of Quran 19:17 as Gabriel as well, so the two traditions even agree on the messenger. Both record Mary's astonished question in nearly identical words: "How can I have a boy while no man has touched me?" in the Quran; "How can this be, seeing I am a virgin?" in Luke. Both give God's power as the only explanation. Both call Jesus the Messiah. Both exalt Mary among women — "Blessed are you among women!" in Luke; "chosen you above the women of the worlds" in the Quran.

The divergence begins at the interpretation. Luke's annunciation includes the words "will be called the Son of the Most High" and "the Son of God," and Christianity built its reading of the virgin birth around them: the miraculous conception is the moment the eternal Son entered the world as a man. Islam reads the same miracle through Quran 3:47 — "Such is Allah; He creates what He wills" — and through the Adam comparison of Quran 3:59.

The Adam argument deserves to be spelled out, because it is the Quran's own logic. If a fatherless conception proved divinity, Adam would have a stronger claim than Jesus, since Adam had neither father nor mother. Yet no one worships Adam or calls him God's literal son. A fatherless conception, by itself, proves one thing only: that God creates however He wills. The virgin birth makes Jesus a sign and a mercy — the Quran's exact words — but it does not make him God.

A Muslim reader will also note that sonship language in the Jewish scriptures was not always literal: the Hebrew Bible applies "son" language to Israel and to its kings as a mark of closeness and chosenness, not of shared divine nature. So the phrase "Son of God" in Luke's Jewish setting did not have to mean what later creeds made it mean. Christians respond that the rest of the New Testament points to a stronger, unique sonship — which shows where the argument really lies: not in the manger, but in the doctrine each community brings to it.

It is also honest to note what Christian theology itself concedes: since the Son's divinity is held to be eternal, the virgin birth is not, even for Christians, the proof of Jesus's divinity — it is its manner. The miracle itself, taken on its own terms, is fully at home in either theology. Islam's contention is that its reading requires nothing beyond what the texts describe: a creation by God's command, like Adam — an explanation both simpler and consistent with the absolute oneness of the God whom Jesus called his Lord.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
"Muslims deny the virgin birth." This is perhaps the most common misconception of all, and it is exactly backwards. The Quran teaches the virginal conception explicitly and defends Mary's chastity emphatically — she is "the one who guarded her chastity" (Quran 21:91). A Muslim who denied the virgin birth would be denying the plain text of the Quran.

"The Quran only rejects a crude idea of sonship that Christians never held." Mainstream Christian doctrine does deny any physical fatherhood on God's part, and fairness requires saying so. But the Quran's rejection is broader: it denies that God has offspring in any sense, physical or metaphysical, because attributing a son to God compromises His absolute self-sufficiency and uniqueness. The disagreement is real; it is just not the cartoon version.

"Islam diminishes Mary." The opposite is true. She is the only woman named in the Quran, a chapter of the Quran carries her name, and the Quran calls her chosen "above the women of the worlds" (Quran 3:42) and a model of devotion for believers (Quran 66:12).

"A child with no human father must be the Son of God." The Quran answers this directly with the case of Adam (Quran 3:59), who had no father and no mother. Careful Christian theology agrees that the virgin birth alone does not establish divinity — it locates Jesus's sonship in his eternal nature, not in the mode of his conception. So both traditions reject the inference here; they part ways over the separate claim of eternal sonship.

"The Quran and the Gospels disagree about who visited Mary." Luke names Gabriel; the Quran says God sent "Our Spirit," who appeared to her as "a well-proportioned man" (Quran 19:17), and Muslim commentary has overwhelmingly identified this Spirit as Gabriel. This is convergence, not contradiction.

"The Holy Spirit means the same thing in both accounts." In Christian doctrine the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity. In Islamic understanding, the Spirit associated with Jesus's conception is the angel Gabriel, a created being who carries God's command. The narrative role is the same; the theology behind the term differs — a good example of why definitions matter in comparative reading.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion: A Sign for the Worlds
sections.body:
The Quran's own summary of the virgin birth is worth repeating: God made Mary and her son "a sign for the worlds" (Quran 21:91), "a sign to the people and a mercy from Us" (Quran 19:21). In Islam, that is precisely what the miracle is — a sign. It points away from itself, toward the One who performed it.

Islam's conclusion protects two things at once. It protects the honor of Jesus and Mary: he is the Messiah, a word from God, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter; she is pure, chosen above the women of the worlds. And it protects the absolute oneness of God — in Arabic, tawhid: God is one, without partners, parents, or offspring. The same God who created Adam from dust created Jesus in a virgin's womb by the same command: "Be," and it is.

To a sincere seeker, the shared miracle is an invitation. Muslims and Christians do not need to argue about whether God acted in Mary's womb; both say He did. The remaining question is which conclusion follows from that act with the fewest assumptions: that God became a man, or that God — who "creates what He wills" (Quran 3:47) — created a man miraculously, as He had done once before at the beginning of the human story. Islam holds that the second reading keeps everything the texts affirm — the angel, the virgin, the sign, the mercy, the Messiah — while keeping worship directed where, in both scriptures, Jesus himself directed it: toward God alone.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims believe Jesus was born of a virgin?
A: Yes, without qualification. The Quran states that Mary conceived Jesus while no man had touched her (Quran 3:47; 19:20), and belief in the virgin birth has been the unanimous position of Islamic scholarship. Denying it would contradict the plain text of the Quran.

Q: Why is Mary so important in Islam?
A: Mary (Maryam) is the only woman mentioned by name in the Quran, and Surah 19 is named after her. The Quran says God chose her and purified her above the women of the worlds (Quran 3:42) and presents her as a model of chastity, faith, and devotion for believers (Quran 66:12).

Q: If Jesus had no father, doesn't that make him the Son of God?
A: The Quran answers this with the example of Adam (Quran 3:59): Adam had neither father nor mother, yet he was a created human being. A miraculous origin shows God's power to create as He wills; it does not make the created one divine. Notably, classical Christian theology also holds that Jesus's divine sonship is eternal rather than caused by the virgin birth, so both traditions agree the miracle alone does not establish divinity.

Q: Who was the spirit or angel that appeared to Mary?
A: Luke names the angel Gabriel. The Quran says God sent 'Our Spirit,' who appeared to Mary in the form of a man (Quran 19:17), and Muslim commentators have overwhelmingly identified this Spirit as Gabriel. The two accounts converge on the same messenger.

Q: Do the Quran and the Bible describe the same annunciation?
A: The parallels are striking: an angel announces a son to a virgin, she asks how this can be when no man has touched her, and the answer appeals to God's power. Both accounts also call Jesus the Messiah and exalt Mary among women. The two faiths differ mainly in the theological conclusion they draw, not in the event they describe.

Q: Does the Quran call Jesus the Messiah?
A: Yes. In Quran 3:45 the angels announce him as 'the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary,' distinguished in this world and the Hereafter. Islam affirms Jesus as the Messiah sent to Israel while understanding that title as a mark of his mission, not of divinity.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The books below treat the virgin birth and the wider place of Jesus and Mary in Islam and Christianity. They range from accessible introductions to detailed scholarship, and they include Christian as well as Muslim authors so that each tradition can be heard in its own voice.

Geoffrey Parrinder — Jesus in the Qur'an. A respectful, widely used survey by a Christian scholar of religion covering the Quranic passages about Jesus and Mary, including the annunciation narratives.

Tarif Khalidi — The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature. A collection showing how deeply Jesus is loved and quoted in the Islamic tradition beyond the Quran itself.

Mustafa Akyol — The Islamic Jesus. An accessible modern discussion of what the Quran says about Jesus and Mary and how it relates to Jewish and Christian views.

Raymond E. Brown — The Birth of the Messiah. A classic, detailed Christian scholarly commentary on the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke; useful for seeing how Christian scholarship itself reads these chapters.

Gabriel Said Reynolds — The Qur'an and the Bible: Text and Commentary. A verse-by-verse academic resource comparing Quranic passages with their biblical parallels, including the Mary narratives.

title: The Second Coming of Jesus
subtitle: Both faiths await his return — what each expects him to do reveals everything
summary: Islam and Christianity both teach that Jesus is alive with God and will return before the end of the world — one of the deepest agreements between the two faiths. The Quran ties Jesus to “the Hour” and Muslim narrations describe his descent as a just ruler, while the New Testament promises that he will come back the way he ascended. Both traditions insist that no one knows when. The decisive difference is what he returns to do: Christianity awaits him as divine judge, Islam as God’s human servant and Messiah — and that difference distills the whole question of who Jesus is.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body:
Islam and Christianity disagree about many things concerning Jesus, but on one striking point they agree: both teach that he is alive with God and will return before the end of the world. The Quran calls Jesus a matter of “knowledge of the Hour,” which classical commentators overwhelmingly understood to mean that his return will signal that the end is near, and well-known Muslim narrations describe him descending to rule with justice.

The New Testament promises that “this Jesus” will come back the same way he was seen going, and historic Christian creeds affirm that he will come again to judge the living and the dead. Both traditions also insist, in their own scriptures, that no one knows when.

This article sets out each tradition’s expectation from its own sources, shows how much they share, and then asks what the one great difference — whether he returns as God’s servant or as God — reveals about the deeper question of who Jesus is.

sections.title: The Agreement Nobody Expects
sections.body:
Ask a devout Christian what she is waiting for, and somewhere near the top of the list will be the return of Jesus. Ask a devout Muslim the same question, and you may be surprised to hear the same answer.

The disagreement between Islam and Christianity about Jesus is real and serious, and this library does not soften it. But it sits alongside an agreement that startles many people on both sides: the world’s two largest religions both teach that Jesus, the son of Mary, is alive with God and will return before the end of history. No other figure is awaited by so much of humanity.

This article lays out what each tradition actually teaches about that return, from its own sources. Following this library’s method, scripture is quoted exactly as published translations render it, classical interpretation is labelled as interpretation, and well-known Muslim narrations are described rather than quoted. The aim is that a Christian reader should recognize her own belief in the description of it, and a Muslim reader his — and that both should see clearly where, and why, the two expectations part ways.

sections.title: The Question Behind the Question
sections.body:
The question this article asks is not “will Jesus return?” On that, mainstream Islam and mainstream Christianity answer yes together.

The real questions lie one layer down. What does the Quran itself say, and what comes from hadith — the recorded narrations of the Prophet Muhammad’s teachings — and from classical commentary? What did Jesus’ own disciples expect, according to the New Testament? And where do the two pictures overlap? As we will see, they overlap far more than most people on either side assume.

Then comes the decisive question: when he returns, what will he come to do? Will he come as the servant and prophet of God, or as God coming to judge the world? The answer each tradition gives is a compressed summary of everything it believes about who Jesus is. That is why a chapter about the end of the story turns out to be a chapter about the heart of it.

sections.title: Two Communities, One Long Wait
sections.body:
The expectation of Jesus’ return is as old as Christianity itself. The letters of Paul, commonly dated to around the middle of the first century and among the earliest Christian documents we possess, already comfort believers with the promise that the Lord will come. The Gospels record Jesus speaking at length about the coming of “the Son of Man,” and the book of Acts opens with the disciples being promised that he will come back. By the fourth century the mainstream churches had fixed the expectation into their creeds: Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. Christians have disagreed among themselves about the surrounding details — whether there will be a visible thousand-year reign, whether believers will be taken up before a final tribulation — but the core conviction of a real, personal return has been constant across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christianity.

The Muslim expectation is nearly as old as Islam. The Quran, delivered in the early seventh century, ties Jesus to “the Hour” — its name for the end of the world — and Muslim scholars from the earliest generations transmitted narrations describing his descent in the last days. Belief in the return of Jesus became a standard article of mainstream Sunni faith; classical creedal texts, such as the widely memorized statement of faith by the Egyptian scholar al-Tahawi, include the descent of Jesus among the signs of the Hour. Shia Islam likewise awaits his return alongside the Mahdi, a righteous leader expected at the end of time.

One further historical parallel is worth noticing. Both communities have repeatedly produced confident date-setters, and both communities’ scholars have repeatedly rebuked them — because both scriptures, as we will see, place the timing of the end beyond human knowledge.

sections.title: What the Quran Says
sections.body:
The Quran speaks of Jesus’ connection to the end of the world in a handful of brief, weighty verses. In Surah Az-Zukhruf, at the close of a passage about him, God says:

وَإِنَّهُۥ لَعِلْمٌۭ لِّلسَّاعَةِ فَلَا تَمْتَرُنَّ بِهَا وَٱتَّبِعُونِ ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٌۭ مُّسْتَقِيمٌۭ

“And indeed, Jesus will be [a sign for] knowledge of the Hour, so be not in doubt of it, and follow Me. This is a straight path.” (Quran 43:61)

A word about translation is owed here. The Arabic says literally “and indeed he” — or, on another reading of the pronoun, “it” — “is knowledge of the Hour.” The bracketed words “Jesus” and “a sign for” are the translators’ clarification, following the reading that dominated classical Quran commentary: the pronoun refers to Jesus, and his return to earth will be one of the great signs by which people will know the Hour has drawn near. A minority of commentators took the pronoun to refer to the Quran itself. This library flags such matters honestly: the connection of this verse to Jesus’ return is early, dominant, and mainstream — and it is interpretation.

A second verse appears in Surah An-Nisaa, immediately after the Quran’s famous denial that Jesus was killed on the cross and its statement that God raised him to Himself:

وَإِن مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا لَيُؤْمِنَنَّ بِهِۦ قَبْلَ مَوْتِهِۦ ۖ وَيَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ يَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ شَهِيدًۭا

“And there is none from the People of the Scripture but that he will surely believe in Jesus before his death. And on the Day of Resurrection he will be against them a witness.” (Quran 4:159)

Here too the translators have made an interpretive choice visible: the Arabic says “believe in him,” and “Jesus” is the translators’ identification of the pronoun. Classical commentary preserves two main readings of “before his death.” On one, it means the death of each Person of the Book: before dying, every such soul glimpses the truth about Jesus, too late to act on it. On the other reading — the one tied most naturally to the raising mentioned in the verses just before — it means the death of Jesus himself: he did not die on the cross, he will return, and before his eventual death the People of the Scripture will come to believe in him as he truly is. Both readings are old; the second became an anchor for the doctrine of his return. Either way, the verse’s ending is unambiguous: on the Day of Resurrection, Jesus will stand as a witness concerning those who received scripture before.

The foundation beneath both verses is what God says to Jesus in Surah Aal-i-Imraan:

إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَىٰٓ إِنِّى مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَىَّ وَمُطَهِّرُكَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ وَجَاعِلُ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّبَعُوكَ فَوْقَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۖ ثُمَّ إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ فَأَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ

“[Mention] when Allah said, "O Jesus, indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself and purify you from those who disbelieve and make those who follow you [in submission to Allah alone] superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ.” (Quran 3:55)

Jesus, in the Quran, was not killed. God took him and raised him to Himself. A man who is alive with God can return — and, on the mainstream Muslim understanding, will.

What the Quran states briefly, the hadith literature fills out. Narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — the two most rigorously authenticated Sunni collections — describe the son of Mary descending among the Muslims in the last days, ruling with justice, and breaking the cross: a vivid image classically understood as his personal correction of beliefs that grew up around him after he was raised. Other well-known narrations describe him confronting and defeating the false messiah (al-Masih ad-Dajjal, a great deceiver expected before the end), an era of peace and plenty following his victory, and, in some reports, his living out his remaining years on earth and dying as every human being dies. Following this library’s rules, these narrations are described here rather than quoted; readers will find them in the standard collections in the chapters on the tribulations and the signs of the Hour. Their standing should not be understated: many classical hadith specialists judged the reports of Jesus’ descent to be so numerously transmitted that the expectation belongs to settled mainstream doctrine, not folklore.

sections.title: What the New Testament Says
sections.body:
The New Testament’s expectation begins at the moment Jesus leaves. The book of Acts describes the disciples watching him ascend, and two men in white addressing them:

“who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”” (Acts 1:11, World English Bible)

The promise is concrete: the same Jesus, returning the same way — personally and visibly.

The Gospels place the fullest teaching about that return on Jesus’ own lips, in the discourse he gave on the Mount of Olives. Matthew records:

“and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory.” (Matthew 24:30)

The phrase “Son of Man” — Jesus’ habitual way of referring to himself — echoes a vision in the book of Daniel of one like a son of man brought on the clouds before God. Christians read Matthew 24 as Jesus’ promise that he himself will appear in glory at the end of the age, and the historic creeds state the purpose: he will come again to judge the living and the dead. For mainstream Christianity — Catholic, Orthodox, and most Protestant churches — this is a single, visible, bodily return. Some Protestant traditions add further structure around it, such as a rapture of believers or a literal thousand-year reign, and Christians debate these details among themselves; the return itself is common ground.

Then comes a verse that has echoed through this discussion for two thousand years. Asked when these things would come to pass, Jesus answers — in Mark’s Gospel:

“But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.” (Mark 13:32)

Matthew’s Gospel carries the same teaching:

“But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only.” (Matthew 24:36)

Attentive readers will notice that the translation of Matthew quoted here lacks the words “nor the Son” found in Mark. Ancient manuscripts of Matthew differ over whether the phrase appears, which is why translations vary; its presence in Mark is not in dispute.

Two things stand out in these verses. First, the hour is unknowable, and Jesus shuts the door on the calculating spirit — a prohibition his followers have honored unevenly. Second, and remarkably, the Son himself is placed among those who do not know. Christians and Muslims read that second point very differently, as the next section explains.

sections.title: Shared Waiting, Different Roles
sections.body:
Set side by side, the two expectations agree on far more than either community usually realizes.

Both await a real, personal return — not a metaphor, not a movement, but the man himself. Acts promises that “this Jesus” will “come back in the same way” he was seen going; Muslim narrations describe a bodily descent. Both tie his return to the end of history: on the dominant classical reading the Quran makes him “knowledge of the Hour,” and Matthew places his coming at the climax of the age. Both declare the timing sealed — “of that day or that hour no one knows,” says Jesus in Mark, and the Quran consistently places knowledge of the Hour with God alone. And both therefore command the same posture: not calculation but readiness. Live now as you would wish to be found living then.

The parting of ways is over the role of the one who returns. In Christian teaching, the returning Jesus comes “with power and great glory” as divine judge; the creeds say he will judge the living and the dead, which makes his return the return of God incarnate to close the books of history. In Muslim teaching, the returning Jesus comes as what Islam holds he always was: the Messiah, a human servant and messenger of God. He will defeat deception, establish justice, restore the pure worship of the One God — and then he will die, as every human being dies, to be raised on the Last Day with everyone else. Judgment on that Day belongs to God alone.

The Quran’s own wording draws this line finely. In 3:55 God tells Jesus, “Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ” — God is the judge, and the centuries-long dispute about Jesus is among the things He will judge. And in 4:159 Jesus appears on the Day of Resurrection not as the court but as “a witness.” Testimony is given before a judge, not by one.

This is where Mark 13:32 becomes more than a footnote. If the Son does not know the day or the hour, Muslims ask, in what sense is he the all-knowing God? Christian theology has a considered answer — that Christ has two natures, divine and human, and spoke here from the human nature, whose knowledge was limited — and fairness requires saying that this answer is ancient and carefully worked out. But fairness also permits the Muslim reply: the two-natures reading is required by the doctrine, not by the sentence. Taken on its own terms, the verse describes exactly what Islam says Jesus is — an honored creature whose knowledge, like his life, is granted by God and bounded by God.

And that is what the difference finally reveals. Eschatology — the doctrine of last things — is theology in miniature. Tell someone what you expect Jesus to do when he returns, and you have told them who you believe he is. Christianity awaits its God; Islam awaits God’s servant. Everything else the two traditions dispute about Jesus is folded inside that sentence.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
“The second coming is a Christian idea that Muslims borrowed.” The Muslim expectation rests on the Quran’s own verses and on narrations transmitted from Islam’s earliest generations, and it entered the classical creeds long before modern polemics between the two communities. A Muslim would also invert the premise: on the Islamic account both expectations descend from the same source — authentic prophetic teaching — so agreement is not borrowing but shared inheritance.

“The Quran describes the second coming in vivid detail.” It does not, and honesty about this strengthens rather than weakens the Muslim case. The Quran’s references — 43:61 and 4:159 above — are brief, and their application to the return is classical interpretation: dominant, early, but interpretation. The vivid details — the descent, the false messiah, the just rule — come from hadith. This article labels each layer as what it is.

“If Jesus returns, he must bring a new revelation, contradicting Islam’s belief that Muhammad is the final prophet.” Mainstream Muslim scholarship holds the opposite. Jesus returns not to found anything but to complete his own interrupted human span and to rule by the final revelation already given. He comes back as a prophet God already sent, not as a new one, so his return leaves the finality of Muhammad’s prophethood intact.

“Muslims who await Jesus are half-worshipping him.” Islam gives Jesus titles it gives no one else — the Messiah, a word from God, born of a virgin — and awaits his return, yet directs every act of worship to God alone. Reverence and worship are different categories; collapsing the two is precisely the error Islam believes later generations made about Jesus.

“The signs are all here; the date can be worked out.” Both traditions bar that door with their own scripture. “But of that day or that hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Mark 13:32); and in the Quran, knowledge of the Hour rests with God — Jesus is its sign, not its schedule.

sections.title: The Islamic Conclusion
sections.body:
Seen from inside Islam, the return of Jesus is God’s public vindication of a wronged prophet.

He was not abandoned to a criminal’s death; God said to him, “indeed I will take you and raise you to Myself” (Quran 3:55). He was neither the failure his enemies proclaimed nor the deity his later admirers proclaimed; in the Muslim expectation he will return to correct both errors in person — the narrations’ image of him breaking the cross is classically read as his own hand dismantling the theology built in his absence. And on its classical reading, 4:159 holds out an extraordinary promise: before his death, the People of the Scripture will at last believe in him as he truly is — one community gathered around one prophet, worshipping the One God whom he worshipped.

Then he will die. That quiet ending may be the most Islamic sentence in the whole expectation. Jesus’ story finishes not on a throne of universal judgment but in the earth, like Abraham, like Moses, like Muhammad — a complete human life, resumed and completed, with judgment left where the Quran leaves it: “Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that in which you used to differ” (Quran 3:55).

To the Christian reader who loves Jesus and awaits him: that love and that waiting are not what Islam disputes. Islam’s invitation is to await him as — in the Muslim account — he would ask to be awaited: as the servant and Messiah of the One God, whose own recorded words in the Gospels place the knowledge of the hour with the Father alone. The Quran’s verse about him ends by addressing all of us: “so be not in doubt of it, and follow Me. This is a straight path” (Quran 43:61).

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims really believe Jesus will return?
A: Yes. It is mainstream doctrine in both Sunni and Shia Islam, grounded in Quranic verses such as 43:61 and 4:159 as classically interpreted, and in numerous narrations in the most authenticated hadith collections.

Q: Does the Quran state the second coming explicitly?
A: The Quran’s references are brief. It calls Jesus “knowledge of the Hour” (43:61) and speaks of the People of the Scripture believing in him “before his death” (4:159); reading these as his return is the dominant classical interpretation, and the detailed picture comes from hadith. This article labels each layer honestly.

Q: Will Jesus bring a new religion or a new scripture when he returns?
A: No. Mainstream Muslim teaching holds that he returns as a prophet God already sent, ruling by the final revelation rather than bringing a new one — which is why his return does not conflict with Muhammad being the final prophet.

Q: What is the Dajjal?
A: Al-Masih ad-Dajjal, often rendered “the false messiah,” is a great deceiver whom Muslim narrations expect before the end and whom Jesus is expected to defeat. Christians will recognize a broad parallel in their own tradition’s expectation of a final deceiver often called the antichrist.

Q: Do all Christians expect the same sequence of end-time events?
A: No. The core conviction — a real, visible return of Christ as judge — is shared across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Christianity, but details such as a rapture or a literal millennium are debated among Christians themselves.

Q: Can anyone calculate when Jesus will return?
A: Both traditions say no. Jesus in the Gospels says no one knows that day or hour, and the Quran places knowledge of the Hour with God alone. Both traditions call for readiness, not arithmetic.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The scripture quoted in this article comes from the Saheeh International translation of the Quran (via api.alquran.cloud, with the Uthmani Arabic text) and the World English Bible (via bible-api.com). Muslim narrations were described, not quoted, in line with this library’s sourcing rules; readers can locate them in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim in the chapters on tribulations and the signs of the Hour.

For readers who want to go deeper, the works listed below approach Jesus in Islam from several angles: a Christian scholar’s survey of the Quranic material, an anthology of how Muslim civilization remembered Jesus, a Muslim argument about his status, and a secular historian’s reconstruction of the earliest Christian expectation of the end. None of them is required to accept this article’s conclusions; each helps test them.

title: The Day of Judgment
subtitle: Resurrection, the Scale, and the Books of Deeds in the Quran and the Bible
summary: Islam and Christianity both teach that history ends in a bodily resurrection and a final judgment before God, where every soul's deeds are examined and nothing is hidden. The Quran pictures this Day of Resurrection through a scale weighing even an atom's weight of good or evil and a record of deeds placed in each person's hand. The Bible pictures Jesus separating the nations like a shepherd separating sheep from goats, with books of deeds opened before God's throne. This article compares both pictures in detail, showing what the two faiths share and where they differ over who judges and how mercy is granted.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
Islam and Christianity agree on something enormous: this life is not the end of the story. Both faiths teach that a day is coming when every person who has ever lived will be raised from death, stand before God, and answer for how they lived.

The Quran calls this event the Day of Resurrection, or simply "That Day." It pictures a moment when even the smallest deed, as small as a single atom, is weighed on a scale of perfect justice and recorded in a book each person receives in their own hand. The New Testament pictures Jesus returning in glory to gather all nations before him, separating people the way a shepherd separates sheep from goats, while books recording every deed are opened before God's throne.

This article compares what each scripture actually says: the scattering of deeds and the scale of justice in the Quran, and the sheep and goats, the opened books, and the judgment seat of Christ in the New Testament. It closes by asking why Islam frames that day as both perfectly just and directly merciful, without needing anyone else to stand in a person's place.

sections.title: Introduction: A Day Neither Faith Lets You Forget
sections.body:
A shared conviction runs through mosque sermons and church sermons alike: what you do in this life matters forever, because a day of reckoning is coming. In English this is called the Day of Judgment, and it is one of the few doctrines where Islam and Christianity stand closer to each other than either does to many other worldviews.

Both scriptures reject two comforting but very different ideas: that death simply ends everything, and that a person may do as they wish because no final account will ever be settled. Instead, both describe a specific future event: the resurrection of the dead, followed by a judgment before God in which nothing is hidden and nothing is forgotten.

For someone new to either faith, this doctrine often lands as the most serious part of the religion. It turns everyday choices - honesty, generosity, cruelty, neglect - into matters of eternal consequence.

sections.title: The Question This Article Answers
sections.body:
The question at the center of this article is: how does the Quran describe the Day of Judgment, how does the Bible describe it, and what do the similarities and differences reveal about how each faith understands justice, mercy, and mediation between the sinner and God?

Both scriptures agree on the basic architecture of the event: a bodily resurrection, a gathering of all humanity before God, an examination of deeds symbolized by scales in the Quran and opened books in the Bible, and a permanent separation into two final destinies.

Where the two traditions differ is in the mechanics of the verdict: what exactly is weighed, who stands between the sinner and God, and how forgiveness reaches an imperfect human being. The Quran presents direct, personal accountability before God alone. The Bible presents Jesus Christ seated on the throne of judgment, with much of historic Christian theology holding that a believer's standing before that throne depends on their relationship to Christ as well as their deeds.

sections.title: Resurrection and Reckoning Before and After Muhammad
sections.body:
Belief in bodily resurrection and a final moral reckoning was not universal in the ancient world. Many ancient societies imagined the dead continuing in a shadowy existence, with little connection between how a person lived and what happened afterward. Against that backdrop, both the biblical and Quranic pictures of a coming Day of Judgment stand out as a far more morally charged vision of the afterlife.

The New Testament assumes bodily resurrection and final judgment as settled convictions. The book of Acts records that this had already become a live debate among Jewish groups in the first century, some affirming a future resurrection and some denying it. The Gospels and letters of the New Testament consistently teach that Jesus himself will return to judge the living and the dead.

The Quran was revealed in seventh-century Arabia, where many of the Prophet Muhammad's pagan contemporaries in Mecca found bodily resurrection almost absurd, doubting that decayed bones could ever be raised again. Because of that skepticism, many of the Quran's earliest revealed chapters, including the short Surah al-Zalzalah quoted below, insist on the reality, certainty, and exact fairness of the coming Day. For early Muslims, as for early Christians, the Day of Judgment was never a peripheral idea.

sections.title: The Day of Judgment in the Quran
sections.body:
The Quran's short ninety-ninth chapter, Surah al-Zalzalah, "The Earthquake," opens with the world convulsing at the end of time, the earth shaking and giving up what is inside it. Out of that upheaval comes a description of what happens to human beings:

يَوْمَئِذٍۢ يَصْدُرُ ٱلنَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًۭا لِّيُرَوْا۟ أَعْمَٰلَهُمْ

"That Day, the people will depart separated [into categories] to be shown [the result of] their deeds." (Quran 99:6)

People do not face judgment as an undifferentiated crowd; they leave already sorted, according to their deeds, into distinct outcomes. The next two verses make the standard of that sorting startlingly precise:

فَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًۭا يَرَهُۥ

"So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it," (Quran 99:7)

وَمَن يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍۢ شَرًّۭا يَرَهُۥ

"And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it." (Quran 99:8)

Nothing is too small to count: not a private kindness no one else noticed, and not a small cruelty a person hoped had been forgotten.

This precision is not left abstract; the Quran gives it a concrete image, the scale (mizan). In Surah al-Anbiya, "The Prophets," God says:

وَنَضَعُ ٱلْمَوَٰزِينَ ٱلْقِسْطَ لِيَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ فَلَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌۭ شَيْـًۭٔا ۖ وَإِن كَانَ مِثْقَالَ حَبَّةٍۢ مِّنْ خَرْدَلٍ أَتَيْنَا بِهَا ۗ وَكَفَىٰ بِنَا حَٰسِبِينَ

"And We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be treated unjustly at all. And if there is [even] the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as accountant." (Quran 21:47)

The mustard seed, like the atom of the earlier verses, says no unit of good or evil is too small to register. The verse names God directly as the Accountant, needing no witness to correct His count.

Alongside the scale, the Quran describes a written record (kitab) handed to each person individually. Surah al-Inshiqaq, "The Splitting Open," describes the reception of that record:

فَأَمَّا مَنْ أُوتِىَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِيَمِينِهِۦ

"Then as for he who is given his record in his right hand," (Quran 84:7)

فَسَوْفَ يُحَاسَبُ حِسَابًۭا يَسِيرًۭا

"He will be judged with an easy account" (Quran 84:8)

Receiving the record in the right hand is a sign, throughout the Quran, of a life that met God's approval, and the reckoning that follows is gentle rather than crushing. The same passage describes a different reception for those whose record testifies against them. Together, the scale and the record give Quranic eschatology its shape: an individual, exact accounting before a Judge who needs no one else to establish the truth.

The record in the right hand shows that the accounting is individual; a separate verse states just as directly that the guilt behind a bad record cannot be shifted onto someone else. Surah al-Isra, "The Night Journey," says:

مَّنِ ٱهْتَدَىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَهْتَدِى لِنَفْسِهِۦ ۖ وَمَن ضَلَّ فَإِنَّمَا يَضِلُّ عَلَيْهَا ۚ وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌۭ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ ۗ وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِينَ حَتَّىٰ نَبْعَثَ رَسُولًۭا

"Whoever is guided is only guided for [the benefit of] his soul. And whoever errs only errs against it. And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And never would We punish until We sent a messenger." (Quran 17:15)

This, rather than the description of the record in the right hand, is the Quran's explicit statement that one soul's guilt is never transferred to or borne by another - a claim the conclusion below returns to directly.

sections.title: The Day of Judgment in the Bible
sections.body:
The New Testament's clearest single picture of the final judgment comes in Jesus's own words in the Gospel of Matthew. Describing his own return, Jesus says:

"But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.

Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats." (Matthew 25:31-32)

In the parable that follows, the sheep and goats are separated according to how they treated the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, and the imprisoned - a standard of practical mercy many readers, Christian and Muslim alike, recognize as close to the Quran's own commands to feed the poor and care for the orphan.

The book of Revelation describes the same event from a different angle, using courtroom imagery rather than a pasture:

"I saw the dead, the great and the small, standing before the throne, and they opened books. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. The dead were judged out of the things which were written in the books, according to their works." (Revelation 20:12)

Here the record-keeping motif of the Quran's scale and written record reappears in similar form: books opened before the divine throne, containing the deeds of "the great and the small" alike, judged "according to their works." A further book, the book of life, is named alongside the books of deeds, tying the verdict to belonging as well as behavior.

The apostle Paul reinforces the same expectation in two of his letters. To the Corinthians he writes:

"For we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ; that each one may receive the things in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad." (2 Corinthians 5:10)

And to the Romans, warning believers against judging one another prematurely, he states the same principle even more simply:

"So then each one of us will give account of himself to God." (Romans 14:12)

Together, these passages describe a final judgment that is universal, based on deeds, and presided over by Christ, named as the one seated on the throne of judgment. Mainstream Christian theology holds that Jesus is not only the coming Judge but, in this life, the believer's advocate and the ground of their acquittal, so the verdict a Christian expects is shaped by their relationship to Christ as much as by an independent tally of deeds. Christian traditions differ on how faith and works relate to that verdict, but all agree no one is exempt from standing before that throne.

sections.title: What the Two Pictures Share, and Where They Part
sections.body:
Set the two pictures side by side, and the agreement is striking before the disagreement even comes into view. Both scriptures teach a literal, bodily resurrection - not a vague survival of the soul, but people standing before God. Both teach a judgment that is total and universal: the Quran's "whoever does an atom's weight" (Quran 99:7-8) and Revelation's "the dead, the great and the small" (Revelation 20:12) refuse to let anyone imagine themselves too insignificant, or too important, to be judged. Both use the image of a written record: the Quran's book placed in the hand (Quran 84:7), and Revelation's books opened before the throne (Revelation 20:12). Both insist that deeds form part of the evidence: "according to what he has done" (2 Corinthians 5:10) parallels "to be shown [the result of] their deeds" (Quran 99:6) almost precisely. And both name a moment of separation into two final groups, whether Matthew's sheep and goats (Matthew 25:32) or the Quran's people "departing separated [into categories]" (Quran 99:6).

The difference that matters most is the identity of the judge. In the Quran, God alone judges and keeps account, described directly as "sufficient... as accountant" (Quran 21:47), with no figure standing between the individual and God as the ground of acquittal. The Quran itself makes this conditional character of intercession explicit; in Ayat al-Kursi, God asks, "Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?" (Quran 2:255). Any intercession granted to the Prophet is therefore not an independent ground of acquittal but something that operates only within limits God sets, and it does not change the deeds actually weighed. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ is seated on "the throne of his glory" (Matthew 25:31) and before his "judgment seat" all must appear (2 Corinthians 5:10); Christ is understood not only as judge but as the means by which a believer's sins are covered, a role Islam does not accept, since it holds each soul answers directly for itself before God.

A second difference is emphasis: the Quran's scale gives Islamic eschatology an almost mathematical precision, while the biblical picture leans more on shepherding imagery.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
First: "Islam teaches that a person earns Paradise purely by good deeds, with no room for mercy." This is a mistaken caricature. Narrations in the major hadith collections describe the Prophet Muhammad teaching that no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, but only by God's mercy; the weighing of deeds (Quran 21:47, 99:7-8) establishes perfect justice, but entry into Paradise depends on mercy responding to faith and sincere effort, not deeds as a purchase price.

Second: "Christianity teaches that a believer's deeds do not matter at the final judgment, since salvation is by faith alone." This oversimplifies. The passages quoted above - "each one will give account of himself to God" (Romans 14:12), judgment "according to what he has done, whether good or bad" (2 Corinthians 5:10), and "judged... according to their works" (Revelation 20:12) - show that mainstream Christian teaching holds every believer accountable for their deeds. Theologians differ on how that fits with justification by faith, but none deny that works are examined.

Third: "The Quran only cares about deeds, and the Bible only cares about who Christ is." Both foreground deeds heavily - the Quran's atom's weight of good or evil (Quran 99:7-8) and the Bible's books "according to their works" (Revelation 20:12). The real dividing line is whether a mediating figure stands between the sinner and the verdict, not whether deeds matter.

Fourth, some assume the sheep-and-goats parable is only about correct doctrine. In the fuller parable, the criterion Jesus names is mercy shown to the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, and the imprisoned - close to the Quran's own commands to feed the poor and care for the orphan and the traveler.

sections.title: Conclusion: A Just and Merciful Reckoning, With No One Bearing Another's Burden
sections.body:
From an Islamic point of view, the Quran's picture of the Day of Judgment answers a question every serious person eventually asks: if life so often feels unfair, is there a court where the account will finally, exactly be set right? The Quran's answer is yes, and it is emphatic about the precision of that court. Nothing is too small to matter - not an atom's weight of good, not an atom's weight of evil (Quran 99:7-8) - and no soul will be wronged even by the weight of a mustard seed (Quran 21:47).

Muslims find something theologically satisfying in the directness of this picture. Each person stands before God carrying their own record (Quran 84:7), and the Quran states the deeper principle behind that record explicitly: "no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" (Quran 17:15). No one else's righteousness covers their failures, and no one else's guilt is punished in their place. God alone is sufficient as the Accountant (Quran 21:47) - not because Islam denies that mercy is real, but because it holds that mercy does not require an intermediary's suffering to be activated. A repentant sinner is forgiven because God chooses to forgive, directly, the same God who set the scale.

This is where the Islamic case is made most confidently: a Day of Judgment in which perfect justice and perfect mercy sit together without needing a mediator who bears a penalty meant for someone else. Christians rightly cherish their own scripture's insistence that Christ will judge the nations and that every person will give account of themselves. Islam asks readers to consider whether that same seriousness about accountability points most naturally toward a Judge who deals with each soul directly, without needing anyone else to stand in the accused's place.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do Muslims and Christians actually agree that a Day of Judgment is coming?
A: Yes. Both scriptures teach a bodily resurrection of the dead, a universal judgment before God, and a final separation between two ultimate destinies.

Q: What is the "scale" (mizan) mentioned in the Quran?
A: The mizan is the Quran's image of a scale of justice on which every deed is weighed. Quran 21:47 says God places these "scales of justice" so precisely that "no soul will be treated unjustly at all," down to a mustard seed.

Q: Does the Bible teach that people are judged by their good and bad deeds?
A: Yes. Revelation 20:12, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and Romans 14:12 all describe judgment based on a person's actual deeds - "according to what he has done, whether good or bad" - not merely stated beliefs.

Q: Who acts as judge on the Day of Judgment in each faith?
A: In the Quran, God alone judges, sufficient "as accountant" (Quran 21:47). In the New Testament, Jesus Christ returns "in his glory" to judge all nations (Matthew 25:31-32), and before his "judgment seat" everyone must appear (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Q: What is the "book" or "record" of deeds?
A: Both scriptures use a written record of a person's life. The Quran describes a record given into the right or left hand (Quran 84:7); Revelation 20:12 describes books opened before God's throne, alongside a separate "book of life."

Q: Does Islam believe in intercession on the Day of Judgment?
A: Many Islamic scholars affirm that intercession (shafa'ah) by the Prophet Muhammad on behalf of believers will occur, but the Quran ties any such intercession strictly to God's own permission - "Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?" (Quran 2:255) - so it is read as an added mercy, not a substitute payment that changes the deeds weighed on the scale.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
The following works are offered as further reading, listed for orientation rather than as sources for specific claims in this article.

Jane I. Smith and Yvonne Y. Haddad — The Islamic Understanding of Death and Resurrection: a study of Islamic eschatology drawing on the Quran, hadith, and classical commentary.

Seyyed Hossein Nasr (general editor) — The Study Quran: A New Translation and Commentary: an English translation with commentary on the Quran's passages about resurrection and judgment.

N.T. Wright — Surprised by Hope: a widely read study of the Christian doctrine of resurrection and final judgment.

Jerry L. Walls (editor) — The Oxford Handbook of Eschatology: a scholarly survey of afterlife beliefs across religious traditions, including Islam and Christianity.

John L. Esposito — Islam: The Straight Path: a standard introductory overview of Islamic belief and practice.

title: The Final Message
subtitle: Why Islam holds that Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets, and how that claim relates to the Christian conviction that God's word culminated in Christ
