In response, many Islamic scholars reinterpret the term as metaphorical or symbolic (a token, non-injurious gesture signaling final disapproval rather than a beating), point to hadith reports restricting any such act to something that leaves no mark and forbids striking the face, and situate it as the last of a three-stage de-escalation sequence (advise, separate, then this minimal step) rather than a license for punishment; a minority of scholars, classical and modern, argue the root can mean "to separate from" rather than to strike at all, while others candidly acknowledge that some historical practice and jurisprudence did permit corporal correction and that reformist and conservative scholars remain divided on how far reinterpretation can go. The interpretive diversity on this verse alone spans centuries of Islamic jurisprudence, and it remains among the passages most frequently raised by critics of the Quran's treatment of women. Beyond guardianship within an ongoing marriage, the Quran also sets out specific legal provisions for women navigating divorce. Quran 65:4 specifies the waiting period (idda) required before a divorce becomes final: three months for women who no longer menstruate or have not yet begun menstruating (where pregnancy status is uncertain), and, for pregnant women, until they give birth. Read alongside the surrounding verses of Surah At-Talaaq, this waiting period obligates the husband to continue housing and financially supporting the wife during this time, and it serves practical functions recognized by classical and modern jurists alike: establishing legal certainty about paternity and lineage should the wife be pregnant, and allowing a window for reconciliation before the separation is final. Some scholars and critics note that this framework, whatever its protective intent, still places the burden of proof and waiting on the woman rather than the man, reflecting the same asymmetrical marital structure discussed above.

sections.title: Quranic Partnership and Mutual Care
sections.body: Beyond the guardianship framework, the Quran establishes mutual care and alliance between believing men and women. Surah At-Tawba 9:71 describes believers—both male and female—as awliya (allies or protectors) of one another, jointly commanding good and forbidding evil, establishing prayer, giving charity, and obeying Allah. This verse emphasizes reciprocal moral and spiritual responsibility without hierarchy. Surah Al-Ahzaab 33:35 takes this further by listing virtues for both men and women in parallel language—Muslim men and women, believing men and believing women, obedient men and obedient women—affirming that spiritual achievement is gender-inclusive. Women are not subsumed under male categories but addressed directly and equally in their spiritual aspirations. Surah Aal-i-Imraan 3:195 reassures all believers that God will never waste their effort, explicitly emphasizing "whether male or female," signaling that gender does not diminish the value of one's service to God. Together, these verses frame Islamic women as active moral agents, co-builders of the believing community, and directly accountable to God for their spiritual lives.

sections.title: Biblical Submission, Headship, and Mutuality
sections.body:
Pauline letters in the New Testament, particularly Ephesians and Colossians, establish complementarian structures in household relationships. Ephesians 5:22-25 instructs wives to be subject to their husbands and describes the husband as the head of the wife, using the analogy of Christ and the church. 1 Corinthians 11:3 articulates a hierarchical structure: the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. 1 Peter 3:1-7 similarly directs wives to be in subjection to their husbands, with instructions on inner beauty and spiritual quietness. Titus 2:3-5 directs older women to train younger wives to love husbands and children, with submission to husbands listed as a virtue. Critics argue that hierarchical headship language—particularly the framing of the husband as "head" and the description of the wife as "the weaker vessel" in 1 Peter 3:7—establishes a structural subordination that is incompatible with equal dignity, regardless of how practitioners intend to exercise it. However, the complementarian structure in these texts is consistently qualified by reciprocal obligations. Ephesians immediately follows its submission instruction with a command to husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it—a sacrificial, self-giving love that mirrors the wife's submission. 1 Peter 3:7 commands husbands to live with their wives "according to knowledge," giving honor to women as fellow heirs of grace, with prayer consequences tied to how men treat their wives. This reciprocal framework distinguishes these texts from assertions of one-sided male authority; the headship is contextualized within mutual honor and self-sacrificial love.

Beyond household submission, two further Pauline texts go further still by restricting women's teaching authority and public speech in the gathered church, and these are among the most contested passages in the entire debate over women's roles. 1 Timothy 2:11-15 states plainly, "I don’t permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness," grounding the restriction in the creation order ("Adam was first formed, then Eve") and in Eve's deception in the garden, and adding the difficult claim that a woman "will be saved through her childbearing." 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 similarly instructs that "the wives be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking... it is shameful for a wife to be talking in the assembly." Critics press this objection at full strength: unlike the reciprocal household codes above, these texts categorically bar women from teaching or exercising authority over men and tie that exclusion to Eve's culpability in the Fall—a rationale that, on its face, extends a punitive judgment onto all women rather than describing a voluntary or mutual arrangement, and that appears to sit in direct tension with the spiritual equality affirmed in Galatians 3:28 and with the female prophets, deacons, and co-workers named elsewhere in Paul's own letters. For many readers this is the single hardest passage in the Bible's treatment of women's status, not a minor tension to be waved away.

Mainstream Christian responses to these texts fall into two broad camps, each with serious scholarly defenders. Complementarian scholars read 1 Timothy 2 as establishing a transcultural, creation-order principle rather than a Fall-based punishment—arguing that Paul's appeal to "Adam was first formed, then Eve" points to an abiding pattern of male teaching authority in the church that predates the Fall and therefore cannot be dismissed as a first-century cultural accommodation; they read 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 as addressing disorderly conduct specific to the Corinthian assembly (such as wives publicly interrupting to question their husbands' teaching), and note that the same letter assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in the gathered church (1 Corinthians 11:5), so the silence commanded in chapter 14 cannot mean total silence in every circumstance. Egalitarian scholars respond that both texts are occasion-specific responses to concrete local problems rather than universal, transcultural directives: 1 Timothy, they argue, addresses a particular crisis of false teaching in Ephesus—where inexperienced women had reportedly been targeted and misled by the false teachers described earlier in the letter—so Paul's reference to Eve functions as a cautionary parallel for those specific women rather than a blanket ontological claim about all women for all time. They further point to Junia, whom Paul names as "notable among the apostles" (Romans 16:7), and to the prophesying women of 1 Corinthians 11:5, as evidence that Paul did not regard women's public teaching and spiritual authority as inherently forbidden, arguing that the wider church must have permitted forms of authoritative speech by women for these examples to make sense. The broader interpretive fault line—whether these apparently absolute prohibitions are transcultural directives binding for all times and places, or occasion-specific responses to local first-century problems—runs through this entire debate and has no scholarly consensus; both readings are held by serious, non-fringe biblical scholars, and denominational practice today spans the full range of this disagreement.

sections.title: Biblical Assertions of Spiritual Equality
sections.body: The most direct statement of gender equality in the New Testament appears in Galatians 3:28, where Paul declares, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." This verse is understood by many Christian scholars as a fundamental spiritual principle that transcends social categories—including gender. In the Gospels, women appear in roles of spiritual leadership and discipleship that were counter-cultural for first-century Judaism: Mary of Bethany sits at Jesus' feet to learn, a posture reserved for rabbinical students, and Jesus affirms her choice as the "good part." Women are the first witnesses to the Resurrection and are commissioned to proclaim the news to the male disciples—a detail scholars note as counter-cultural precisely because women's testimony did not carry full legal weight in Jewish legal practice of the period. The Acts of the Apostles and Paul's letters name women as deacons, prophets, and church leaders. Proverbs 31:10-11 portrays a capable woman who manages commerce, property, and household with her husband's trust and recognition. Genesis 1:27 establishes that both male and female are created in God's image. Christian interpreters who emphasize these texts argue that Galatians 3:28 establishes an eschatological or spiritual principle that should inform how Christians view gender roles, even if first-century cultural practices were accommodations to their time. Others contend that household codes (like Ephesians and 1 Peter) establish enduring structures; the debate centers on whether these are culturally situated applications of a deeper principle or universal directives.

sections.title: Interpretive Frameworks and Historical Development
sections.body: In Islamic tradition, women's roles have been interpreted across a spectrum. Classical Islamic jurisprudence developed detailed frameworks for women's rights in marriage, inheritance, divorce, and property ownership—rights that many scholars describe as revolutionary compared to many pre-Islamic and contemporary societies, though historians of late antiquity note that some pre-Islamic Arabian women (such as Khadija) already held independent property and business standing, making comparative claims about the period a matter of ongoing scholarly debate. Modern Islamic scholars range from those advocating strict adherence to traditional role distinctions to those arguing that principles like justice, consultation (shura), and community good allow or require flexible interpretation of Quranic directives in changed circumstances. Feminist Islamic scholars have highlighted women's agency in early Islamic history—women merchants, poets, hadith scholars, and political actors—and argue that a return to principle-based interpretation rather than medieval jurisprudential crystallization would recover a more egalitarian vision. In Christian tradition, the debate over female leadership and roles has intensified in recent centuries. Complementarian churches maintain that male headship reflects creation order and God's design, though they increasingly emphasize mutual submission and sacrificial love as essential qualifications. Egalitarian or feminist Christian interpreters argue that Paul's affirmations of equality and his praise of women leaders throughout his letters represent his true position, and that household codes are first-century compromises that should not bind modern churches. Both communities have produced scholarly literature grappling seriously with textual interpretation, historical context, and theological principles. The existence of this diversity does not make one side definitively right; it reflects the genuine complexity of scriptural texts that contain both equality affirmations and role directives.

sections.title: Contemporary Expressions and Lived Experience
sections.body: Modern Muslim-majority and Muslim-minority communities exhibit considerable variation in how women's roles are practiced and understood. Some emphasize formal equality in law and workplace while maintaining traditional family structures; others have integrated women into religious scholarship, leadership, and judiciary. Many Muslim women scholars, activists, and theologians engage in ijtihad (independent reasoning) to argue for women's full participation in all aspects of community life, grounding their positions in Quranic principles rather than medieval interpretations. Similarly, Christian denominations range from those ordaining women to senior leadership to those maintaining male-only pastoral roles. Women serve as theologians, biblical scholars, missionaries, activists, and church leaders across the Christian world, and many of these women root their participation in Christian theology itself. What remains consistent across both traditions is that no mainstream Islamic or Christian authority advocates for women's spiritual worthlessness or exemption from moral accountability; the scriptural foundations of women's dignity are not in dispute. The disagreements center on the implications of scriptural texts for social roles, the relationship between equality and difference, how to interpret culturally situated passages in modern contexts, and whether specific role directives are universal or provisional.

title: Worshiping God Alone: Islamic and Christian Approaches
subtitle: Exploring how both traditions emphasize exclusive devotion to God
summary: Both Islam and Christianity emphasize that worship belongs to God alone, though they differ on the nature of God's unity. Islam emphasizes strict monotheism (tawhid), centering on the principle of worshiping Allah exclusively. Christianity affirms that God is one while maintaining the doctrine of the Trinity—three persons in one being—and directs worship to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one God. Despite differing theological frameworks, both traditions demand sincere, exclusive devotion to God.

sections.title: Introduction: The Centrality of Exclusive Devotion
sections.body: The concept of worshiping God alone stands as a foundational principle in both Islamic and Christian tradition. In Islam, this principle is known as tawhid—the assertion that God (Allah) is one and deserves worship without any partners or intermediaries. In Christianity, while the understanding of God's nature differs, the demand for exclusive devotion to God remains paramount. Both traditions insist that true worship cannot be divided; it belongs entirely to the one true God. This article explores how each tradition articulates and understands this principle, examining scriptural foundations and practical implications.

sections.title: The Islamic Perspective: Tawhid and Exclusive Worship
sections.body:
In Islamic theology, tawhid (التوحيد)—meaning "unification" or "making one"—represents the cornerstone of faith. It affirms that there is no god but Allah, and therefore no one deserves worship except Him. This principle extends beyond mere intellectual acknowledgment; it demands complete and exclusive devotion in practice. The Quran consistently reinforces this concept, presenting it not as an abstract theological claim but as a lived reality that shapes how believers relate to God and navigate the world.

The opening chapter of the Quran, Al-Fatiha, encapsulates this principle in its most direct form. When Muslims recite the opening chapter five times daily in prayer, they explicitly state their exclusive devotion. Islamic jurisprudence and practice flow from this foundation: no one is invoked in prayer except God, no one intercedes with divine authority except through God's permission, and no acts of worship are directed toward anyone but Allah. This understanding shapes Islamic ethics, law, and spirituality comprehensively.

sections.title: The Christian Perspective: Worship of the One God
sections.body:
Christianity affirms with equal intensity that worship belongs to God alone. From the earliest teachings recorded in the Gospels, Jesus reiterates this principle directly. When tempted by Satan in the wilderness, Jesus responds by quoting Scripture: exclusive devotion must be given to God. Christian theology maintains that there is one God eternally existing in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This doctrine, known as the Trinity, does not introduce multiple gods or objects of worship; rather, it is understood as the Christian explanation of God's own nature and how God reveals Himself to humanity.

In Christian practice, worship is directed to God—understood as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—as a unified whole. Prayer, thanksgiving, praise, and intercession all flow toward the one God. The Apostle Paul emphasizes this principle clearly: there is "one God, the Father" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ," yet both are worshiped as expressions of the single divine being. Christian ethics, like Islamic ethics, demand that believers place God at the absolute center of their lives, allowing no rival loyalty or divided allegiance.

sections.title: Scriptural Foundations: Key Verses from Both Traditions
sections.body:
The Islamic tradition anchors its teaching on exclusive worship in clear Quranic affirmations. The principle appears throughout Scripture in various formulations: from the direct proclamation that there is no god but Allah, to the command to worship God alone, to the warning against arrogance in rejecting this message.

The Christian tradition similarly emphasizes exclusive worship through both Jesus's teaching and apostolic instruction. Jesus himself models and commands worship of God alone, while also receiving worship that Christian theology understands as appropriate because of his divine nature. The apostles teach that unity with God comes through recognizing the one God and the one Lord, Jesus Christ. These scriptural foundations do not contradict the distinctive theological claims of each tradition; rather, they represent how each tradition's own scriptures orient believers toward exclusive devotion.

sections.title: Practical Implications: Living Out Exclusive Devotion
sections.body:
Both traditions understand that declaring exclusive devotion to God has profound practical consequences. In Islam, tawhid demands that Muslims structure their entire lives around obedience to God. Islamic law, ethics, and spiritual practices all flow from this central commitment. A Muslim cannot claim to worship God alone while simultaneously placing trust in wealth, power, status, or other human beings. Such division would contradict the principle of tawhid. Instead, Islamic practice involves the five daily prayers (salat), which are understood as both a declaration and a renewal of exclusive devotion to Allah.

Christian practice similarly demands total allegiance. Jesus teaches that his followers must love the Lord their God with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their mind, as recorded in Matthew 22:37. This represents not a partial commitment but a comprehensive reorientation of one's entire being toward God. Christian spiritual disciplines—prayer, worship, study of Scripture, and service—are all understood as expressions of this exclusive devotion. In both traditions, this exclusivity is not merely about what is consciously affirmed; it extends to how believers actually live, spend their time, direct their resources, and order their priorities.

sections.title: Where the Traditions Differ
sections.body:
While both traditions emphasize exclusive worship of God alone, they articulate fundamentally different understandings of God's nature. Islam teaches strict numerical monotheism: God is absolutely one, without any internal plurality. The affirmation "there is no god but Allah" is understood as excluding any conception of God existing as more than one person or entity.

Christianity teaches that there is one God who eternally exists in three persons. For Christians, saying "God is one" and affirming the Trinity are not contradictory; they represent different aspects of Christian understanding. God is numerically one in being and substance, yet three in person. This is why Christian worship is directed to Father, Son, and Spirit—not as three separate gods, but as three persons of the one God.

Islamic theology rejects the Trinity as a compromise of monotheism, viewing it as a step toward polytheism. Islamic apologists cite Quranic passages such as 4:171 (which emphasizes God's absolute oneness and warns "do not say, Three") and 5:73 (which states "They have certainly disbelieved who say, Allah is the third of three") as scriptural grounds for this position. Islamic theologians argue that true tawhid cannot accommodate internal division within the Godhead. Christian theologians offer a specific response to these two verses rather than only a general defense of the Trinity. They point to Quran 5:116, in the same surah as 5:73, where God asks Jesus on the Day of Judgment whether he told people to take himself and his mother as deities "besides Allah" - pairing Allah, Jesus, and Mary as the implied "three." Since the Trinity as defined at the Council of Nicaea (325 CE) consists of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not Father, Son, and Mary, many Christian scholars argue that 4:171 and 5:73 may be targeting a distorted folk conception of the Trinity - one in which Mary was mistakenly venerated as a divine third person, a misunderstanding historically associated with certain fringe groups - rather than refuting the Nicene formulation itself. Muslim theologians typically respond that the Quran's language in 4:171 ("do not say, Three") is not narrowly restricted to any single triad but rejects any plurality within the Godhead as such, so the Nicene formulation remains implicated regardless of which three persons are in view. This exchange over precisely what conception of "three" the Quran addresses remains a live and specific point of disagreement between the traditions, rather than one side leaving the other's textual argument unanswered.

Despite this fundamental theological difference, both traditions insist that their respective understanding best preserves the principle of exclusive devotion to God alone. Each claims to offer the truest expression of monotheism, though on different grounds. Muslims emphasize numerical simplicity; Christians emphasize the relational nature of God's being.

sections.title: Points of Convergence
sections.body:
Despite their theological differences, Islamic and Christian traditions converge on several crucial points regarding worship:

(1) **Rejection of Idolatry**: Both traditions categorically reject the worship of idols, created objects, or false gods. Both condemn polytheism and the direction of worship toward anyone or anything other than the true God.

(2) **Necessity of Sincere Intention**: Both traditions emphasize that worship must flow from genuine heart commitment, not mere external conformity. Islamic teaching stresses the concept of niyyah (intention), while Christian teaching emphasizes worshiping "in spirit and in truth." Both reject hollow ritual detached from sincere devotion.

(3) **All-Encompassing Allegiance**: Neither tradition permits a compartmentalized faith where God receives worship on certain occasions while other loyalties govern daily life. Both demand comprehensive reorientation of one's entire existence around exclusive devotion to God.

(4) **Rejection of Intermediaries with Divine Authority**: While Christian theology permits intercessory prayer and the veneration of saints, and Islamic practice acknowledges the spiritual authority of prophets and leaders, both traditions maintain that only God possesses ultimate authority and receives the submission of worship. No creature stands between the believer and God as a rival object of devotion.

(5) **Transformation of the Worshiper**: Both traditions teach that genuine worship transforms the person who offers it. True devotion to God alone changes how one thinks, acts, and relates to others. It produces moral reform and spiritual growth.

sections.title: Conclusion: A Shared Emphasis with Different Foundations
sections.body:
Islamic and Christian traditions, despite their significant theological differences, share a profound conviction: worship belongs to God alone. For Muslims, this principle is expressed through tawhid—the affirmation of God's strict oneness and the exclusive devotion that flows from this belief. For Christians, this principle is affirmed through the recognition that the one God deserves and receives all worship, whether directed to Father, Son, or Spirit, understood as three persons of one divine being.

These two traditions offer different answers to the question: "What does it mean that God is one?" Islam emphasizes numerical singularity without any internal complexity. Christianity emphasizes numerical oneness coexisting with personal multiplicity. Yet both agree that this God alone is worthy of worship, that human loyalty cannot be divided, and that authentic faith transforms every aspect of life.

For believers within each tradition, understanding why the other tradition emphasizes exclusive devotion to God, even while disagreeing about the nature of God's unity, can foster greater mutual respect. Both traditions take seriously what they see as the gravest spiritual danger: the dilution of faith through compromise, the division of allegiance, or the worship of anything or anyone other than God. In this shared concern lies both common ground and a clear demarcation of what each tradition holds most fundamental to authentic faith.

title: Celestial Signs: Orbits, Stars, Iron, and Light in the Quran
subtitle: Seven frequently cited Quran-and-science passages, read through classical tafsir and modern science with an honest strength assessment for each
summary: This article examines seven commonly cited Quran passages from the "scientific miracles" (i'jaz) literature — on orbiting celestial bodies, the oath by the stars' positions, mountains passing like clouds, paired plant life, water and life, iron "sent down," and the sun's versus the moon's light — giving the classical tafsir reading, the modern scientific gloss, and an honest assessment of each. It applies the site's caution framework throughout, showing that resonance ranges from strong to interpretively flexible to genuinely contested.

sections.title: Introduction: Seven More Signs, One Framework
sections.body:
Alongside the more heavily debated passages on embryology, cosmology's "Big Bang" resonance, mountains as stabilizers, and the barrier between seas — each treated in its own dedicated article on this site — the Quran contains a further set of frequently cited nature verses: on the orbiting of celestial bodies, the oath by the "positions" of the stars, mountains "passing like clouds," paired plant life, water as the origin of living things, iron "sent down," and the differing terms used for the light of the sun and the moon. These verses circulate widely in popular Muslim apologetics (often called the i'jaz 'ilmi, or "scientific miraculousness," genre) as evidence that the Quran anticipated discoveries unavailable to a seventh-century audience.

This article treats each of the seven passages in turn, using the same caution framework laid out in "How to Approach Scientific Claims in Scripture Carefully": distinguishing scientific accuracy from prescience from theological meaning, insisting that a claim to prescience requires genuine temporal impossibility rather than mere compatibility, and taking seriously that words carry the semantic range available to their own language and era before they carry any modern one. For each verse this article gives the classical tafsir reading, the modern scientific gloss that popular apologetics builds on it, and an honest strength assessment along the three-tier scale used elsewhere on this site: strong resonance, interpretively flexible, or overclaimed/contested inference. None of these labels is a verdict on the Quran's truth as scripture; they are judgments about how much evidentiary weight a specific scientific argument can bear.

It is worth noting at the outset that the Quran itself typically frames these very passages as ayat — "signs" meant to provoke reflection (tafakkur) and gratitude in an already-believing or open audience, not as forensic proofs addressed to a skeptical scientific committee. Two of the passages discussed below end with exactly that language: Quran 13:3 closes, "Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought," and Quran 10:5 closes, "He details the signs for a people who know." Keeping that self-described purpose in view is not a way of lowering the bar for these verses; it is a way of applying the right bar.

sections.title: 1. "Each in an Orbit, Swimming": Quran 36:40 and 21:33
sections.body:
Quran 36:40 states that "it is not allowable for the sun to reach the moon, nor does the night overtake the day, but each, in an orbit (falak), is swimming (yasbahun)." Quran 21:33 makes the same claim more broadly: "it is He who created the night and the day and the sun and the moon; all [heavenly bodies] in an orbit are swimming."

Geocentric astronomy was dominant across late antique and medieval learned traditions, but it was not literally universal or intellectually static. A small number of ancient and medieval thinkers discussed Earth's rotation, and later Islamic astronomers critically revised Ptolemaic devices even while usually retaining geocentrism. The Quranic image of celestial bodies swimming in an orbit is compatible with observed regular motion, but it does not by itself choose between geocentric and heliocentric models.

The modern scientific gloss is considerably broader than what any seventh-century reader could have had in mind: not only do the sun and moon appear to move across the sky, but the Earth and every other planet genuinely orbit the sun under gravity, the moon orbits the Earth, and — a fact unavailable to any observer before twentieth-century astronomy — the sun itself orbits the center of the Milky Way galaxy, moving at roughly 220–230 kilometers per second and completing one full circuit (sometimes called a "galactic year") in something on the order of 225 to 250 million years. In that sense, "each in an orbit, swimming" describes the universe at every scale humans have so far been able to measure it, from moons to stars to the sun's own path through the galaxy.

A devotional resonance some later Muslim writers and preachers draw out — though it belongs to homiletics rather than to formal classical tafsir on these specific verses — is the parallel between the swimming or circling of the heavenly bodies and the tawaf, the ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba performed by pilgrims. On this reading, the orbiting of creation itself becomes a kind of cosmic worship, echoing the Quran's broader theme (as in 22:18 and 13:15) that all created things, willingly or unwillingly, submit and "prostrate" to God; the pilgrim who circles the Kaaba enacts in miniature what the sun and moon are imagined to enact on a cosmic scale.

The honest caveat is that the verses' own vocabulary is exactly as compatible with the old geocentric cosmology as with the modern heliocentric and galactic one — which is precisely why generations of readers before Copernicus took the same words as confirmation of an earth-centered universe, and readers after Copernicus and Hubble take them as confirmation of a sun-centered, then galaxy-embedded, universe. A form of words flexible enough to fit both pictures is functioning as a broad and lasting poetic truth about a universe full of motion, not as a specific prediction of any one physical model. **Assessment: strong resonance** with the general modern fact that virtually everything in the universe orbits something — tempered by the fact that the same wording was read, just as confidently, within an incompatible ancient cosmology for most of its interpretive history.

The Hebrew Bible offers its own poetic image of solar motion rather than a scientific claim. Psalm 19:4-6 describes the sun as being like "a bridegroom coming out of his room, like a strong man rejoicing to run his course," whose "going out is from the end of the heavens, his circuit to its ends." Read plainly, this too reflects the phenomenology of a sun that rises, crosses the sky, and returns to begin again — a literary circuit rather than a claim about orbital mechanics, and one that Biblical scholars generally read within the same observational, earth-centered framework common to the ancient Near East, rather than as an anticipation of heliocentric or galactic astronomy.

sections.title: 2. The Oath by the "Positions of the Stars": Quran 56:75-78
sections.body:
Quran 56:75-76 reads: "Then I swear by the setting of the stars (mawaqi' al-nujum) — and indeed, it is an oath, if you could know, [most] great." The passage continues in 56:77-78 to specify what the oath is actually about: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Register well-protected."

The Arabic mawaqi' is the plural of mawqi', from the root waqa'a, "to fall, to occur, to happen" — the same root that gives the Quran's vocabulary for the stars "falling" or "being scattered" at the Last Hour (as in 81:2). This is why classical and modern English translations of the phrase spread across a real semantic range rather than converging on one word: Saheeh International and Yusuf Ali both render it "the setting of the stars," Pickthall and Shakir render it "the places of the stars" and "the falling of stars" respectively. Classical exegetes offered several readings in the same spirit — the times and points on the horizon where stars rise and set, their fixed positions and courses across the sky, or (echoing 81:2) their scattering on the Day of Resurrection. The verse's own next line clarifies that its point is the greatness of the oath itself and, by extension, of what is being sworn upon (the Qur'an's protected transmission) — not a technical claim about stellar mechanics.

Modern popular apologetics nonetheless finds real scientific resonance in the idea of stellar "positions." Two facts are genuinely striking, if read into the term: first, because light takes a finite time to travel, the position at which we observe a distant star is never its current position — for the nearest stars this lag is a few years, for others many millennia, so that naked-eye and telescopic astronomy of "the positions of the stars" is, by necessity, always an exercise in observing where a star used to be. Second, stars in orbit — whether members of binary systems or, like the sun, orbiting a galactic center — are, in the language of general relativity, in a state of continuous free fall, following the curvature of spacetime rather than being pulled by a classical "force"; their apparent fixed "position" is itself the outcome of constant motion. Both of these are genuinely profound modern facts about what a stellar "position" even means.

The honest assessment has to weigh this resonance against how open-ended the term mawaqi' is and against what the passage's own continuation identifies as the actual point of the oath. An oath phrased broadly enough to be filled with almost any subsequently discovered fact about stars — their light-travel-time delay, their orbital free-fall, their gravitational dynamics, or simply their rising and setting — is exactly the kind of alignment the caution framework warns against treating as prediction: compatibility is not the same as impossibility-to-have-known. **Assessment: evocative resonance rather than a scientific prediction** — the linguistic openness of mawaqi' is what allows it to be filled with whatever modern astronomy an interpreter already has in mind.

Job 38:31-33 offers a striking Biblical parallel in register, if not in claim: God challenges Job, "Can you bind the cluster of the Pleiades, or loosen the cords of Orion? Can you lead the constellations out in their season? ... Do you know the laws of the heavens?" Both passages use the stars rhetorically, to humble the listener's claim to knowledge before the vastness of the sky, rather than to transmit specific astronomical data. Neither text is best read as a scientific claim about stellar positions; both use the stars as a rhetorical figure for what lies beyond ordinary human comprehension.

sections.title: 3. Mountains "Passing Like Clouds": Quran 27:88
sections.body:
Quran 27:88 reads: "And you see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they will pass as the passing of clouds. [It is] the work of Allah, who perfected all things. Indeed, He is Acquainted with that which you do."

The verse's own immediate context is unambiguous about its setting. The verse before it, 27:87, describes the Day the Horn (Trumpet) will be blown, when "whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified except whom Allah wills," and the two verses after it, 27:89-90, describe the reward of "whoever comes [at Judgement] with a good deed" and the punishment of whoever comes with an evil one. Mainstream classical tafsir — al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and al-Qurtubi among them — accordingly reads the mountains "passing like clouds" as one more description of the cosmic upheaval of the Last Day, in the same register as other Quranic images of that day: mountains becoming "like fluffed-up wool" (101:5), removed and vanishing "as if it were a mirage" (78:20), or flattened into "a leveled plain" (20:105-106). On this reading, which is the plain and dominant sense of the verse in its own literary setting, the mountains that appear so solid to the living will be set into unimaginable motion at the Resurrection specifically — not a statement about ordinary geological process in the present age.

The modern popular-apologetic reading, prominent since the mid-to-late twentieth-century growth of the i'jaz 'ilmi genre, proposes instead that the verse describes plate tectonics: mountains, though rigid-looking, are in fact riding on tectonic plates that drift a few centimeters per year, so that over geological time they truly do "pass" like slow-moving clouds. Plate tectonics is itself a genuine, well-established twentieth-century scientific discovery. But applying it to this verse requires detaching "you see the mountains... while they pass" from the Day-of-Judgment frame that its immediately surrounding verses establish, and relocating it instead to describe the present geological era — a move the grammar and literary context do not themselves suggest, and one the classical exegetical tradition, working from the same Arabic text, did not make. This is a case where a mainstream classical reading exists, states plainly that the referent is the Last Day, and is simply set aside by the modern scientific reading rather than engaged with or refuted.

**Assessment: interpretively flexible at best.** The plate-tectonics gloss is a real reinterpretation of a verse whose own context, and whose classical tafsir, point elsewhere — toward eschatology rather than plate geology.

The Bible uses closely related imagery for exactly the eschatological purpose classical tafsir assigns to 27:88. Micah 1:4 describes divine judgment in similarly dramatic terms: "The mountains melt under him, and the valleys split apart, like wax before the fire, like waters that are poured down a steep place." No one reads Micah's melting mountains as an early description of volcanism or erosion; it is transparently apocalyptic imagery of judgment. The shared convention — mountains that appear permanent being dissolved, moved, or leveled as a sign of divine intervention at the end of history — is common currency across the ancient and late-antique Near East, which strengthens the case that Quran 27:88 belongs to that same genre rather than to a scientific description of the present geological era.

sections.title: 4. "Two Mates" Among the Fruits: Quran 13:3 and 36:36
sections.body:
Quran 13:3 describes God as the one "who spread the earth and placed therein firmly set mountains and rivers; and from all of the fruits He made therein two mates (zawjayn ithnayn)... Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought." Quran 36:36 states more broadly: "Exalted is He who created all pairs — from what the earth grows and from themselves and from that which they do not know."

Classical tafsir on these verses tends to read "pairs" broadly — as contrasting varieties within a single fruit (sweet and sour, light and dark, large and small), or simply as the general principle that God has built complementary duality into creation (as in the pairing of male and female humans, mentioned in the same verse, 36:36, alongside plants) — rather than as a specific technical claim about floral reproductive anatomy. The phrase in 36:36, "and from that which they do not know," is an open acknowledgment by the text itself that further categories of pairing exist beyond the audience's knowledge; later commentators and popular writers sometimes extend this to modern discoveries of paired phenomena in physics (such as particle-antiparticle pairs), though that is a homiletical extension well beyond the verse's plant-and-human context rather than a claim the classical tradition made about it.

Ancient Near Eastern reliefs are sometimes interpreted as showing artificial pollination of date palms, but the scenes may also carry ritual or royal symbolism and their precise action is debated. They can support the general point that people long understood practical differences between productive palms, but they should not be treated as an uncontested visual record of botanical theory without a specialist archaeological citation.

**Assessment: modest resonance, honestly qualified.** The Quran's "pairs" language touches a real botanical phenomenon that was already part of the practical, working knowledge of its first audience through date-palm cultivation; it does not itself state the general scientific principle of plant sexuality later established by early modern botany, and classical exegesis read "pairs" more broadly than reproductive biology alone.

sections.title: 5. "Every Living Thing" From Water: Quran 21:30
sections.body:
Quran 21:30 reads: "Have those who disbelieved not considered that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them, and made from water every living thing? Then will they not believe?" This article's companion piece on cosmology treats the verse's first clause — the heavens and earth as an originally "joined entity" later "separated" — at length, including the contested resonance some readers find with modern cosmology's expanding, once-unified early universe; readers interested in that half of the verse should consult the "Cosmology: Creation and the Universe" article.

The clause relevant here — "We made from water every living thing" — states a biological dependency that modern science fully confirms: every known form of life, from single cells to complex organisms, requires water for its basic chemistry, and water remains the medium in which the biochemical reactions of life take place. In that narrow sense the claim is scientifically accurate and remains so today.

The honest caveat, consistent with the caution framework's emphasis on distinguishing accuracy from prescience, is that this was also intuitively available knowledge to the Quran's original desert-dwelling audience, and indeed to virtually every agrarian and pastoral society in history. Anyone who has watched crops wither without rain, watched livestock and travelers die of thirst in the desert, or seen an oasis sustain abundant life against a backdrop of lifeless sand has direct experiential grounds for concluding that water is what makes living things possible. Other ancient Near Eastern cultures reached similar conclusions through their own cosmologies — Egyptian civilization built its entire understanding of fertility and renewal around the life-giving Nile flood, and Mesopotamian myth placed the primordial waters (Apsu and Tiamat) at the origin of all things. This is a case, in the caution framework's terms, of accurate observation rather than prescient or otherwise inaccessible knowledge: it required no instrument, no theory, and no information unavailable to the text's own time and place to arrive at. **Assessment: accurate but not prescient** — true both to modern biology and to what careful observation had already taught desert and agrarian peoples for millennia.

Genesis 1:20-21 shows the same association of water with the origin of living creatures: "Let the waters abound with living creatures... God created the large sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed." Like the Quranic verse, this reflects the ancient and cross-culturally common recognition that water and life are inseparable; it is best read, on both sides, as theologically framed observation rather than as biochemical prescience.

sections.title: 6. Iron "Sent Down": Quran 57:25
sections.body:
Quran 57:25 reads, in relevant part: "...And We sent down (anzalna) iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for the people, and so that Allah may make evident those who support Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might."

The modern scientific gloss draws on stellar nucleosynthesis: iron sits at the peak of nuclear binding energy, meaning it is the heaviest element that ordinary nuclear fusion inside the cores of massive stars can efficiently produce, with iron and heavier elements reaching interstellar space chiefly through the deaths of those stars in supernova explosions. In this precise sense, essentially all of Earth's iron — including the iron in its molten core and in every iron tool ever forged — is stellar in origin and predates the Earth itself, formed inside stars that lived and died before the solar nebula that became the Sun and its planets ever collapsed into being. Read with maximal literalness, "We sent down iron" is a striking match for the idea that iron genuinely arrived in the material that built Earth from beyond it, rather than originating here.

The linguistic counterpoint that the caution framework requires be weighed alongside this resonance is that anzala/nazzala ("to send down") is Quranic vocabulary used well beyond contexts of literal descent from the sky. Quran 39:6 uses the same verb for livestock: "...and He produced (anzala) for you from the grazing livestock eight mates..." — cattle plainly do not fall from the sky, so anzala here functions as "provided" or "brought into being for your benefit." Quran 7:26 uses the related anzalna for clothing: "We have sent down (anzalna) to you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment" — garments are manufactured by human hands from plant and animal fiber, not literally lowered from heaven. Classical Arabic usage and tafsir recognize this broader idiomatic sense of anzala as divine provision or bestowal, distinct from its more literal use for revelation and rain.

Two readings therefore genuinely compete for 57:25. A maximalist reading takes "sent down" as a literal, physically descriptive statement about iron's cosmic origin — a striking resonance with modern astrophysics if adopted. A linguistically conservative reading treats anzala here exactly as it functions for livestock and clothing elsewhere in the Quran: a general idiom for divine provision, making a claim about iron's usefulness to human civilization (metallurgy, tools, weaponry) rather than about its astrophysical origin at all. Because the same verb demonstrably carries the non-literal sense elsewhere in the same text, the inference to a literal cosmic claim cannot be treated as settled by the word choice alone. **Assessment: striking resonance, but a contested inference** — the astrophysics of iron's stellar origin is not in question; whether 57:25 is actually asserting it is.

It is worth noting, for comparative purposes, that the Bible frames iron in the opposite direction. Job 28:2, part of a poem about mining and human ingenuity, states plainly: "Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted out of the ore." Where the Quran's phrasing (on the maximalist reading) points outward, toward the heavens, for iron's origin, the Biblical text's plain sense points downward, toward the ground beneath human feet — describing the ordinary, observable experience of ancient mining and metallurgy rather than any claim about cosmic origins. Neither framing was making a claim about nucleosynthesis; the contrast simply illustrates how differently two ancient texts can describe the same metal depending on their immediate rhetorical purpose.

sections.title: 7. Lamp and Reflected Light: Quran 25:61, 71:16, and 10:5
sections.body:
Three passages consistently distinguish the vocabulary used for the sun from that used for the moon. Quran 25:61 describes God as the one "who has placed in the sky great stars and placed therein a [burning] lamp (siraj) and luminous moon (qamaran muniran)." Quran 71:16 states that God "made the moon therein a [reflected] light (nur) and made the sun a burning lamp (siraj)." Quran 10:5 states that God "made the sun a shining light (diya') and the moon a derived light (nur), and determined for it phases — that you may know the number of years and account [of time]." Across all three, the sun consistently receives the more intense vocabulary — siraj (blazing lamp) or diya' (radiant, burning light) — while the moon consistently receives nur or its related form munir (light, luminosity), a comparatively softer and more general term. Saheeh International's translation signals its own interpretive leaning by inserting the bracketed gloss "[reflected]" before "light" for the moon in 71:16.

Modern astronomy is not in doubt on the underlying physical fact: the sun generates its own light through nuclear fusion, while the moon has no light of its own and shines purely by reflecting sunlight off its surface. What is genuinely debated — including within the Islamic exegetical tradition itself, independent of any outside polemic — is whether the Quran's terminological distinction is best read as encoding that specific mechanism. Ibn Kathir's tafsir on 10:5 comments that God "made the rays that come forth from the bright sun as the source of light, and made the beams that come forth from the moon as light," made "of two different natures so they would not be confused with one another" — a real distinction, though stated without explicitly invoking reflection as a physical mechanism. The twentieth-century Ma'arif-ul-Qur'an commentary of Mufti Muhammad Shafi goes further in urging caution: it notes that some commentators propose diya' denotes intrinsic light and nur denotes light "derived from something else," but adds that "this semantic approach appears to be influenced by Greek thought, otherwise it has no lexical basis," and that "the Qur'an too has not given any categorical verdict about it" — preferring instead the more modest explanation that diya' simply denotes strong, work-enabling daylight while nur denotes general light of any intensity or source, a difference of degree and function rather than of physical mechanism.

A further honest caveat concerns how available this idea already was. Greek astronomers as early as Anaxagoras (fifth century BCE) had proposed that the moon shines by reflected sunlight, and the idea became a standard part of later Hellenistic astronomy, transmitted through late-antique Alexandria, Syriac Christian scholarship, and the Sasanian Persian court — all of which stood in cultural contact with the wider late-antique Near East, even if precisely what reached the Hijaz by the seventh century is difficult to establish with certainty. The insight was not, in other words, exotic or unreachable in principle for a late-antique audience.

**Assessment: a genuine and consistent terminological distinction whose significance is debated even among the Quran's own classical and modern commentators** — some read it as anticipating the sun/moon light difference science later confirmed in mechanism; others, working from the same Arabic text, caution that the vocabulary supports only a difference of intensity and function, not a claim about reflection as such.

By contrast, Genesis 1:16 makes no terminological distinction at all between the two bodies' light: "God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night." Both sun and moon are simply "lights" (the Hebrew me'orot), differentiated only by relative size and by day/night function, not by any linguistic marker of intrinsic versus derived luminosity. This is a useful comparative data point: it shows that a text can describe the sun and moon accurately and reverently, as Genesis does, without drawing the terminological distinction the Quran draws — which means the Quran's distinction, whatever its ultimate significance, is not the only way an ancient Near Eastern scripture handled the topic.

sections.title: Applying the Framework: Signs, Not a Physics Textbook
sections.body:
Laid side by side, these seven passages resist a single verdict, which is itself the honest finding: the orbiting of celestial bodies is a strong resonance whose wording is equally at home in the geocentric cosmology it was first read within; the "positions of the stars" is evocative but linguistically open enough to fit whatever astronomy a reader already holds; mountains "passing like clouds" carries a plain classical meaning about the Day of Judgment that the plate-tectonics reading sets aside rather than builds on; paired fruits touch a real but only partially known ancient practice; water as life's origin is accurate but was already available to unaided observation; iron "sent down" rests on a striking astrophysical fact paired with a live linguistic counter-reading from the Quran's own usage elsewhere; and the sun/moon light distinction is real in the text but its significance is contested by the very tafsir tradition that transmits it.

What unites the two verses that close with an explicit statement of purpose — 13:3's "signs for a people who give thought" and 10:5's "He details the signs for a people who know" — is that the Quran's own stated aim for this material is ayat: prompts toward reflection, gratitude, and recognition of a Creator, addressed most directly to an audience already inclined to look for them. That is a theological and rhetorical purpose, not a scientific one, and the distinction matters in both directions. It means these verses should not be dismissed as failures simply because they do not read like a modern astronomy or geology textbook — that was never their genre or aim. But it equally means that treating them as forensic scientific predictions, capable of settling debates about the Quran's origin, asks them to bear a kind of evidentiary weight their own context does not claim for them. As the companion article on approaching scientific claims carefully argues, overclaiming here does not strengthen the religious case being made for these verses; by inviting exactly the scrutiny under which alignment collapses into either geocentric-compatible poetry, contested linguistics, or knowledge the original audience already possessed, it can weaken it. The more durable claim — available whether or not any given scientific resonance holds up — is the text's own: that a reflective observer, looking at orbiting bodies, a star-strewn sky, standing mountains, fruit-bearing plants, water-dependent life, useful metal, and the different lights of day and night, might reasonably be moved to wonder about their maker.

title: Civilian Protection in Islamic Law and the Biblical Tradition
subtitle: Who May Be Fought, and Who May Never Be Targeted, Across Two Textual Traditions
summary: Islamic jurisprudence developed an explicit doctrine of non-combatant immunity grounded in Quranic verses, the Prophet Muhammad's recorded practice, and a genuine cross-school juristic consensus — a doctrine this article examines honestly alongside the difficulty posed by Quran 9:5. The Hebrew Bible's herem texts, by contrast, describe the total destruction of conquered populations including women and children, presented here at full strength alongside the mainstream Jewish and Christian responses to them. A closing section considers, with careful attribution, how both traditions' ancient war texts have surfaced in modern conflicts — a question about adherents' conduct that is distinct from what the founding texts themselves establish.

sections.title: Introduction: Who May Be Fought, and Who May Never Be Targeted
sections.body:
Every tradition that permits warfare at all must answer two distinct questions: who may licitly be fought, and who may never be targeted regardless of the cause. Islamic jurisprudence and the Hebrew and Christian scriptures both address this question, but through very different textual histories. Islamic law developed an explicit, detailed doctrine of non-combatant immunity grounded in Quranic verses, in the Prophet Muhammad's recorded practice, and in centuries of juristic elaboration across the four Sunni schools of law. The Bible, by contrast, contains texts that establish comparable protections and also a small number of texts — the herem, or "ban," passages describing the conquest of Canaan — that appear to command the opposite: the total destruction of entire populations, explicitly including women and children.

This article examines both traditions at full strength. On the Islamic side, it presents the Quranic and hadith basis for civilian protection, the near-unanimous juristic consensus that followed, and the honest difficulty posed by Quran 9:5, the so-called "sword verse," including both the mainstream contextual reading and a genuine classical abrogation-based reading. On the biblical side, it presents the herem texts at full strength, alongside the mainstream Jewish and Christian interpretive responses to them and the distinct question of the New Testament's ethic of enemy-love. A closing section considers, with careful attribution, how both traditions' ancient war texts have surfaced in modern conflicts and modern warfare more broadly — a question about adherents' and states' conduct that is separate from, and does not resolve, what the founding texts themselves establish.

sections.title: The Qur'an on the Limits of Fighting
sections.body:
Quran 2:190 states: "Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors." Addressed to the early Muslim community facing armed conflict with Mecca, the verse frames permission to fight in narrowly conditional terms: only against those actively fighting, and only within a limit — "do not transgress" (la ta'tadu) — that classical and modern exegetes alike read as encompassing restrictions on methods and targets, later elaborated in detail by the jurists discussed below. The verse does not itself list protected categories, but its structure — permission bounded by an explicit non-transgression clause — is the textual seed from which Muslim jurists developed the more detailed rules of engagement examined in this article.

Quran 5:32 states: "Because of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely. And our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, [even] after that, throughout the land, were transgressors." This verse's immediate subject is individual homicide law as given to the Children of Israel, with a stated exception for lawful capital punishment or the suppression of "corruption in the land" — it is not, in its primary sense, a rule of war. Muslim jurists and preachers have nonetheless invoked it consistently, across the classical and modern periods, as underwriting a general Quranic principle: that the sanctity of a single human life carries the moral weight of humanity as a whole, and that killing outside strictly bounded exceptions is a graver matter than an isolated act. That principle, applied to the conduct of war, is one of the sources jurists cite alongside 2:190 and the hadith material below when explaining why non-combatants may not be killed as a matter of course.

sections.title: The Prophet's Practice and Abu Bakr's Instructions to the Army
sections.body:
The clearest evidence for a specific prohibition on killing women and children comes from the Prophet Muhammad's own recorded practice rather than from Quranic text alone. Ibn Umar reported that during one of the Prophet's military expeditions, a woman was found among the slain; when this was reported to the Prophet, he denounced it and forbade the killing of women and children in war. This report is recorded, in closely similar wording, in both Sahih al-Bukhari (hadith 3014) and Sahih Muslim (hadith 1744), a status hadith scholars term muttafaqun 'alayhi — agreed upon by the two most rigorously vetted hadith collections in Sunni Islam. Related reports on the same prohibition are attributed to additional narrators, including Buraydah, al-Aswad ibn Sari', Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama, giving the rule an unusually broad base of transmission for a single point of law.

This categorical rule sits alongside a separate, frequently discussed report attributed to that same companion, al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama, recorded in Sahih Muslim (hadith 1745) under the chapter heading "Permissibility of killing women and children in night raids, so long as it is not done deliberately." Asked about women and children of polytheists killed during night raids, the Prophet is reported to have replied, "They are of them" (hum minhum). Classical commentators treated this as a narrow qualification rather than a reversal of the general rule: al-Nawawi, in his commentary on Sahih Muslim, and Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani, in Fath al-Bari, both explain the remark as addressing incidental deaths occurring in the dark, when combatants and non-combatants could not be visually distinguished from one another, rather than as license to target women and children knowingly; where such a distinction could be made, jurists held, the categorical prohibition continued to govern. The report is one classical jurists had to reconcile with the general rule, via this distinction between incidental and deliberate killing, rather than one that simply reinforces the prohibition without complication, and it continues to be cited in modern discussions of incidental civilian harm in warfare.

The principle was carried into institutional practice within roughly a year of the Prophet's death. According to Imam Malik ibn Anas's Muwatta (Book of Jihad) and al-Tabari's History, when Caliph Abu Bakr al-Siddiq dispatched the Muslim armies toward Syria, he walked alongside Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, one of the appointed commanders, and gave him a set of instructions before the army marched. He is reported to have said, in substance: do not kill a woman, a child, or an aged and infirm person; do not cut down fruit-bearing trees; do not destroy an inhabited dwelling; do not slaughter a sheep or a camel except for food; do not burn or scatter bees; do not steal from the spoils of war; and do not act with cowardice. He is further reported to have told Yazid that the army would encounter people who had devoted their lives entirely to worship in monasteries — monks — and that these were to be left undisturbed, along with what they had devoted themselves to.

The same reported instruction, in the same breath, continues with a considerably less comfortable clause that this article should not pass over: Abu Bakr is also recorded telling Yazid that the army would find people who had shaved the middle of their heads, leaving a ring or band of hair around it, and that the army was to strike what they had shaved with the sword. This second group is not the monastics protected in the preceding clause. Commentators on the passage generally identify the described hairstyle with a distinctive tonsure worn by certain Byzantine-affiliated clergy and monastic orders in Roman Syria, and treat it as marking a group distinct from the ascetic, world-renouncing monks addressed immediately before — but the primary sources do not themselves explain the basis for the distinction, and this article is not in a position to resolve, from the text alone, why one tonsured religious group was to be left alone and another struck. What can be said plainly is this: the single passage most often cited as Abu Bakr's founding charge for protecting monastics also authorizes killing a second group identified by a religious marker, in the very next clause, and a fair presentation of this precedent has to include that rather than quoting only its more comfortable half.

Later jurists treated this episode as an authoritative early precedent, alongside the Quranic and hadith material above, for extending protection to categories — the elderly and monastics explicitly, and, in the juristic elaboration that followed, hired laborers and other non-combatants — not individually itemized in the Quran's own war verses. The same episode, read in full rather than selectively, is a reminder that even this centerpiece precedent is not a clean, uncomplicated protection list.

sections.title: Juristic Consensus Across the Four Schools — and Its Limits
sections.body:
By the classical period, jurists across the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools had converted this Quranic and hadith foundation into detailed doctrine. The Andalusian jurist Ibn Rushd (Averroes), in his comparative law survey Bidayat al-Mujtahid, records that the schools held no disagreement on two specific points: it is permissible to fight adult male polytheists who are actively waging war, and it is not permitted to kill women or children so long as they are not themselves fighting. This narrow point — the immunity of non-combatant women and children specifically — functioned as a genuine ijma, or scholarly consensus, across the classical schools, and it is the strongest textually and historically attested claim this article makes about Islamic law's protection of civilians.

Ibn Rushd also records that the schools disagreed on the underlying legal rationale for the rule, and that this disagreement had real consequences for less clear-cut categories. Jurists who held that the basis for permitting killing was disbelief itself were, on his account, more willing to extend permissible targeting to non-combatant adult men, including peasants and hired laborers who took no part in the fighting. Jurists who held instead that the basis was the capacity to fight — a position associated particularly with the Hanafi school — extended protection more broadly to anyone lacking that capacity: the elderly, the disabled, monastics, and unarmed peasants and laborers alike. In practice, most later fiqh manuals absorbed the more protective reading into their standard lists of categories exempt from deliberate targeting — women, children, the elderly, the insane, monks and other non-combatant religious figures, and hired laborers — while the underlying scholarly disagreement about why these categories were protected persisted. Contemporary academic treatments of Islamic laws of war, such as the Yaqeen Institute's paper "War, Islam, and the Sanctity of Life: Non-Aggression in the Islamic Code of Combat" and John Kelsay's Arguing the Just War in Islam, generally present the fuller protective list as the settled classical doctrine, even though the point of strict, cross-school ijma recorded by Ibn Rushd is narrower — limited specifically to non-combatant women and children.

sections.title: Quran 9:5 in Its Textual Neighborhood: Two Classical Readings
sections.body:
No honest discussion of civilian protection in Islamic law can omit Quran 9:5, sometimes called ayat al-sayf, the "sword verse." It reads: "And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they should repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them [go] on their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." Read in isolation, this verse states an apparently unconditional command to kill polytheists unless they repent, without explicit restriction to combatants — and it is the single most frequently cited Quranic verse both by critics who argue that the Qur'an licenses indiscriminate violence and, historically, by some classical jurists who argued that it superseded earlier, more restrictive verses.

The verse does not stand alone. It opens a short, tightly connected passage near the beginning of Surah at-Tawba. The verse immediately before it, Quran 9:4, reads: "Excepted are those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and then they have not been deficient toward you in anything or supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term [has ended]. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous [who fear Him]." This explicitly exempts from the following command any polytheist group that had kept its treaty obligations with the Muslims in full. The verse immediately after, Quran 9:6, reads: "And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know." This instructs that any individual polytheist who sought protection was to be granted it, given the opportunity to hear the Quran, and then delivered safely to a place of security. Verse 9:7, not quoted here at length, reaffirms a similar treaty exception. Read as a textual unit, then, the very passage that contains the "sword verse" also contains, in the same breath, both a treaty-honoring exemption and an individual asylum guarantee.

The mainstream contextual reading, held by the majority of classical and nearly all contemporary exegetes, ties 9:5 to its stated occasion: the surrounding verses of the same sura identify the target as specific Arabian polytheist tribes who had repeatedly broken treaties with the Muslim community and initiated hostilities, not polytheists or non-Muslims as a category. This reading is associated especially with the Hanafi school of law and has been argued at length by modern scholars including the Egyptian Grand Mufti Mahmoud Shaltut and the Syrian jurist Wahbah al-Zuhayli, both well documented as proponents of a contextual, defensive reading of the Quran's war verses generally; 9:4 and 9:6 sitting inside the same short passage as 9:5 is, independent of any single scholar's precise wording, the internal textual evidence contextual readers most often point to for the claim that the chapter did not intend a general command against all non-combatants.

A second, minority-but-genuinely-classical reading held that 9:5 abrogated (naskh) a substantial number of earlier, more conciliatory verses. Ibn Kathir's tafsir records this position as held by the early exegete al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who is reported to have said the verse abrogated every peace agreement, treaty, and fixed term the Prophet held with idolaters; the jurist Ibn al-'Arabi went further, holding that 9:5 abrogated some 124 verses counseling patience or forbearance toward unbelievers; and al-Tabari's tafsir presents the verse, drawing on companion-era narrations, as a general command to fight polytheists until conversion. Surveys of the classical abrogation literature record the total number of Quranic verses considered abrogated by some other verse — not solely by the sword verse, but across the whole Qur'an — growing across the medieval period, from roughly 138 in the work of al-Nahhas to as many as 238 in that of Ibn Salama. Al-Nahhas's list is not commonly broken down by which specific verse did the abrogating in each case, but of Ibn Salama's 238 total, roughly half are specifically attributed to the sword verse itself, with the remainder attributed to a range of other abrogating verses. This was a genuine position within classical Islamic legal theory, held by identifiable named scholars, not a modern invention, and it should be presented as such. It was not, however, the only or majority classical position: most classical jurists and virtually all contemporary scholarship hold the contextual reading instead, and 9:4 and 9:6 remain part of the same textual unit under either interpretation.

sections.title: Casualty Estimates Across the Prophet's Military Campaigns
sections.body:
A separate, empirical line of argument for the practical scope of restraint during the Prophet's lifetime comes from historians' attempts to tally total casualties across the roughly eighty military expeditions (ghazawat and saraya) traditionally counted during his prophethood, the great majority of which involved no fighting at all. The historian and jurist Muhammad Hamidullah, in his study Battlefields of the Prophet Muhammad: A Contribution to Muslim Military History, calculated Muslim battle deaths across the entirety of the Prophet's campaigns at approximately 150. Other scholars working from the same classical maghazi (campaign-narrative) sources have produced a comparable combined total: the Indian scholar Maulana Wahiduddin Khan arrived at a combined figure of 259 Muslims and 759 non-Muslims killed (1,018 total), a figure he presents as covering the Prophet's campaigns as a whole, though the underlying combat deaths are concentrated overwhelmingly in a handful of major engagements — chiefly Badr, Uhud, and Hunayn — since the great majority of the roughly eighty expeditions saw no fighting at all. These two figures converge on a widely cited order-of-magnitude estimate of roughly one thousand total combat deaths, on every side, across more than two decades of intermittent warfare touching a rapidly expanding community.

These numbers should be read with the caution appropriate to any casualty estimate drawn from ancient sources. They rest on the maghazi and sira literature compiled by Muslim historians — chiefly Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet as preserved by Ibn Hisham, and al-Waqidi's Kitab al-Maghazi — one to two centuries after the events they describe, using methods of transmission and verification that differ substantially from modern casualty accounting, and specialists in early Islamic history do not treat every individual figure in these sources as precise. The estimate is best understood as an order-of-magnitude claim, advanced primarily within Muslim scholarship as evidence of the restrained character of the era's warfare relative to the scale of territorial and political change it produced, rather than as an audited casualty count in the modern sense.

sections.title: The Herem Texts: Total Destruction Commanded
sections.body:
The Hebrew Bible's conquest narratives contain a small number of texts that, read at face value, describe the opposite of non-combatant protection: a divine command to destroy entire populations, explicitly including those who would elsewhere be classified as civilians. Deuteronomy 20:16-18 states: "But of the cities of these peoples, that Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes; but you shall utterly destroy them: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; as Yahweh your God has commanded you; that they not teach you to follow all their abominations, which they have done to their gods; so would you sin against Yahweh your God." Here the herem, or "ban" — the practice of devoting a conquered population entirely to destruction — is commanded specifically against the named Canaanite peoples, without an exception for women, children, or any other otherwise-protected category; the stated rationale is the prevention of religious contamination, not military necessity.

1 Samuel 15:3 records an instance where a comparable command is applied outside Canaan proper. The prophet Samuel relays a divine instruction to King Saul concerning the Amalekites: "Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey." This explicitly extends destruction to infants and nursing babies alongside livestock, and Saul's later partial non-compliance — sparing King Agag and the best of the animals — is presented in the subsequent narrative as the reason his kingship was rejected, meaning the text frames obedience to the command, not deviation from it, as the righteous course. The larger command to "remember what Amalek did" and to blot out the memory of Amalek, which Samuel's instruction to Saul carries out, is itself set out earlier in Deuteronomy 25:17-19: "Remember what Amalek did to you by the way as you came out of Egypt; how he met you by the way, and struck the rearmost of you, all who were feeble behind you, when you were faint and weary; and he didn’t fear God. Therefore it shall be, when Yahweh your God has given you rest from all your enemies all around, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it, that you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under the sky. You shall not forget."

A third, smaller-scale text is sometimes cited alongside the herem passages, though it is a different kind of text — an individual act of prophetic judgment rather than a war law or command to a national army. 2 Kings 2:23-24 states: "He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, 'Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!' He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in Yahweh’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods, and mauled forty-two of those youths." Unlike the Deuteronomy and 1 Samuel passages, this incident does not concern warfare or a divine command to an army; it is presented in the narrative as an act of prophetic retribution against mockery of the prophet Elisha, and it belongs to a broader set of ancient Near Eastern narrative conventions in which prophets pronounce curses that come to pass. It is nonetheless one of the texts most frequently raised in popular debate over violence against children in the Bible, and is included here at full strength alongside the war texts for that reason.

sections.title: Jewish and Christian Responses to the Herem Texts
sections.body:
Jewish and Christian interpreters have not treated the herem texts as settled or comfortable, and mainstream responses within both traditions engage them directly.
