One influential line of Christian response, developed by the philosopher Paul Copan in Is God a Moral Monster? Making Sense of the Old Testament God, and further with the philosopher Matthew Flannagan in Did God Really Command Genocide? Coming to Terms with the Justice of God, argues that the herem commands employ standard ancient Near Eastern conquest rhetoric — a genre in which total-destruction language ("utterly destroy," "save alive nothing that breathes") functioned as a stock hyperbolic formula for decisive victory, comparable to similar total-annihilation language in other ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions (such as the Moabite Mesha Stele) whose underlying events, on independent reconstruction, involved more limited routs and displacement than the literal wording suggests. On a related but distinct line of argument, the biblical scholar John Walton, with J. Harvey Walton, in The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest, argues that the Hebrew term herem itself means something closer to "removal from ordinary use" than "annihilate," pointing to internal biblical evidence — Joshua 11 describes northern cities as herem, yet only Hazor is actually burned; Leviticus 27:21 treats a herem field not as destroyed but as becoming priestly property — as evidence that the term functioned as a covenantal and theological category, marking the conquest as God's action rather than Israel's material gain, rather than as a literal mass-killing directive in every application.

This reading is contested within Christian and Jewish scholarship itself, not only by outside critics. The philosopher Randal Rauser, among others, has argued that the hyperbole and removal-from-use readings do not adequately answer the plain sense of commands directed at named categories, including infants and nursing children in 1 Samuel 15:3, and that treating the language as convention risks minimizing a textually explicit command rather than resolving the moral difficulty it raises. Jewish tradition, for its part, has generally treated the herem commands as bound to a specific, non-repeatable historical circumstance. Maimonides, reasoning from the biblical account that the Assyrian king Sennacherib mixed and displaced the ancient Near Eastern populations centuries later, ruled that the seven named Canaanite nations could no longer be reliably identified — rendering the command, in normative Jewish law, inapplicable in practice rather than a live instruction for any later era.

Within Christian theology specifically, a further line of response holds that the New Testament develops or reframes the ethic of the conquest texts. Matthew 5:44 records Jesus instructing his followers: "But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you." Mainstream Christian interpreters across a wide range of traditions read this instruction, part of the Sermon on the Mount, as establishing the governing ethic for Christian conduct — one that stands in visible tension with the herem texts. That tension is one Christian theologians have long debated rather than resolved by simple harmonization. The church's mainstream, across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions, has rejected the second-century teacher Marcion of Sinope's position that the Old Testament's God and law should be set aside altogether as belonging to a different, lesser deity than the New Testament reveals — a view condemned as heretical by the early church. Instead, the mainstream position has held both testaments as scripture while treating the New Testament's ethic of active enemy-love as, at minimum, the standard governing Christian conduct now, whatever conclusion one reaches about the original moral status of the conquest commands. This is a live and openly debated question within Christian scholarship, not a settled harmonization, and serious, faithful interpreters land in different places on it.

sections.title: Modern Invocations: Ancient Texts in Live Conflicts
sections.body:
Ancient religious war texts do not stay confined to ancient contexts. News organizations reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a statement issued by his office on October 28, 2023, at the start of Israel's Gaza ground operation, told troops, in the government's own published English-language rendering, that they must "remember what Amalek has done" — a reference to the Deuteronomy and 1 Samuel texts discussed above — and that "we do remember and we are fighting." The remark, along with other statements by Israeli officials, was subsequently cited in South Africa's application to the International Court of Justice alleging incitement to genocide, an allegation Israel's government has denied, stating the reference was to Hamas rather than to Palestinians as a people. This article does not adjudicate that legal dispute; the point relevant here is narrower — that a specific ancient total-destruction text was invoked, on the public record, in a live twenty-first-century conflict, which is a different question from what the text was originally understood to require of ancient Israel.

On the human cost of a separate modern conflict, the Costs of War Project at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs, Brown University, estimates that direct violence in post-9/11 United States wars and counterterrorism operations in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen, and Pakistan — countries with majority-Muslim populations — killed more than 940,000 people between 2001 and 2023, of whom over 432,000 are estimated to have been civilians. The project separately estimates, using a multiplier methodology developed by the Geneva Declaration Secretariat (roughly four indirect deaths — from disease, displacement, and the destruction of health and economic infrastructure — for every direct death), that indirect deaths in these conflicts likely number 3.6 to 3.8 million, for a combined total the project describes as at least 4.5 to 4.7 million. The project's own researchers describe the direct-violence figure as a conservative undercount of the true toll and caution that the indirect-death estimate carries wide uncertainty inherent to the multiplier method used to produce it; these are the Costs of War Project's own stated figures and caveats, reported here with attribution rather than independently verified by this article.

A further modern comparison sometimes raised alongside religious war-ethics texts is the American atomic bombing of the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 — an act of state warfare, not one framed by its planners in the religious terms discussed elsewhere in this article. Historians' estimates of the death toll vary considerably, given the destruction of civil records and the ongoing deaths from burns and radiation sickness through the end of 1945. The United States Manhattan Engineer District's contemporaneous 1946 tally put combined deaths at roughly 105,000 (66,000 at Hiroshima and 39,000 at Nagasaki), while later reassessments incorporating Japanese municipal records — including the Hiroshima Peace Memorial's estimate of roughly 140,000 dead by December 1945, and a later Japanese reassessment of roughly 70,000 dead at Nagasaki by the same date — put the combined total closer to 210,000. Historians commonly cite this full range, roughly 110,000 to 210,000, reflecting the gap between the earliest official tally and later, higher reconstructions. The large majority of the dead in both cities are estimated to have been civilians — in Hiroshima, an estimated 90 percent of deaths despite a military garrison of some 24,000 troops stationed in the city.

None of these modern episodes settles the textual and juristic questions addressed earlier in this article, and this article does not treat them as doing so. They are included because both religious traditions examined here have, at different points, been invoked by their own adherents, or by state and political actors operating within societies those traditions have shaped, in ways that sit uneasily beside the traditions' own texts of restraint. How a tradition's stated doctrine relates to the conduct of those who invoke its name, or its cultural inheritance, in a given era is a genuinely open question that recurs across both Islamic and Jewish/Christian history, and it is a different question from what the traditions' founding texts themselves say.

sections.title: Conclusion: Texts and Adherents, Judged Separately
sections.body:
Both traditions examined in this article contain strong resources for civilian protection, and both contain texts that sit uneasily beside that protection. Islamic law's textual and juristic case for non-combatant immunity is unusually explicit and well attested: Quranic verses restricting fighting to those who fight; a hadith on the prohibition of killing women and children carried by an unusually wide set of narrators; an early caliphal precedent, Abu Bakr's instructions to Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan's army, naming specific protected categories including monastics; and a genuine cross-school juristic consensus on the immunity of non-combatant women and children specifically. That case sits alongside the honest difficulty of Quran 9:5, which a real, named strand of classical exegesis read as abrogating much of this restraint — a reading disputed by the majority of scholars, ancient and modern, but not invented by modern extremists.

The Bible's herem texts present something like the reverse difficulty: read at face value, they describe exactly what Islamic law and modern international humanitarian law alike categorically forbid — the deliberate killing of women, children, and infants, framed as obedience to a divine command whose refusal costs a king his throne. Mainstream Jewish and Christian scholarship has not ignored this difficulty; it has produced substantial, contested interpretive work — the ancient-Near-Eastern-hyperbole reading, the removal-from-use reading of herem itself, the claim that Jewish law renders the command inapplicable in the absence of an identifiable Canaanite nation, and the claim that the New Testament's ethic of active enemy-love reframes or supersedes the conquest texts — none of which commands universal assent even within the traditions that produced it.

Neither tradition's founding texts, honestly read, hand their adherents an uncomplicated brief for or against civilian protection. Both offer real resources for restraint, and both contain material that must be interpreted, historically contextualized, or theologically reframed to arrive at a fully categorical protection doctrine. In the modern world, adherents of both traditions, and the political and military actors who invoke them, have — at various points and to greatly differing degrees — both honored and violated whatever protective doctrine their texts support: from extremist groups claiming Islamic warrant for attacks on civilians that classical jurists across every school would have called unlawful, to political rhetoric that reaches for ancient total-destruction language in a live war, to state violence, carried out by actors from across the religious spectrum, whose civilian death tolls in specific modern conflicts dwarf the casualty figures associated with the founding-era texts examined here. Whether a tradition should be judged chiefly by the most protective reading of its own founding texts, by its most permissive classical reading, or by the conduct of those who invoke its name in a given era is a question this article leaves open in both directions, for both traditions, because it is a fair question to put to each.

title: Eve in Islam and Christianity
subtitle: Two tellings of the first disobedience — who is blamed, what is inherited, and what each structure has meant for women
summary: Genesis narrates a fall in which the woman acts first, and later Christian texts — from 1 Timothy to Tertullian — built arguments about all women on that priority, arguments most churches today qualify or reject. The Quran retells the same primal scene in the grammatical dual: Satan whispers to the couple together, both eat, both repent, both are forgiven, and the one verse of individual reproach names Adam. This article quotes the core texts of both traditions and lays out the structural differences — inherited condition versus clean slate, woman-first versus joint address — without declaring a winner.

sections.title: Why Eve Is the Starting Point
sections.body:
No single figure has shaped the two traditions' conversations about women more than the first woman herself — Eve in the Bible, Hawwa in Islamic tradition (named in hadith literature, though not named in the Quran). In Christian history, Genesis 3, read through 1 Timothy 2 and amplified by some early church writers, became the story of the woman who was deceived first — and, in the harshest patristic rhetoric, the story of a guilt her daughters share. In the Quran, the same primal scene is retold with a different grammar: Satan whispers to the couple together, both eat, both repent, both are forgiven, and the one verse of individual reproach names Adam.

This article works through the primary texts in order. It quotes the Genesis narrative and the key New Testament passages; it quotes, verbatim and in context, the most severe historical statement of the Eve-blaming reading and the mainstream Christian responses to it; it then quotes the Quranic tellings and deals honestly with the Eve-negative material that exists in later Islamic literature. It closes by stating the structural differences precisely. Whether one structure is truer or better than the other is left to the reader; what the texts actually say is not left vague.

sections.title: The Genesis Narrative: The Woman Acts First
sections.body:
Genesis 3 opens with the serpent questioning the woman about God's command concerning the tree. The eating itself takes a single verse: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate; and she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.” (Genesis 3:6, World English Bible). Two details here have carried enormous interpretive weight. The woman acts first — she sees, takes, eats, and gives. And the phrase “her husband with her” has been read by many commentators to mean Adam was present throughout the exchange, a detail that complicates later retellings in which Eve seeks out and seduces an absent Adam.

When God questions the pair, each deflects blame downward: “The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”” (Genesis 3:12-13). God then pronounces consequences on the serpent, the woman, and the man in sequence. The address to the woman is the verse that has echoed longest: “To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. In pain you will bear children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”” (Genesis 3:16). Pain in childbearing and the husband's rule enter the story here, as words spoken to the woman within the judgment scene. The man's address follows in the same scene: the ground is cursed on his account and his labor becomes toil until he returns to dust.

What Genesis 3 itself does not say is also important for what follows: it contains no statement that the woman's descendants inherit her act, and no ranking of the two transgressions. Those moves came later, in different directions, in both the New Testament and post-biblical interpretation.

sections.title: Two New Testament Trajectories: Eve Deceived, Sin Through Adam
sections.body:
Two New Testament passages fixed the terms of the later Christian debate, and they pull in different directions.

The first is from the first letter to Timothy: “Let a woman learn in quietness with full submission. But I don’t permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in quietness. For Adam was first formed, then Eve. Adam wasn’t deceived, but the woman, being deceived, has fallen into disobedience;” (1 Timothy 2:11-14). The passage grounds a restriction on women's teaching and authority in two claims about Eden — Adam was formed first, and it was the woman, not Adam, who was deceived. For much of Christian history this text was read as establishing a permanent order between the sexes, with Eve's deception as standing evidence.

The second passage runs the other way. When Paul explains in Romans how sin and death entered the world, he names one person, and it is not Eve: “Therefore as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; and so death passed to all men, because all sinned.” (Romans 5:12). The fall-theology of Romans 5 is built entirely on Adam — sin enters “through one man,” and Christ is presented as the counterpart of Adam. When Christian doctrine later formalized the transmission of the fall as original sin, it followed Romans and made Adam, not Eve, the channel.

Both strands are canonical. Which one governs the reading of the other is among the questions that still divides Christian interpreters, and it matters directly for the question this article asks: whether anything from Eden attaches to women as women.

sections.title: The Patristic Legacy: Tertullian’s Indictment and Irenaeus’s Reversal
sections.body:
The harshest surviving statement of the Eve-blaming reading comes from Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155–c. 220), writing around the turn of the third century in a treatise on women's dress. Addressing the Christian women of his congregation, he wrote: “And do you not know that you are (each) an Eve? The sentence of God on this sex of yours lives in this age: the guilt must of necessity live too. You are the devil's gateway: you are the unsealer of that (forbidden) tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law: you are she who persuaded him whom the devil was not valiant enough to attack. You destroyed so easily God's image, man. On account of your desert — that is, death — even the Son of God had to die.” (On the Apparel of Women, Book I, ch. 1, trans. S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4). The logic is explicit and total: every woman is an Eve; God's sentence on “this sex” lives on, and so does the guilt; and even the death of the Son of God is laid at woman's door. Other early writers argued in a similar register — John Chrysostom's homilies on 1 Timothy, for example, treat Eve's deception as evidence of a weakness shared by the sex — though the fathers were not unanimous in this.

The patristic record also contains the opposite motif, and it is older than Tertullian's treatise. Irenaeus of Lyons set Eve beside Mary as parallel and reversal: “And thus also it was that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary.” (Against Heresies, Book III, ch. 22, sec. 4). In this strand, which became central to Catholic and Orthodox devotion, Eve's story is answered rather than perpetuated: Mary is honored as the “new Eve” whose obedience unties what disobedience knotted. Both motifs — woman as the devil's gateway and woman as the agent of reversal — descend from the same Genesis text, through different interpretive choices.

sections.title: How Mainstream Christianity Answers the “Devil’s Gateway” Reading
sections.body:
Fairness requires stating the mainstream Christian responses at full strength, because on this topic they are substantial.

First, Tertullian is not scripture. No ecumenical council adopted his rhetoric; he ended his life aligned with the Montanist movement, and no major church confesses that women bear Eve's guilt as women. His words are quoted today mostly as a warning specimen of how far one reading could go.

Second, where churches do teach a transmitted fall, the channel is Adam and the content is carefully qualified. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (secs. 404-405) teaches that original sin is “contracted,” not “committed” — a deprived state of human nature that, in its own words, does not have the character of a personal fault in Adam's descendants. Eastern Orthodoxy speaks of ancestral sin: what humanity inherits is mortality and a damaged condition, not guilt. Reformed confessions retain a stronger doctrine of imputed guilt — but imputed from Adam, following Romans 5:12, not from Eve.

Third, much modern exegesis, including official Catholic teaching, reads Genesis 3:16 as description rather than prescription. On this reading, “he will rule over you” describes the disordered condition that follows the rupture between humanity and God — a distortion redemption works against, not a norm God endorses. John Paul II's apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem (1988, sec. 10) argues exactly this: the domination of the words “he shall rule over you” breaks the original equality of man and woman and diminishes both.

Fourth, 1 Timothy 2:11-14 is contested within Christianity itself. Complementarian interpreters take its appeal to creation order as a permanent arrangement for church teaching offices, while explicitly denying that it implies women's inherited guilt or lesser worth. Egalitarian interpreters locate the instruction in a specific first-century Ephesian situation — unlearned women and circulating false teaching — and point to the women Paul greets as co-workers and a deacon in the greetings of Romans 16. Many churches today ordain women; many others do not; both camps claim the New Testament.

Finally, Mary. In Catholic and Orthodox thought the most consequential woman in the story of salvation is not Eve but the new Eve, and the tradition's liturgical instinct — honoring a woman as higher than the angels — is itself offered as the answer to Tertullian's rhetoric.

sections.title: The Quranic Narrative: Told in the Dual
sections.body:
The Quran tells the Eden story in several surahs, and its most consistent feature is grammatical. Arabic possesses a dedicated dual form — verbs and pronouns that refer to exactly two people — and the Quranic fall is narrated almost entirely in it.

In Surah al-Baqara the command is given to both at once: “And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise and eat therefrom in [ease and] abundance from wherever you will. But do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers."” (Quran 2:35). The fall likewise happens to both: “But Satan caused them to slip out of it and removed them from that [condition] in which they had been. And We said, "Go down, [all of you], as enemies to one another, and you will have upon the earth a place of settlement and provision for a time."” (Quran 2:36).

Surah al-A'raf sustains the dual through the entire temptation. “But Satan whispered to them to make apparent to them that which was concealed from them of their private parts. He said, "Your Lord did not forbid you this tree except that you become angels or become of the immortal."” (Quran 7:20). “And he swore [by Allah] to them, "Indeed, I am to you from among the sincere advisors."” (Quran 7:21). “So he made them fall, through deception. And when they tasted of the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten together over themselves from the leaves of Paradise. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?"” (Quran 7:22). Satan whispers to them both, swears to them both, deceives them both; they taste together, are exposed together, and are called to account together — “Did I not forbid you” is addressed, in the Arabic dual, to the two of them.

At no point in the Quran does the woman eat first, tempt her husband, or receive a separate address of blame or punishment. The tempter is Satan; the tempted are the pair. The Quran also never names her — Hawwa is her name in hadith and tafsir literature — and never uses her as an argument about other women.

sections.title: Reproach Falls on Adam; Both Repent; Both Are Forgiven
sections.body:
Where the Quran does single out one of the two, the singling-out runs in the opposite direction from 1 Timothy. In Surah Ta-Ha the forgotten covenant is Adam's: “And We had already taken a promise from Adam before, but he forgot; and We found not in him determination.” (Quran 20:115). After narrating that both ate and both began covering themselves, the verse of individual censure names him alone: “And Adam and his wife ate of it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves from the leaves of Paradise. And Adam disobeyed his Lord and erred.” (Quran 20:121). And the resolution follows in the very next verse: “Then his Lord chose him and turned to him in forgiveness and guided [him].” (Quran 20:122).

In Surah al-A'raf the repentance is explicitly joint, spoken in the dual voice: “They said, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers."” (Quran 7:23). The story thus closes inside itself — disobedience, joint repentance, acceptance, guidance. The descent to earth is not narrated as an unhealed curse: Quran 2:36 pairs it with “a place of settlement and provision for a time,” and Quran 20:122 with being chosen, forgiven, and guided. In Islamic theology Adam is not only forgiven but becomes the first prophet.

The contrast in narrative mechanics is worth stating neutrally: Genesis 3 ends with expulsion and consequences pronounced; the arc of repair unfolds across the rest of the Christian Bible and centers on Christ. The Quranic tellings compress fall, repentance, and forgiveness into the same passage, so that no unresolved debt leaves Eden with the couple.

sections.title: No Inherited Burden, and Childbirth Reframed
sections.body:
Islamic theology draws a doctrinal line under this narrative closure: nothing of the episode transmits to anyone. The Quran states it as a general principle of moral accounting: “And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to [carry some of] its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he should be a close relative. You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen and have established prayer. And whoever purifies himself only purifies himself for [the benefit of] his soul. And to Allah is the [final] destination.” (Quran 35:18) — a principle repeated in similar words in several other surahs. Sunni and Shia theology alike hold that every human being is born morally clean; Sahih al-Bukhari 1385 states that every child is born upon the fitra, the innate God-given disposition. There is, accordingly, no Islamic doctrine of original sin, no baptism to remove an inherited stain, and no category of guilt attaching to women as daughters of Eve.

Childbirth pain — which Genesis 3:16 places inside the judgment addressed to the woman — appears in the Quran in a different register entirely. “And We have enjoined upon man, to his parents, good treatment. His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship, and his gestation and weaning [period] is thirty months. [He grows] until, when he reaches maturity and reaches [the age of] forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents and to work righteousness of which You will approve and make righteous for me my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed, I am of the Muslims."” (Quran 46:15). The hardship of pregnancy and labor is cited here as the ground of a lifelong debt of gratitude the child owes the mother, and Islamic tradition builds the mother's elevated status partly on this verse. No Quranic verse connects the pain of labor to Eve, to Eden, or to punishment.

On the specific question this article asks — does anything from the first disobedience follow all women? — the Quranic answer is structural, not incidental: the fall is joint, the repentance is joint, the forgiveness is explicit, and the accounting of every later human being starts at zero.

sections.title: An Honest Caveat: Eve in Hadith and Tafsir
sections.body:
Honesty requires a caveat on the Islamic side, and a Christian reader is entitled to press it. While the Quran never blames Eve alone, some later Islamic literature does contain Eve-negative material. Sahih al-Bukhari 3330, with a close variant in Sahih Muslim 1470a, reads, in the USC-MSA English translation: “Narrated Abu Huraira: The Prophet said, 'But for the Israelis, meat would not decay and but for Eve, wives would never betray their husbands.'” Classical tafsir works — al-Tabari's commentary among them — also transmit narratives in which Eve tempts Adam, generally paralleling Genesis and later Jewish elaborations; Muslim scholarship labels much of this imported narrative material Isra'iliyyat and has long treated it with reserve, since it derives from earlier communities' traditions rather than from the Quran or the Prophet.

How Muslims read the Bukhari hadith varies. Classical commentators generally took it as an observation that Eve set a precedent her daughters sometimes follow — betrayal here being read as concealment or acting against a husband's wishes, on the model of Eve encouraging Adam to eat — rather than as a doctrine that women inherit her guilt; and it is a fact of Islamic law and creed that no ruling about women's nature or standing was ever derived from it. Modern academic work, notably Barbara Freyer Stowasser's Women in the Qur'an, Traditions, and Interpretation (1994), documents both sides of this record: the Quran's strictly joint narrative, and the entry of Eve-blaming motifs into hadith commentary and tafsir through post-Quranic channels.

The fair symmetry should be stated plainly. Just as Christians distinguish scripture from Tertullian, Muslims distinguish the Quran from transmitted reports and exegetical folklore. This article therefore draws its comparison where each tradition locates its highest textual authority — Genesis and the New Testament on one side, the Quran on the other — while acknowledging that both traditions' secondary literatures absorbed harsher material about Eve than their scriptures required.

sections.title: The Structural Comparison, Stated Precisely
sections.body:
Set side by side, the foundational texts differ at four precise points.

1. Who is blamed in the primal scene. In Genesis 3:6 the woman sees, takes, eats, and gives; the judgment words addressed to her in Genesis 3:16 include childbirth pain and her husband's rule; and 1 Timothy 2:11-14 later builds an argument about women's roles on her having been deceived. Yet Romans 5:12 assigns the entry of sin to Adam, and formal Christian doctrine followed Romans. In the Quran the narration is dual throughout (2:35-36; 7:20-23), and where one party is singled out for reproach it is Adam (20:115; 20:121).

2. What is inherited. Classical Western Christianity teaches a transmitted condition: imputed guilt in Augustinian and Reformed formulations, a “contracted” deprivation that is not personal fault in current Catholic teaching, inherited mortality and corruption in Orthodoxy. Islam teaches that nothing transmits: no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another (35:18), and every child is born clean.

3. Childbirth. Genesis 3:16 places the pain of childbearing inside the judgment scene, addressed to the woman. Quran 46:15 presents the same pain as the mother's merit and the child's debt, with no connection to Eden.

4. The repair. Christianity answers Eve outside Eden — through Christ, the counterpart of Adam in Romans 5, and through Mary, honored as the new Eve. Islam answers the fall inside the story itself: both repent (7:23), forgiveness is granted (20:122), and the account is closed before human history begins.

Two caveats keep the comparison honest. Christianity is not monolithic: inherited guilt in the strict sense is denied by Orthodoxy and carefully qualified by Rome; many churches read Genesis 3:16 as description of a broken condition rather than divine mandate; and no major church today teaches Tertullian's claim that women share Eve's guilt. And the Islamic tradition is not spotless in practice: Eve-blaming motifs entered tafsir, and a sound hadith links wives' betrayal to Eve's precedent. But at the level of the founding texts — the level each tradition itself treats as decisive — the structures genuinely differ: a narrative in which the woman moves first, on which later canonical and post-canonical texts built durable arguments about women; and a narrative told in the dual, with individual reproach directed at the man, joint repentance, and a slate wiped clean. What follows from each structure for women's actual lives has been argued in both directions for centuries. That argument is the reader's to weigh; the texts above are its raw material.

sections.title: Sources and How to Verify Them
sections.body:
Bible quotations (Genesis 3:6; 3:12-13; 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:11-14; Romans 5:12) are from the World English Bible, fetched from bible-api.com; the WEB is a public-domain modern translation. Quran quotations (2:35-36; 7:20-23; 20:115; 20:121-122; 35:18; 46:15) are from api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani Arabic text with the Saheeh International English translation.

Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women (De cultu feminarum), Book I, chapter 1, is quoted from the S. Thelwall translation in Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 4; the text is freely available at newadvent.org (fathers/0402.htm) and at tertullian.org. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book III, chapter 22, section 4, is quoted from Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 1, at newadvent.org (fathers/0103322.htm).

Sahih al-Bukhari 3330 is quoted in the USC-MSA English translation (Volume 4, Book 55, Number 547); the reference on sunnah.com is bukhari:3330. The Catechism of the Catholic Church, sections 404-405, and John Paul II's Mulieris Dignitatem, section 10, are paraphrased rather than quoted; both documents are available in full at vatican.va. Readers are encouraged to check every quotation in this article against these sources directly.

title: James, Josephus, and the Earliest External Evidence for Jesus
subtitle: What the Testimonium Flavianum, the James passage, and Tacitus actually attest — and what they cannot settle
summary: Two passages in Josephus and one in Tacitus form the earliest non-Christian testimony about Jesus of Nazareth. This article quotes each passage in full, maps the scholarly debate over their authenticity — including the majority view that the Testimonium Flavianum contains a genuine core with Christian insertions — and examines James, "the brother of the Lord," whose death Josephus records. It closes by asking what this external evidence can and cannot establish for Christians and for Muslims, who affirm Jesus' historicity while contesting the crucifixion.

sections.title: Why External Evidence Matters — and What Counts as External
sections.body:
Almost everything written about Jesus in the first century comes from people who believed in him. The Gospels, Paul's letters, and the other New Testament documents are the earliest and fullest sources, but they are testimony from inside the movement. Historians therefore attach special interest to the small number of passages about Jesus written by outsiders — authors with no stake in Christian claims, or with active hostility to them. Two such authors stand at the head of the list: Flavius Josephus, a Jewish priest and historian writing in Greek under Roman patronage in the 90s CE, and Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman senator and historian writing around 115-120 CE.

Josephus mentions Jesus in two places in his twenty-book history, the Antiquities of the Jews: a famous and fiercely disputed paragraph in Book 18 known as the Testimonium Flavianum, and a brief, widely accepted notice in Book 20 that identifies a man named James as "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ." Tacitus mentions Jesus once, in his account of Nero's persecution of Christians after the great fire of Rome in 64 CE.

This article examines each passage in turn: what it says, how it has been transmitted, what scholars across the spectrum make of it, and — crucially — what it can and cannot establish. The question of whether these texts are authentic is separate from the question of what they prove, and both questions look different from within the Christian and Islamic traditions. Both distinctions are kept in view throughout.

sections.title: Who Josephus Was
sections.body:
Yosef ben Mattityahu — later Flavius Josephus — was born in Jerusalem around 37 CE into a priestly family. When the Jewish revolt against Rome broke out in 66 CE, he commanded rebel forces in Galilee, was captured at the siege of Jotapata, and famously predicted that his captor, the general Vespasian, would become emperor. When Vespasian did, Josephus was freed, took the imperial family's name, and spent the rest of his life in Rome writing history under Flavian patronage. His major works are The Jewish War (written in the late 70s CE) and the Antiquities of the Jews, a twenty-book history of the Jewish people from creation to the eve of the revolt, completed around 93-94 CE.

Josephus matters to this question for three reasons. First, chronology: he wrote within living memory of the events, roughly sixty years after Jesus' death and about thirty years after the death of James. Second, position: he was a Jerusalem aristocrat and priest who was a young man in Judea in exactly the period when James led the Jerusalem church, so events like a high-profile execution ordered by a high priest were the kind of thing he could know directly or from eyewitnesses. Third, independence: Josephus was not a Christian, a point on which the church father Origen is explicit (discussed below), so whatever he wrote about Jesus was not written to serve Christian preaching.

The difficulty is that Josephus' works were copied for over a millennium almost exclusively by Christian scribes, because Christians — not the rabbinic Jewish community — treasured and transmitted him. That transmission history is precisely what makes the authenticity debate over the Testimonium Flavianum possible, and it must be kept in mind at every step.

sections.title: The Testimonium Flavianum: The Text as We Have It
sections.body:
In Book 18 of the Antiquities (18.63-64 in the modern numbering; Book 18, chapter 3, section 3 in William Whiston's classic English edition), amid a series of episodes involving Pontius Pilate, the received text reads as follows in Whiston's translation:

"Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was [the] Christ. And when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him; for he appeared to them alive again the third day; as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him. And the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day."

Read as a whole, this is astonishing: a non-Christian Jewish historian apparently affirming that Jesus was the Messiah, that his death was foretold by the prophets, and that he rose from the dead on the third day. And that is exactly the problem. Three phrases in particular read like a Christian confession of faith rather than the voice of a Pharisee-aligned priest writing for a Roman audience: "if it be lawful to call him a man," "He was [the] Christ," and the sentence reporting the resurrection appearance "the third day" as fulfilled prophecy. A Jew who sincerely believed those three statements would, by the definitions of the first century, have been a Christian — and everything else we know about Josephus indicates he was not.

This tension between the passage's existence and its wording is the engine of a debate that has run since the seventeenth century, when scholars such as Lucas Osiander and later critics first pressed the case against authenticity. The logically possible positions are three: Josephus wrote all of it; Josephus wrote none of it; or Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral notice that Christian copyists later embellished. All three positions have living defenders, and they are not equally populated.

sections.title: The Authenticity Spectrum: Three Positions, Honestly Stated
sections.body:
The majority position: partial authenticity. Most specialists today hold that Josephus wrote a genuine notice about Jesus which Christian scribes later retouched. The most influential modern statement is John P. Meier's in A Marginal Jew, volume 1 (1991). Meier argued that if one simply removes the three confessional phrases — "if it be lawful to call him a man," "He was [the] Christ," and the resurrection sentence — what remains is a coherent, dispassionate paragraph whose vocabulary and syntax are characteristically Josephan and whose mildly complimentary but non-committal tone ("a wise man," "a doer of wonderful works") fits a curious outsider far better than a forger, who would likely have written something far more glowing. Louis Feldman, the leading twentieth-century Josephus specialist, surveyed the vast literature (his Josephus and Modern Scholarship, 1937-1980 catalogues the debate) and reported that the intermediate position — a genuine core with interpolations — commands the majority. Scholars as different as Geza Vermes, James D. G. Dunn, and Bart Ehrman have endorsed versions of this reconstruction. Supporters also point to an indirect witness: the tenth-century Arabic chronicle of Agapius of Hierapolis preserves a version of the Testimonium — published by Shlomo Pines in 1971 — that lacks the flat confession "He was the Christ," saying instead only that Jesus was perhaps, or was thought to be, the Messiah; and Jerome's fourth-century Latin rendering (On Illustrious Men 13) likewise says Jesus was believed to be the Christ rather than asserting it. Some scholars read these as fossils of a more neutral original.

The fabrication position: a minority holds that the entire passage is a Christian composition inserted into Josephus. Ken Olson ("Eusebius and the Testimonium Flavianum," Catholic Biblical Quarterly 61, 1999) argued that the passage's vocabulary and phrasing match the style of Eusebius of Caesarea — the first author ever to quote it — more closely than the style of Josephus, suggesting Eusebius or someone in his milieu composed it. Richard Carrier has pressed the case further, arguing that the passage interrupts its narrative context (the surrounding episodes are calamities involving Pilate, into which a notice about Jesus fits awkwardly) and that the argument from Josephan style is weaker than defenders claim. Earlier advocates of wholesale interpolation include G. A. Wells. On this view, the silence of every Christian writer before the fourth century is not an accident: there was nothing there to quote.

The full-authenticity position: a smaller minority defends the passage essentially as it stands. Ulrich Victor (Novum Testamentum 52, 2010) argued on linguistic grounds that the whole text is Josephan and that phrases like "He was the Christ" can be read as reporting a designation ("this was the man called Christ") rather than a confession. Alice Whealey, whose Josephus on Jesus (2003) is the standard history of the controversy, occupies the far edge of the majority camp: she argues the text is very nearly all authentic, with perhaps only "He was the Christ" altered from an original "He was believed to be the Christ."

Fairness requires saying plainly: none of these positions can be proven, because no manuscript of the neutral core exists. The majority reconstruction is a hypothesis — a widely held, carefully argued hypothesis, but a hypothesis. Equally, the fabrication thesis must explain why a Christian forger produced so restrained a text when unconstrained forgers of the period produced far more extravagant ones. Each side has real arguments; the debate is genuinely open at the edges even if the center of scholarly gravity sits with partial authenticity.

sections.title: Manuscripts, Origen's Silence, and Eusebius' First Quotation
sections.body:
The transmission history is where the hardest evidence lies, and it cuts in both directions.

First, the manuscripts. Every surviving Greek manuscript of Antiquities Book 18 contains the Testimonium — there is no copy without it. But the earliest of those manuscripts (Codex Ambrosianus) dates to the eleventh century, roughly a thousand years after Josephus wrote. A thousand years is ample time for an interpolation made in late antiquity to become universal in the surviving copies, so the unanimity of the manuscripts proves less than it might first appear. Conversely, it also means there is no direct textual evidence for any shorter version: every reconstruction of a "neutral core" is inference, not collation.

Second, Origen. Writing around 248 CE, the Christian scholar Origen — who demonstrably knew Antiquities Book 18, since he cites its passage on John the Baptist — states twice that Josephus did not accept Jesus as the Messiah. In Against Celsus 1.47 he describes Josephus as "although not believing in Jesus as the Christ," and in his Commentary on Matthew (Book 10, chapter 17) he says the same while praising Josephus' testimony to the righteousness of James. This is powerful evidence that Origen's copy of Josephus did not contain the sentence "He was [the] Christ" — which is precisely why even most defenders of a genuine core concede that phrase is an insertion. Origen's silence about the rest of the Testimonium is harder to weigh: he had occasions where quoting a neutral notice of Jesus might have served him, and he did not; but arguments from silence about what an ancient author chose not to quote are notoriously fragile. There is a further puzzle: in both passages Origen attributes to Josephus the view that Jerusalem fell as divine punishment for the killing of James — a statement found nowhere in our manuscripts of Josephus. Scholars on all sides note this (some suggest Origen was loosely paraphrasing, or confusing Josephus with the second-century Christian writer Hegesippus), and it is a standing caution about how precisely Origen was quoting anything.

Third, Eusebius. The first author in history to quote the Testimonium is Eusebius of Caesarea, in the early fourth century, who cites it in three works: the Demonstration of the Gospel (3.5), the Ecclesiastical History (1.11), and the Theophany. What does that prove? For the fabrication camp, it identifies the earliest possible witness — and, on Olson's argument, the likeliest author. For the majority, it proves only that Eusebius is the first surviving writer with a reason and occasion to quote it; most of Christian literature before Eusebius has perished, and apologists before him wrote mainly against pagans, for whom a Jewish historian's neutral notice carried limited weight. Both readings of the Eusebius datum are defensible; the datum itself is simply that quotation begins with him.

sections.title: Antiquities 20.200: "The Brother of Jesus, Who Was Called Christ"
sections.body:
The second Josephan passage is shorter, quieter, and far more widely accepted. In Book 20 of the Antiquities (20.200 in the modern numbering; Book 20, chapter 9, section 1 in Whiston), Josephus narrates a crisis in Jerusalem in 62 CE. The Roman procurator Festus had died in office, and his successor Albinus was still en route from Rome. In that interval of vacant Roman oversight, the newly appointed high priest Ananus — son of the Ananus (Annas) who appears in the Gospel passion narratives — acted on his own authority. In Whiston's translation, Ananus "assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others"; and "when he had formed an accusation against them as breakers of the law, he delivered them to be stoned." Josephus goes on to relate that this act outraged fair-minded citizens, who complained to King Agrippa II and to the incoming procurator, and that Ananus was deposed from the high priesthood after only three months.

Most scholars regard this passage as authentic, and many regard it as the strongest single piece of external evidence for Jesus. The reasons are cumulative. The passage's subject is not Jesus or James but Ananus and high-priestly politics; Jesus is mentioned only as an identifying tag, which is not how Christian interpolators wrote. The phrase "who was called Christ" is studiously non-committal — it reports a designation without endorsing it — and Josephus needed some such tag because his history mentions many men named Jesus (including, a few lines later, Jesus son of Damneus, who received the high priesthood after Ananus' removal). The account of James's death disagrees with later Christian legend (see below), which tells against Christian authorship. And Origen, a century before Eusebius, already knew a passage in Josephus about James "the brother of Jesus who is called Christ," showing the reference predates the era in which the Testimonium first surfaces. Louis Feldman observed that few scholars have doubted the genuineness of this passage; John P. Meier and Robert Van Voorst treat its authenticity as close to secure as such things get.

There is a dissent, and honesty requires stating it. Richard Carrier ("Origen, Eusebius, and the Accidental Interpolation in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 20.200," Journal of Early Christian Studies 20.4, 2012) argues that "who was called Christ" began as a marginal gloss by a Christian scribe that was accidentally copied into the text, and that the James whom Ananus executed was actually James the brother of Jesus son of Damneus, the man who became high priest in the aftermath. Mainstream reviewers have generally found this reconstruction speculative — it requires the gloss to land in exactly the right place, and it must explain why Josephus would introduce the Damneus family so obliquely — but it is a genuine argument by a credentialed scholar and readers should know it exists. The majority judgment stands on the other side: a short, sober, contextually embedded notice that Jesus called Christ existed and had a brother named James whom a high priest had stoned in 62 CE.

sections.title: Who Was James? The New Testament Portrait
sections.body:
The James of Antiquities 20.200 is not a marginal figure conjured from nowhere; he is independently and abundantly attested in the earliest Christian sources, which is precisely why the Josephus notice carries such weight — the two bodies of evidence interlock.

Paul, writing in the late 40s or 50s CE about a visit to Jerusalem that took place within a few years of the crucifixion, says: "But of the other apostles I saw no one, except James, the Lord's brother." (Galatians 1:19). This is a first-person report by a man who says he met James — as close to primary evidence as ancient history offers. Paul elsewhere lists James among the witnesses of the risen Jesus: "Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles" (1 Corinthians 15:7), in a passage most scholars regard as quoting an early creed.

The Gospels name James among Jesus' brothers. In Matthew's account, the crowd in Nazareth asks: "Isn't this the carpenter's son? Isn't his mother called Mary, and his brothers, James, Joses, Simon, and Judas?" (Matthew 13:55). The Gospels also report that Jesus' brothers did not believe in him during his ministry — a detail preserved despite its awkwardness, which historians generally take as a mark of authenticity.

By the time of the Jerusalem council, however, James appears as the presiding voice of the mother church: "After they were silent, James answered, 'Brothers, listen to me.'" (Acts 15:13). Paul in Galatians 2 names him first among the "pillars" of the Jerusalem community. Later Christian tradition remembered him as "James the Just," renowned for piety. The second-century writer Hegesippus (whose account survives in quotation in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.23) gives an elaborate martyrdom narrative — James is thrown from the temple parapet, stoned, and finally clubbed to death — which differs in manner and legal setting from Josephus' brief judicial account. Where the two conflict, historians generally prefer Josephus' sober, nearly contemporary report of a Sanhedrin condemnation and stoning under Ananus in 62 CE, while noting that both traditions agree on the core: James, brother of Jesus, leader in Jerusalem, violently killed.

sections.title: "Brother of the Lord": Three Christian Readings, Fairly Stated
sections.body:
What did "brother" mean? The Greek word adelphos most naturally means a sibling, but Christian tradition has read these texts in three distinct ways, each driven by real exegetical observations and, for two of them, by the ancient doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.

The sibling reading (often called Helvidian, after the fourth-century writer Helvidius): James and the other named brothers were children of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus. This is the plain-sense reading of Matthew 13:55 and Galatians 1:19, and it is the view of most Protestant interpreters and most historical-critical scholars, including many Catholic historians writing in a purely historical register (John P. Meier argues in A Marginal Jew that, judged by historical method alone, sibling is the most probable sense).

The step-brother reading (Epiphanian, after Epiphanius of Salamis; the standard Eastern Orthodox view): the brothers were Joseph's children from a marriage prior to his betrothal to Mary — making James an older step-brother of Jesus. This reading appears as early as the second-century Protoevangelium of James, which, whatever its historical value, shows that some Christians very early understood the brothers this way. It preserves Mary's perpetual virginity without straining the word adelphos, since step-brothers are brothers in ordinary usage.

The cousin reading (Hieronymian, after Jerome, who argued it in his treatise Against Helvidius, c. 383 CE; historically the dominant Catholic view): adelphos here means kinsman — Semitic languages routinely use "brother" for cousins, and the Septuagint does the same (Genesis 13:8 calls Abraham and his nephew Lot "brothers"). Jerome identified James the brother of the Lord with James son of Alphaeus and made the brothers cousins through a sister or kinswoman of Mary.

Each reading has strengths and costs. The sibling reading is lexically simplest but collides with a doctrine held across most of Christian history. The Epiphanian reading has early attestation but rests partly on a non-canonical source. The cousin reading has genuine Semitic parallels, but critics note that Paul, writing in Greek, had a perfectly good word for cousin (anepsios, which he uses in Colossians 4:10) and did not use it of James. For the purposes of external evidence, the debate changes little: on any of the three readings, Josephus' "brother of Jesus" refers to a close kinsman of a real, recently living man — Josephus, writing in Greek for Romans, gives no sign of meaning anything but ordinary kinship. Islamic sources, for their part, affirm Mary's virginity in conceiving Jesus but simply do not address whether she had later children; the question of James's exact relation is an intra-Christian debate with no Quranic stake.

sections.title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: The Roman Witness
sections.body:
The third major external text comes from Cornelius Tacitus, widely regarded as Rome's greatest historian, writing around 115-120 CE. Narrating the great fire of Rome in 64 CE and the rumor that Nero had ordered it, Tacitus reports (Annals 15.44, in the Church and Brodribb translation): "Consequently, to get rid of the report, Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace. Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus, and a most mischievous superstition, thus checked for the moment, again broke out not only in Judaea, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome..."

What this attests is specific and limited: that a man called Christus was executed under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius; that his movement originated in Judaea; that it had reached Rome and grown large enough by 64 CE for Nero to scapegoat; and that Tacitus himself despised it. The passage is manifestly not a Christian interpolation in its tone — no Christian would call the faith a "most mischievous superstition" or its adherents "hated for their abominations" — and its authenticity as genuine Tacitus is accepted by virtually all classicists.

The honest caveats are two. First, distance: Tacitus wrote roughly eighty-five years after the crucifixion, and he does not name his source. He may have consulted official records, but he may equally have reported what was common knowledge in Rome — knowledge ultimately derived from what Christians themselves said about their founder. If so, Tacitus independently attests the existence, scale, and persecution of the movement in 64 CE, but his sentence about Pilate may not be an independent line of evidence for the execution itself. Second, a small anachronism: Tacitus calls Pilate a "procurator," whereas the inscription discovered at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 (the "Pilate Stone") shows Pilate's actual title was prefect. Skeptics read this as evidence Tacitus was not copying an official record; defenders reply that Tacitus was simply using the title current in his own day for equestrian governors, a usage found elsewhere. Most historians conclude that Tacitus provides solid, hostile, non-Christian confirmation that the movement's founder was executed under Pilate — while granting that it is confirmation of a public fact as understood in Rome, not an archival document from Judea.

sections.title: What the External Evidence Establishes — and What It Cannot
sections.body:
Taken together, and weighed with the majority of specialists, the external sources support a short list of claims: that Jesus of Nazareth existed; that he was called Christ by his followers; that he was executed by decision of Pontius Pilate (Tacitus directly; the reconstructed Josephan core as well); that he had a brother named James who led his followers in Jerusalem and was stoned to death in 62 CE at the instigation of the high priest Ananus; and that within a generation the movement bearing his name had spread from Judaea to Rome. This is why the view that Jesus never existed remains a fringe position in professional scholarship — the James anchor in particular, interlocking with Paul's first-person testimony in Galatians 1:19, is very hard to explain on the hypothesis that Jesus was a purely mythical figure. At the same time, honesty requires the inverse list: these texts cannot establish that Jesus worked miracles, that he rose from the dead, that he was the Messiah, or that he was divine. Josephus (on the majority reconstruction) affirmed none of those things; Tacitus was contemptuous of all of them. External evidence attests a man, a movement, an execution, and a brother — not a theology.

The two traditions this library compares receive that result very differently, and it is worth stating each reception in its own terms. For Christians, the external attestation of the crucifixion under Pilate corroborates the historical event on which the entire theology of redemption rests; Tacitus and Josephus are welcomed as hostile witnesses to the fact, even though the meaning of the cross remains a claim of faith beyond their reach.

For Muslims, the calculus is different. The Quran affirms Jesus' historical reality, his messiahship, and his honored status without reservation: "[And mention] when the angels said, 'O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary - distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near [to Allah].'" (Quran 3:45). Muslims therefore have no quarrel with — indeed, positive support for — the core finding that Jesus existed and towered over his time. But the Quran contests the crucifixion: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it." (Quran 4:157). Muslim scholars addressing Tacitus and Josephus typically observe that both authors report, decades later and at second hand, what was publicly believed to have happened in Jerusalem — and that the Quranic phrase "it was made to appear so to them" speaks precisely to the level of public appearance that such reports transmit. On this reading, external evidence that people in the first century believed Jesus had been crucified is exactly what the Quran itself presupposes. Historians working by ordinary critical method reply that public, proximate, multiply attested testimony is precisely what historical probability is built from, and that method cannot make room for an appearance-substitution it has no tools to detect. Both statements are correct within their own frames: the historical method yields probabilities from testimony; the Islamic position rests on revelation that claims to correct testimony. The external evidence, in other words, matters differently to each tradition — it cannot adjudicate between them, and this article does not attempt to.

sections.title: Notes on Citations, Translations, and How to Weigh This Evidence
sections.body:
Citation conventions. Antiquities 18.63-64 and 20.200 follow the modern (Niese) numbering; the same passages are Book 18, chapter 3, section 3 and Book 20, chapter 9, section 1 in William Whiston's eighteenth-century English edition, which is quoted here because it is the standard public-domain translation. Tacitus is quoted from the public-domain Church and Brodribb translation of the Annals. Origen is cited from the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation (Against Celsus 1.47; Commentary on Matthew 10.17). Bible quotations are from the World English Bible; Quran quotations are Saheeh International with the Uthmani Arabic text.

Three distinctions to keep in mind when weighing any of this. First, authenticity versus independence: a passage can be genuinely from Josephus or Tacitus and still depend, at some remove, on what Christians said about themselves — authenticity is about who wrote the words, independence about where the information came from. Second, attestation versus proof: ancient history deals in converging probabilities, not demonstrations; the majority reconstruction of the Testimonium is a strong hypothesis, not a recovered manuscript. Third, historical claims versus theological claims: the strongest reading of the external evidence establishes existence, execution, and kinship — matters in principle open to any historian — while messiahship, resurrection, and the Quranic account of the crucifixion are claims that no Roman archive or Jewish historian could settle in either direction.

Readers who want to test the arguments should read the primary texts whole: Antiquities Book 18 and Book 20 (any complete Whiston or Loeb edition), Annals Book 15, Origen's Against Celsus Book 1, and Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History Book 1 (for the first quotation of the Testimonium) and Book 2 (for Hegesippus on James). The scholarly positions summarized above are argued at full strength in the works listed under Further Reading.

title: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
subtitle: Books written in another's name — the scholarly debate over New Testament authorship, the case of 2 Peter, and how two traditions police attribution
summary: Mainstream New Testament scholarship holds that several canonical books were written in the name of an apostle by someone else — a practice known as pseudepigraphy — with 2 Peter as the most widely cited case. This article lays out the critical arguments and the reception history in the early church, then presents the conservative defenses of authenticity at full strength. It closes with a comparative Islamic lens: the Quran’s condemnation of writing texts and attributing them to God, its single-generation compilation, and the honest parallel of Islam’s own hadith-criticism sciences.

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body:
Pseudepigraphy means writing a work in someone else’s name. Mainstream New Testament scholarship — a field populated largely by Christian scholars — concludes that several canonical books carry apostolic names their actual authors did not bear. The scholarly picture is usually described in tiers: seven letters of Paul are accepted as genuine by essentially everyone; three more (Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians) are seriously disputed; and the Pastoral Epistles (1-2 Timothy, Titus) are regarded by most critical scholars as written after Paul’s death in his name. The book most widely judged pseudonymous is 2 Peter, which was also the most hesitantly received book in the early church’s own canon lists.

This article sets out the critical case in detail — dating, dependence on Jude, the delayed-parousia problem, and the reception history recorded by Eusebius — and then presents the conservative responses at full strength, including the secretary (amanuensis) hypothesis, the testament-genre debate, and scholars such as Michael Kruger and E. M. B. Green who defend Petrine authorship. It then turns to the Islamic comparative angle: the Quran’s explicit condemnation of writing texts and calling them God’s word (Quran 2:79), the contrast with the Quran’s single-generation compilation, and the honest parallel that Islam built its own vast authenticity science — hadith criticism — precisely because false attribution is a universal problem. The two traditions differ most in where each locates its divinely guaranteed core. No winner is declared; readers are given the arguments and the sources.

sections.title: What Is at Stake in a Name
sections.body:
An ancient letter that opens “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus” is making a claim: that the words which follow carry the authority of a specific, known man. If Paul wrote it, the claim is straightforward. If someone else wrote it a generation later and attached Paul’s name, historians call the result a pseudepigraphon — literally, a “falsely inscribed” writing. Whether such a text can still be considered honest, authoritative, or inspired is a separate and much-debated question; but the historical question of who actually wrote each New Testament book is one that modern scholarship treats as open to evidence.

The stakes are real for both faith traditions this library compares. For Christianity, the New Testament canon was assembled in significant part on the criterion of apostolicity — the early church asked whether a book came from an apostle or an apostle’s close associate before admitting it. If some canonical books are pseudonymous, then a criterion the early church itself applied would, on the critical view, have been unknowingly unmet. For Islam, the Quran directly condemns the writing of texts that are then presented as God’s word, and Islamic civilization built one of history’s largest critical apparatuses — the hadith sciences — to police exactly this problem of false attribution.

Two cautions frame everything that follows. First, the scholars who built the critical consensus described here were and are mostly Christians; this is standard seminary material, not polemic. Second, every judgment of pseudonymity is probabilistic — an inference from style, vocabulary, historical setting, and reception history — and serious scholars defend the traditional attributions. Both sides are presented here.

sections.title: Writing in Another’s Name in the Ancient World
sections.body:
Pseudepigraphy was widespread in antiquity. Jewish literature of the Second Temple period produced works in the names of Enoch, Moses, Solomon, and other ancient figures; Greek philosophical schools circulated letters attributed to Plato and Socrates whose authenticity was debated even in ancient times. Scholars disagree, however, about what this prevalence means. David Meade, in Pseudonymity and Canon (1986), argued that within certain Jewish traditions, writing in a revered founder’s name could function as a claim of faithful continuity with his teaching rather than as simple deceit. Bart Ehrman, in Forgery and Counterforgery (2013), argues against this that ancient readers and authors did have a concept of literary forgery and condemned it — works judged falsely attributed were labeled notha (“illegitimate” writings) and excluded.

The early church’s own behavior supports at least part of Ehrman’s point. Around the year 200, Bishop Serapion of Antioch, upon examining the so-called Gospel of Peter, wrote — as Eusebius records in Church History 6.12.3 — “For we, brethren, receive both Peter and the other apostles as Christ; but we reject intelligently the writings falsely ascribed to them, knowing that such were not handed down to us.” The Muratorian Fragment, one of the earliest canon lists, likewise rejects letters it describes as forged in Paul’s name (as translated in standard editions such as Metzger’s The Canon of the New Testament). Whatever pseudepigraphy meant elsewhere, the church that formed the canon did not knowingly accept it.

Strikingly, the New Testament itself attests that forged apostolic letters were a live concern. 2 Thessalonians warns its readers: “Now, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together to him, we ask you not to be quickly shaken in your mind, and not be troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by letter as if from us, saying that the day of Christ has already come” (2 Thessalonians 2:1-2). The same letter closes with an authentication mark: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand, which is the sign in every letter: this is how I write” (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Both sides of the modern debate appeal to these verses. Defenders of traditional authorship read them as Paul protecting his congregations from forgers. Critical scholars note that 2 Thessalonians is itself one of the disputed letters, and some (Ehrman among them) argue that an actual forger would have every motive to include exactly such an authentication device. The verses prove, at minimum, that first- and second-century Christians knew apostolic names could be — and were — falsely claimed.

sections.title: The Three Tiers of the Pauline Letters
sections.body:
Thirteen New Testament letters open in Paul’s name. Standard critical introductions — Raymond E. Brown’s An Introduction to the New Testament (1997) and Bart Ehrman’s The New Testament: A Historical Introduction are representative — describe a three-tier scholarly landscape.

First tier: seven letters are undisputed. Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon are accepted as authentically Paul’s by virtually all scholars, critical and conservative alike, on grounds of consistent style, vocabulary, theology, and historical situation.

Second tier: Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are genuinely disputed. Significant numbers of scholars line up on each side. Doubts rest on differences in sentence style and vocabulary from the undisputed letters, on developed theological themes (for example, the cosmic ecclesiology of Ephesians), and, for 2 Thessalonians, on its relationship to 1 Thessalonians. Defenders reply that Paul’s style could vary with topic, occasion, co-authors, and secretaries, and that the theological development is within one mind’s reach.

Third tier: the Pastoral Epistles — 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus — are regarded by most critical scholars as pseudonymous, written perhaps a generation after Paul. The arguments: a large share of their vocabulary appears nowhere in the undisputed letters; they presuppose a more developed church-office structure (bishops, deacons, an enrolled order of widows) than the undisputed letters reflect; and they are hard to fit into the chronology of Paul’s life as known from his other letters and Acts. Conservative scholars — D. A. Carson and Douglas Moo’s An Introduction to the New Testament is the standard counter-textbook — defend authenticity, arguing that the chronology can be accommodated by a release from Roman imprisonment and later ministry, that vocabulary shifts with subject matter and age, and that greater use of a secretary could account for much of the stylistic difference. Readers should know that the tier language describes the distribution of scholarly opinion, not a settled fact: the majority position on the Pastorals is confident but contested, and it is presented here as exactly that.

sections.title: The Case of 2 Peter: How the Early Church Received It
sections.body:
If the Pastorals are the largest disputed block, 2 Peter is the single book whose traditional attribution is most widely doubted — and the doubt is not a modern invention. It begins in the ancient church’s own records.

No surviving Christian writer clearly cites 2 Peter by name before Origen in the early third century, and Origen himself registers the doubt. As Eusebius preserves his words (Church History 6.25.8), Peter “has left one acknowledged epistle; perhaps also a second, but this is doubtful.” A century later Eusebius gave his own, blunter verdict (Church History 3.3.1): “One epistle of Peter, that called the first, is acknowledged as genuine. And this the ancient elders used freely in their own writings as an undisputed work. But we have learned that his extant second Epistle does not belong to the canon; yet, as it has appeared profitable to many, it has been used with the other Scriptures.”

When Eusebius drew up his famous classification of Christian writings (Church History 3.25), he sorted books into the acknowledged (homologoumena), the disputed (antilegomena), and the rejected. He wrote: “Among the disputed writings, which are nevertheless recognized by many, are extant the so-called epistle of James and that of Jude, also the second epistle of Peter, and those that are called the second and third of John, whether they belong to the evangelist or to another person of the same name.” 2 Peter is also absent from the Muratorian Fragment, the early canon list that already names most other New Testament books.

The hesitation eventually resolved. Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 lists 2 Peter among the seven Catholic Epistles, and the late-fourth-century councils associated with Laodicea and Carthage received it. Jerome accepted it while candidly noting that many doubted it because its style differs from 1 Peter’s — and he proposed, already in the fourth century, that Peter may have used a different secretary for each letter. Doubts resurfaced at the Reformation. Michael Kruger — himself a defender of the letter’s authenticity — opens his study of the question by summarizing this trajectory: 2 Peter “was received into the New Testament canon with hesitation, considered second-class Scripture by Luther, reluctantly accepted by Calvin, rejected by Erasmus, and now is repudiated as pseudonymous by modern scholarship” (“The Authenticity of 2 Peter,” Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society 42/4, 1999, p. 645). Standard reference works, among them The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church (3rd ed.), likewise describe 2 Peter’s admission to the canon as notably hesitant compared with other New Testament books.

sections.title: The Case of 2 Peter: The Critical Argument
sections.body:
Modern critical scholarship adds internal arguments to the ancient hesitation. J. N. D. Kelly’s much-quoted assessment in his 1969 commentary — “scarcely anyone nowadays doubts that 2 Peter is pseudonymous” (as quoted by Kruger, who disputes the verdict) — rests on several converging observations.

First, style. The Greek of 2 Peter differs markedly from that of 1 Peter — a difference so visible that Jerome already had to explain it. Critical scholars judge the two letters unlikely to come from the same hand.

Second, dependence on Jude. Nearly the whole of Jude’s short letter reappears, reworked, in 2 Peter’s second chapter, and most scholars conclude 2 Peter borrowed from Jude rather than the reverse. One parallel is especially discussed. Jude tells its readers: “But you, beloved, remember the words which have been spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said to you that ‘In the last time there will be mockers, walking after their own ungodly lusts’” (Jude 1:17-18) — the apostles’ words are recalled as a past generation’s. 2 Peter presents nearly the same prediction, but in Peter’s own voice as prophecy: “knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come, walking after their own lusts, and saying, ‘Where is the promise of his coming? For, from the day that the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation’” (2 Peter 3:3-4). On the critical reading, a later author has converted an inherited warning into an apostolic prediction after the fact.

Third, the delayed parousia. The scoffers’ taunt quoted above — where is the promised coming, “from the day that the fathers fell asleep”? — is read by most critical scholars as reflecting a time when the first Christian generation (“the fathers”) had died and the expectation of Christ’s imminent return had become an open difficulty requiring pastoral response. That situation, they argue, fits the early second century better than Peter’s lifetime (Peter’s death is traditionally placed in the 60s CE).

Fourth, the view of Paul’s letters. The epistle urges: “Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation; even as our beloved brother Paul also, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you; as also in all of his letters, speaking in them of these things. In those, there are some things that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unsettled twist, as they also do to the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:15-16). Critical scholars note that this presupposes a collected corpus of Paul’s letters, already known widely enough to be twisted by opponents, and already ranked alongside “the other Scriptures” — a situation they judge to postdate Peter.

On these grounds, most critical scholars date 2 Peter roughly between 100 and 150 CE, making it on their view the latest-written book of the New Testament. The dating is not unanimous even among those who accept pseudonymity: Richard Bauckham’s standard commentary (Jude, 2 Peter, Word Biblical Commentary, 1983) argues for the late first century and treats the letter as a “testament” — a recognized genre of farewell discourse written in a great figure’s name — which, on his reading, original audiences would not have mistaken for a letter from Peter’s own hand.

sections.title: The Conservative Case for 2 Peter — at Full Strength
sections.body:
The defense of 2 Peter’s authenticity is a serious scholarly position, not a reflex. Its modern statements include E. M. B.
