Evangelical and traditional scholarship has answered this case point by point, and its arguments deserve statement at full strength.

The most influential is the treaty-form argument, associated with Meredith Kline (Treaty of the Great King, 1963) and developed extensively by the Egyptologist Kenneth A. Kitchen (On the Reliability of the Old Testament, 2003). Ancient Near Eastern treaties changed shape over time. Late-second-millennium Hittite treaties characteristically open with a historical prologue recounting the suzerain’s past benefactions and conclude with both blessings and curses; first-millennium Assyrian treaties, including Esarhaddon’s, typically lack the historical prologue and pronounce curses without corresponding blessings. Deuteronomy has a historical prologue (the retrospect of its opening chapters) and both blessings and curses — a profile Kitchen argues matches the second-millennium pattern, the very age in which Moses is traditionally placed, better than the Assyrian pattern. On this reading, the parallels between Deuteronomy 28 and Esarhaddon’s curses reflect a common and much older ancient Near Eastern curse repertoire rather than borrowing from Assyria.

Second, commentators such as Peter C. Craigie (The Book of Deuteronomy, NICOT, 1976) and J. Gordon McConville (Deuteronomy, Apollos Old Testament Commentary, 2002) argue that the book’s content fits its stated setting better than a Josianic one. The centralization formula never names Jerusalem: “the place which Yahweh your God shall choose” is left open — an odd feature for a document allegedly composed to exalt Jerusalem, and one that these scholars read as genuine pre-monarchic perspective. McConville has argued that Deuteronomy’s provisions for prophets, judges, and a sharply limited kingship read like a constitution for a community about to enter the land rather than a description of Josiah’s centralized state.

Third, the found-book account of 2 Kings 22 is read straightforwardly: an old law book, neglected during two generations of officially sponsored idolatry under Manasseh and Amon, resurfaced during temple repairs. Depositing law texts and inscriptions in temples — and rediscovering them generations later — is a practice attested across the ancient Near East, so the narrative’s own claim is historically plausible on its face.

Finally, many conservative scholars hold a mediating position: the covenant structure, legal core, and speeches derive from Moses, while acknowledged post-Mosaic elements — the death narrative of chapter 34, updated place names, the “to this day” notices, and the final editorial frame — reflect later scribal activity, which such scholars regard as itself carried out under inspiration. On this view the real alternatives are not “all Moses” versus “all seventh century”: an authentically Mosaic tradition was preserved, updated, and eventually promulgated — possibly the very event 2 Kings 22 records. Critics reply that once substantial editing is granted, the disagreement becomes one of degree; conservatives answer that a document’s origin and its later editing are distinct questions, and that the case for denying the Mosaic origin of the substance has not been made. The reader should know that this mediating position, not a rigid word-for-word Mosaic authorship, is what most careful conservative scholarship actually defends.

sections.title: The Comparative Question: Dating Gaps and Authority Claims
sections.body:
Why does a dating question belong on a site comparing Islam and Christianity? Because both traditions make claims about scripture, and composition history is part of how such claims are examined — though the two traditions frame their claims differently, and the comparison is only fair if that difference is kept in view.

Muslim writers regularly point to the contrast in compilation history. On the traditional Islamic account, the Quran was written down piecemeal by scribes during Muhammad’s own lifetime, collected into a complete copy within about two years of his death under Abu Bakr, and standardized as a single consonantal text under Uthman within roughly twenty years — a gap of years and decades between recitation and fixed text, not centuries. Muhammad Mustafa al-Azami’s The History of the Qur’anic Text from Revelation to Compilation (2003) develops precisely this comparison with the Old and New Testaments, arguing that the shortness of the Quran’s transmission chain gives it an evidential character that, in his assessment, the Torah’s history cannot match. The Quran itself claims divine preservation — “Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian.” (Quran 15:9) — and describes its own deliberately staged revelation (Quran 25:32). For writers in this tradition, a book whose scholarly dating places its final form six centuries after its narrative setting cannot carry the same kind of guarantee.

The response from Jewish and Christian scholarship is that this argument measures the Bible against the Quran’s doctrine of scripture rather than the Bible’s own. Islam claims verbatim divine dictation of a single text to a single prophet; on that claim, a short and well-documented compilation history matters enormously, and Muslim theology is right to prize it. Mainstream Judaism and Christianity, in both academic and many confessional forms, locate the Torah’s authority elsewhere: in God’s inspiration working through a people’s long history of tradition, composition, editing, and canonical reception. On that account, a seventh-century crystallization of older Mosaic tradition is not an embarrassment but the expected shape of the process — the community that transmitted the tradition is part of how, on this view, God gave the book. Traditional Jews and confessional Christians who continue to hold Mosaic authorship as doctrine take a different route: they contest the critical dating itself, as the previous section describes. Both responses exist, and they are not the same response.

Fairness also requires the mirror observation: the Quran’s early textual history has its own scholarly discussions — manuscript variants, the canonical readings (qira’at), and finds such as the Sanaa palimpsest — which this site treats in its preservation series rather than glossing over. Whether a centuries-long, community-borne composition or a decades-long, rapidly standardized compilation better fits what a revelation from God should look like is not a question historical evidence alone can settle; it depends on what each tradition understands revelation to be. This article presents the evidence and leaves that judgment with the reader.

sections.title: Where the Evidence Stands: Consensus, Contested, Minority
sections.body:
It helps to sort the claims in this article by how firmly they are held.

Near-consensus in academic biblical studies: the final form of Deuteronomy is later than Moses; chapter 34 was not written by the man whose death it narrates (a point on which the Talmudic rabbis themselves debated, and which most conservative scholars concede in some form); and the book’s centralization program is closely tied, at the latest, to the last century of the Judahite monarchy.

Widely held but contested: the identification of Deuteronomy’s core with the scroll found under Josiah in 622 BCE (the de Wette hypothesis); direct literary dependence of Deuteronomy 13 and 28 on Esarhaddon’s Succession Treaty (affirmed by Steymans and others, doubted by Crouch); and the precise placement of the core in the seventh century rather than under Hezekiah earlier or in the exile later.

Minority positions defended in serious scholarship: substantial Mosaic authorship with limited later updating, argued chiefly in evangelical scholarship (Kitchen, Craigie, McConville) and presupposed in traditional Jewish and classical Christian doctrine.

Primary sources a reader can check directly: the book of Deuteronomy (especially chapters 1, 12, 28, 31, and 34); 2 Kings 22–23; the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a, for the rabbinic discussion of the last eight verses; and Esarhaddon’s Succession Treaty, available in English translation, with the Tell Tayinat copy published by Jacob Lauinger in the Journal of Cuneiform Studies (2012). The scholarly works representing each side are listed under Further Reading. All Bible quotations above were copied exactly from the World English Bible and all Quran quotations from the Saheeh International translation; readers are encouraged to verify every reference against the sources themselves.

title: Why Would God Allow Scripture to Be Corrupted?
subtitle: The question that rebounds: divine faithfulness, human trust, and what each tradition believes God actually promised to protect
summary: After the historical evidence about textual transmission has been laid out, Muslims and Christians often turn to a more basic theological question: if the Torah and Gospel are from God, why would He allow them to be altered at all — and does the same question apply to the Quran? This article presents the Christian argument from divine faithfulness (Isaiah 40:8, Matthew 24:35), the Islamic framework distinguishing scriptures entrusted to human guardianship (Quran 5:44, 2:79) from the Quran's own direct divine guarantee (Quran 15:9), the internal Muslim debate over what "corruption" (tahrif) actually means, and the Christian counter-arguments this raises. It closes with a philosophical look at free will and divine testing, and with what evidence each side would need to strengthen its own case.

sections.title: The Short Answer
sections.body:
After Muslims and Christians work through the historical and manuscript evidence for how the Quran and the Bible were each transmitted, the conversation often lands on a blunter theological question: if the Torah and the Gospel really came from God, why would God allow them to be altered at all? Doesn't a God who is perfectly faithful owe His revelation better protection than that? Christians raise this forcefully, pointing to verses like Isaiah 40:8 and Matthew 24:35, both of which describe God's word as something that endures no matter what happens around it.

The Quran's own answer distinguishes between two different situations rather than treating "preservation" as one fixed promise God always makes the same way. Earlier communities, in the Islamic framework, were entrusted with guarding their own scriptures — the Quran describes rabbis and scholars as answerable "by that with which they were entrusted of the Scripture of Allah" (Quran 5:44) — and the Quran also accuses some individuals of writing things "with their own hands" and calling it revelation (Quran 2:79). Guarding the text, on this reading, was a human responsibility that could be dropped, and Islamic tradition holds that in places it was. The Quran describes its own situation differently: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9) — a direct divine guarantee rather than a delegated human task, tied to the claim that the Quran is God's final revelation with no future prophet left to correct any drift in it.

Christians raise a fair counter-question at exactly this point: why trust a text's own claim about its own preservation? And a second one: doesn't the same logic that indicts earlier scriptures for having any human transmission history apply just as much to the Quran, which also has one? This article lays out the Christian case for divine faithfulness, the Islamic framework of entrustment and guarantee, the classical Muslim debate over what "corruption" (tahrif) even means, and the honest, symmetrical way both traditions answer the deeper question of how God's promises interact with human freedom to fail Him.

sections.title: A Question That Comes After the Evidence
sections.body:
This question tends to surface at a specific point in an Islamic-Christian conversation: after someone has already walked through the manuscript history — the many surviving Greek New Testament manuscripts with their textual variants, the centuries it took to settle the biblical canon, the way Quranic memorization and early manuscripts relate to each other — and a Muslim has argued that the historical evidence shows meaningful change in the Bible's text over time in a way it does not for the Quran. At that point, a Christian will often step back from the details and ask the deeper question directly: if the Torah and the Gospel really are from God, why would God let that happen at all? Isn't the claim that a text was altered, all by itself, a strange thing to say about a book God supposedly wanted people to keep?

This is not a minor objection, and it deserves to be taken at full strength rather than answered with a history lesson alone, because at bottom it is not a historical question — it is a question about God's character and promises. It also, honestly, rebounds: if divine faithfulness requires that a scripture be protected from human tampering, a Muslim has to explain why that same requirement does not fall just as hard on the Quran, which also passed through human hands, memories, and manuscripts. This article tries to take both sides of that exchange seriously, in roughly the order they usually arise.

sections.title: God's Faithfulness to His Word
sections.body:
The Christian argument starts from a straightforward premise: God is not fickle, weak, or absent from history, and Scripture itself repeatedly describes God's own word as something that cannot be defeated by time, human failure, or hostile editing. The prophet Isaiah puts it starkly in the middle of a passage about how frail and temporary human life is: "The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever" (Isaiah 40:8). The contrast is deliberate — everything human is compared to grass that dries up in a season, while God's own speech is placed in a completely different category, one that does not fade with time.

Jesus makes what many Christians read as an even stronger claim about his own words specifically, in the middle of a discourse about the end of the age: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." (Matthew 24:35). Read at face value, this places the durability of Jesus' own teaching above the durability of the physical universe itself. For Christians who hold this text to be trustworthy testimony about what Jesus actually said, it is difficult to square that promise with the idea that his teaching, or the Scriptures that record it, could simply be lost, garbled, or overwritten by later scribes without God doing anything to stop it.

Put together, these verses ground a coherent theological argument: a God who is powerful enough to create the universe and who promises that His word endures forever should be understood to have both the ability and the will to protect that word's actual content, not merely its underlying "message" in some vaguer sense. On this reading, the idea that the text supposedly carrying God's message was significantly altered by human beings, without God intervening, sits uneasily next to God's own stated commitment to His word's endurance. This is the objection at its strongest, and it deserves an answer that engages the actual theological claim, not just the manuscript evidence.

sections.title: Entrusted to Guard, and Failing the Trust
sections.body:
The Islamic framework answers this question by first distinguishing between two very different kinds of relationship a community can have with its scripture: being given a book to guard, versus being given a guarantee that the book cannot be lost. The Quran describes earlier scripture in the first category. Speaking of the Torah, it says: "Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light. The prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged by it for the Jews, as did the rabbis and scholars by that with which they were entrusted of the Scripture of Allah, and they were witnesses thereto. So do not fear the people but fear Me, and do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the disbelievers." (Quran 5:44). On the standard Muslim reading, this verse places responsibility for guarding the Torah's content on the human scholars and rabbis who received and transmitted it — they are described as entrusted with it, not as passive recipients of an automatic divine seal that made tampering impossible regardless of what they did.

The Quran goes further, accusing some individuals of actively breaking that trust rather than simply failing to keep it through neglect: "So woe to those who write the "scripture" with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," in order to exchange it for a small price. Woe to them for what their hands have written and woe to them for what they earn." (Quran 2:79). Read together, these verses present a specific claim: that guarding earlier revelation was a delegated human responsibility, and that at least some of the people entrusted with it did not meet that responsibility — whether through misinterpretation, selective transmission, or, on the reading many classical Muslim scholars held, through actually writing things and attaching God's name to them.

This matters for the theological question at hand because it reframes what "God allowing corruption" would even mean in the Islamic framework. God did not promise, on this reading, that the Torah and Gospel's wording would be automatically protected regardless of human conduct; He entrusted communities with that task and held them accountable for the outcome, the same way the Quran elsewhere holds individuals accountable for other moral and religious failures. Failing to guard something one was trusted with is, in the Quran's own moral vocabulary, a human failure — not evidence that God is either powerless or unfaithful.

sections.title: A Different Promise for the Final Revelation
sections.body:
Having described earlier scripture as entrusted to human guardians, the Quran describes its own situation in different terms entirely. Rather than delegating the task, God states that He personally undertakes it: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Qur'an and indeed, We will be its guardian." (Quran 15:9). The grammar itself marks the shift — the verse uses an emphatic construction ("Indeed, it is We") that Muslim exegetes have long read as underscoring that this guardianship is not shared with, or delegated to, any human community, unlike the Torah's guardianship, which the Quran describes as belonging to "the rabbis and scholars" in 5:44.

Islamic theology ties this different arrangement to a specific claim about religious history: that prophethood itself functioned, across the earlier history described in the Quran and the Bible alike, as the mechanism God used to correct communities that had drifted from His message. A new prophet could be sent to restate, clarify, or correct what earlier generations had lost, misapplied, or altered — part of why, in the Islamic framework, so many prophets appear across the biblical narrative rather than just one. Muhammad, in Islamic belief, is the final prophet, after whom Muslims hold there will be no successor sent to correct any future drift in the message. If that claim is true, then a delegated, humanly-guarded scripture with no future corrective mechanism would leave the final message permanently exposed in a way earlier messages were not — which Islamic theology presents as the reason this one revelation needed, and received, a direct divine guarantee rather than a delegated one.

This is a coherent internal logic: earlier communities were trusted with guardianship because more prophets would come to correct any failure; the final community was given God's own guarantee because no further prophet would come after it. Whether that internal logic is persuasive depends on prior claims — that Muhammad is in fact the final prophet, and that Quran 15:9 is in fact a reliable divine guarantee rather than a human author's confident assertion about his own book — both of which are contested by non-Muslims and examined further below.

sections.title: How Corrupted, Exactly? A Debate Inside Islamic Scholarship
sections.body:
It is worth pausing on a detail often skipped in popular Muslim-Christian debate: Muslim scholars themselves have never spoken with one voice about what "tahrif" (corruption) of the Torah and Gospel actually means, or how far it goes. A detailed academic survey of classical Islamic theology on this question, by Ramazan Biçer ("The Alteration of the Sacred Books According to the Islamic Theologians," RAIS Conference Proceedings, June 2020), traces two competing readings across the classical tradition: tahrif al-lafz (alteration of the actual wording of the text) and tahrif al-ma'na, sometimes called tahrif manawi (distortion of meaning through false interpretation, while the wording itself stays intact).

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 1209), the influential jurist and Quran commentator whose Tafsir al-Kabir remains one of the most cited works of classical Quranic exegesis, addresses this directly when discussing the verses that accuse the People of the Book of tahrif. According to Biçer's survey of that commentary, al-Razi lists several possible senses of the term, including outright substitution of words, but singles out attributing a false interpretation to the text (al-ta'wilat al-batila) as, in his own assessment, the best explanation of what the Quran means by tahrif — that is, tahrif al-ma'na rather than tahrif al-lafz. The same survey finds Abu Mansur al-Maturidi (d. 944), another foundational Sunni theologian, leaning the same direction: toward reading tahrif primarily as misinterpretation rather than physical alteration of the text. Other scholars in the broader tradition, including the ninth-century Zaydi imam al-Qasim al-Rassi, likewise framed the Christian error as a matter of failing to correctly understand their own scriptures rather than possessing a physically falsified text, while later scholars, including Ibn Hazm (d. 1064), argued more forcefully for textual corruption itself (tahrif al-nass).

This internal diversity matters for a fair presentation of the question. It means the claim "the Quran teaches that Jews and Christians physically altered the wording of their scriptures" is not simply "the Islamic view" in any uncontested sense — it is one reading among others that respected classical scholars have held, alongside a competing reading, associated with figures such as al-Razi and al-Maturidi, that the Quran's charge of tahrif is best understood as accusing earlier communities of misinterpreting or misapplying scripture whose wording remained basically intact. Both readings remain live within Islamic scholarship today, and which one a given Muslim scholar or apologist reaches for often shapes how sharply they press the "corruption" argument against the Bible's transmission history.

sections.title: The Christian Response, at Full Strength
sections.body:
Christian theology and scholarship offer several responses to the Islamic framework above, and they deserve to be presented with the same seriousness given to the Islamic case.

The first response leans directly on the internal Muslim debate just described. If respected classical scholars such as al-Razi and al-Maturidi read the Quran's own charge of tahrif as being about misinterpretation rather than textual alteration, then Christians can argue that even by Islamic scholarship's own internal standards, the Quran does not clearly convict the Bible of having a corrupted text — only, at most, of having been misread or misapplied by some of its readers at some point. On this reading, the premise behind the objection this article addresses — "why would God allow the text itself to be altered" — may rest on a stronger reading of tahrif than the Quran itself requires, since a real and respected strand of Islamic exegesis, not merely modern Christian apologetics, treats tahrif as primarily interpretive.

The second response is the reliability argument, made independently of how tahrif is read. Christian textual critics — including scholars such as Bruce M. Metzger and, from an evangelical apologetic angle, F. F. Bruce — argue that the number and antiquity of surviving New Testament manuscripts allow scholars to reconstruct a text substantially identical to the original, with the many documented variants overwhelmingly affecting spelling, word order, or minor wording rather than core doctrine. On this view, God's promise that His word "stands forever" (Isaiah 40:8) does not require that every handwritten copy across centuries of hand-copying be flawlessly identical; it requires that the message God intended to convey survive intact and recoverable, and textual criticism itself is offered as the evidence that it did. Some manuscript variation, on this argument, is compatible with — and even expected within — a text that God has, in the sense that actually matters, preserved well enough.

The third response is the most philosophically pointed, because it turns the Islamic framework's own logic back on itself, and Muslim scholarship has generally engaged it honestly rather than dismissing it. If Quran 15:9's guarantee is what makes the Quran trustworthy where the Bible supposedly is not, a Christian can reasonably ask: why believe that particular verse's claim about itself? A text asserting its own perfect preservation is not, by itself, proof that the assertion is true — every scripture that makes strong claims about itself faces some version of this question. The honest answer, from the Islamic side, is not that Quran 15:9 can be independently verified by some standard entirely external to Islamic revelation; it is a claim of faith, exactly as the claims in Isaiah 40:8 and Matthew 24:35 are claims of faith for Christians. What can be examined without simply assuming the conclusion is the historical record each text actually left behind — the manuscripts, the memorization networks, the compilation history — which is precisely the ground this library's preservation-branch articles were written to examine in detail, rather than settling the question by appeal to either text's self-description alone.

sections.title: Free Will and the Trust God Places in People
sections.body:
Underneath the exegetical and historical arguments sits a shared philosophical commitment that both traditions affirm, even though they apply it to different conclusions. Both Islam and Christianity hold that God gave human beings genuine freedom, including the freedom to fail moral and religious trusts God places in them — and that this freedom is not a flaw in creation but a necessary feature of it, since forced obedience would not be the kind of relationship with God either tradition holds He desires. Both traditions also hold that God tests people, sometimes precisely by placing something valuable in their hands and observing what they do with it, and that God's own faithfulness is not disproven by human beings failing tests He allows them to face.

Where Islam and Christianity diverge is not on whether God permits human failure — both say He does — but on which specific failures each believes actually occurred, and where the line was drawn between what was entrusted to human guardianship and what God guaranteed directly. Islamic theology holds that the trust to guard the Torah and Gospel's wording was placed in the hands of the communities that received them, and that this trust, in at least some places, was not kept, while the final revelation was placed under God's own direct guarantee precisely because no further corrective prophet would follow it. Christian theology holds, by contrast, that God's covenant faithfulness extends to preserving the substance and message of His revealed word across the very same history Muslims describe as compromised, whether that confidence is grounded, as it is for many Catholic and Orthodox Christians, in a Spirit-guided church community carrying the message forward, or, as it is for many Protestants and evangelicals holding to sola scriptura, in the demonstrated textual reliability of the transmitted manuscripts themselves.

Neither position requires denying free will, and neither requires denying that God tests His creatures. What each tradition denies is that God's own promises were broken by the specific failures it believes did or did not happen to its own central text — which means the real disagreement, once the historical and exegetical arguments are laid on the table, is less about whether humans can fail a divine trust and more about the historical question of whether, and where, they actually did.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.body:
One common misconception is that this question only cuts one way, forcing Christians onto the defensive while leaving Islam untouched. In fact, as this article has shown, the same question of "why would God allow His word to be altered by human hands" rebounds directly onto the Quran's own claim in 15:9, since that claim is also a textual self-description that can only be checked against a real transmission history rather than accepted as self-certifying. Fairness requires holding both traditions to the same standard: a scripture's claim about its own preservation is a starting point for historical investigation in both cases, not a substitute for it.

A second misconception is that "tahrif" straightforwardly means, and has always meant, that Jews and Christians physically forged their scriptures word for word. As the classical debate between tahrif al-lafz and tahrif al-ma'na shows, this has never been the only Islamic reading, and influential scholars such as al-Razi and al-Maturidi leaned toward the more modest interpretive reading. Presenting "the Islamic position" as uniformly the harshest possible reading of tahrif overstates the tradition's actual internal diversity.

A third misconception, from the Christian side, is that pointing to New Testament manuscript variants is equivalent to admitting the text was corrupted in the way the Quran describes earlier scripture as corrupted. Mainstream Christian textual criticism, including scholarship produced by Christian scholars themselves, generally holds that documented manuscript variants are real but overwhelmingly minor, and that they are evidence of an ordinary, well-documented hand-copying process rather than of deliberate falsification of the kind Quran 2:79 describes. Conflating "some copying variation exists" with "the text was corrupted by design" flattens a distinction both sides ought to preserve.

sections.title: What Would It Take to Settle This?
sections.body:
This article does not declare a winner, because the disagreement rests on a genuine difference in what each tradition believes God actually promised, and that difference cannot be resolved by evidence about manuscripts alone — such evidence only shows what happened to a text's wording, not what God promised regarding it in the first place. What can be said honestly is what each side would need to show to make its own case stronger, on its own terms.

A Muslim case for the Islamic framework would be strengthened by showing, in detail and against the strongest counter-evidence, that the actual transmission history of the Quran — the interlocking record of memorization and early manuscript compilation examined in this library's preservation-branch articles — matches the specific, verbatim guarantee Quran 15:9 describes, rather than treating that guarantee as self-evidently true because the Quran states it. A Christian case for the Christian framework would be strengthened by showing, with comparable historical rigor, that the New Testament's documented manuscript variants really do fall short of touching the substance of the gospel message, in line with what textual critics such as Metzger and Bruce argue, and by engaging directly with the internal Muslim debate over tahrif al-ma'na rather than treating "the Quran says our scripture was corrupted" as a single, uncontested Islamic claim.

Both sides, in other words, would need to do the same kind of work: test a scripture's claim about itself against the actual, checkable history of how that scripture reached the present day, rather than resolving the question by appeal to the strength of the claim alone. That is the spirit in which this library's preservation-branch articles were written, and it is the same spirit this article has tried to apply to the theological question of why God would allow — or not allow — His word to be altered in the first place.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Does the Quran say the Bible's text itself was physically changed, or just misinterpreted?
A: Classical Islamic scholarship is genuinely divided on this. Some scholars read the Quran's charge of tahrif (Quran 2:79, 5:44, and related verses) as accusing earlier communities of literally altering wording (tahrif al-lafz). Others, including influential commentators such as Fakhr al-Din al-Razi and Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, read it primarily as misinterpretation of scripture whose wording remained largely intact (tahrif al-ma'na). Both readings have real standing within the Islamic tradition.

Q: If God guarantees the Quran in 15:9, why couldn't God have made the same guarantee for the Torah and Gospel?
A: The Islamic answer is that revelation was structured differently across history: earlier scriptures were followed by further prophets who could correct any drift, so their communities were entrusted with guardianship rather than given an unconditional divine guarantee, while the Quran, as the final revelation with no successor prophet to come, is described as directly guarded by God. Whether this explanation is convincing depends on accepting the prior claim that Muhammad is the final prophet, which is itself a matter of faith commitment rather than something the argument can prove on its own.

Q: Isn't it circular for Muslims to use Quran 15:9 to prove the Quran was preserved?
A: Taken alone, yes — a text's claim about its own reliability cannot prove that claim by itself, and this article treats that as an honest problem rather than explaining it away. Muslims typically respond by pointing past the verse itself to the historical record of memorization and manuscript transmission as the actual evidence, which is exactly the kind of evidence this library's preservation-branch articles examine.

Q: Do Christians believe every copy of every Bible manuscript is word-for-word identical?
A: No mainstream Christian scholar claims this. Textual critics openly document many manuscript variants across the New Testament's transmission history. The Christian argument is not that no variation exists, but that the variation which does exist is minor enough, in the judgment of scholars such as Bruce M. Metzger and F. F. Bruce, that the substance of the message God intended has still been reliably preserved.

Q: Does raising this question count as an attack on either faith?
A: It shouldn't be treated that way. Both Christians and Muslims take their scripture's reliability seriously enough to have produced centuries of careful scholarship examining exactly this question from the inside, including Muslim scholars debating tahrif's meaning among themselves and Christian textual critics cataloguing known manuscript variants. Engaging the question in that spirit, rather than as a rhetorical trap, is this article's aim.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body: The works below represent both the Islamic scholarship on tahrif discussed in this article and Christian scholarship on New Testament transmission, so readers can examine the primary arguments on both sides rather than relying on this article's summary alone.

title: Women's Worth: Classical Christian Voices and the Islamic Tradition
subtitle: What Tertullian, Jerome, Aquinas, and Basil wrote about women — verified and in context — read alongside the Quran, the hadith, and both traditions' modern responses
summary: A documentary survey of what four influential classical Christian authorities — Tertullian, Jerome, Thomas Aquinas, and Basil of Caesarea — wrote about women, with every quotation verified against standard scholarly editions and cited by work and section. The same standard of honesty is applied to the Islamic tradition, including the contested "deficient in intellect and religion" hadith and the Quran's equality verses. Both traditions' mainstream responses and internal reform conversations are presented at full strength, with no winner declared.

sections.title: What This Survey Does
sections.body:
This article is a documentary survey. It gathers what four of the most influential classical Christian authorities — Tertullian, Jerome, Basil of Caesarea, and Thomas Aquinas — actually wrote about women, quoting each from a standard scholarly translation and naming the work and section so any reader can check the words. It then places those texts beside the Islamic tradition's own record: the hadith most often raised against Islam on this subject, quoted in full with its precise citation, and the Quranic passages that Muslims cite as the tradition's charter of spiritual equality.

The rules of the survey are strict. Every quotation was verified character-for-character against a named, publicly accessible edition: the Ante-Nicene Fathers and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translations hosted at newadvent.org and tertullian.org, the English Dominican translation of the Summa Theologiae, the World English Bible, the Tanzil Uthmani text with the Saheeh International translation, and the standard English hadith translations following sunnah.com numbering. One famous line commonly attributed to Jerome could not be verified in an accessible primary text; it is reported below as an attribution, with that caveat stated plainly, rather than quoted as verified.

What the survey is not: it is not evidence that either faith, as a faith, despises women, and it is not a scorecard. Both traditions contain harsh texts, generous texts, and long centuries of interpreters arguing over both kinds. The later sections present the mainstream Christian responses to these patristic and medieval passages at full strength, apply the same honesty to the Islamic corpus, and end with the reform conversations happening inside each tradition. The article deliberately declares no winner.

sections.title: The Texts Both Traditions Start From
sections.body:
Classical authorities did not write in a vacuum; they interpreted scriptures their communities already held sacred, through the science and custom of their times. On the Christian side, the baseline texts pull in more than one direction. Genesis 1:27 places male and female together in the creation of God's image: "God created man in his own image. In God's image he created him; male and female he created them." Genesis 2:18 introduces the word that Aquinas would later build on: "It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him." The Levitical purity code, including Leviticus 15:19 on menstrual impurity, shaped later Christian debates about women and sacred space even though most Christians held the ceremonial law fulfilled. In the New Testament, 1 Timothy 2:12-14 grounds a teaching restriction in Eve's creation order and deception, while Galatians 3:28 declares that in Christ "there is neither male nor female." Which of these texts controls the reading of the others is precisely what Christians have argued about for two millennia.

The Islamic baseline shows a parallel structure. Quran 4:1 addresses humanity as created "from one soul" from which its mate was created — with no doctrine of Eve as the first sinner; in the Quranic account of the garden, Adam and his wife err together and are forgiven together. Quran 33:35 lists ten spiritual virtues in deliberately paired masculine and feminine forms and promises both sexes the same forgiveness and reward. Quran 9:71 makes believing men and women awliya — allies and protectors — of one another. Alongside these stand texts Muslims debate internally, notably Quran 2:228, which affirms that wives' rights mirror their obligations "according to what is reasonable" while adding that men have "a degree" over them — a phrase whose meaning (responsibility for maintenance, divorce procedure, or broader authority) is itself a centuries-old interpretive dispute.

With those baselines in view, the classical voices can be heard as what they were: interpreters, not founders.

sections.title: Tertullian: "You Are the Devil's Gateway"
sections.body:
Tertullian of Carthage (c. 155-220) stands at the head of Latin Christianity. He is often called the father of Western theology, and he is generally credited as the first Latin author whose surviving works apply the word trinitas to God — the term that became the Latin church's name for its central doctrine. His treatise On the Apparel of Women (De cultu feminarum) is a two-book exhortation urging Christian women toward plain, penitential dress. Its opening chapter — addressed, in his own words, to his "best beloved sisters" — contains perhaps the most quoted sentence any church father ever wrote about women:

"And do you not know that you are (each) an Eve? The sentence of God on this sex of yours lives in this age: the guilt must of necessity live too. You are the devil's gateway: you are the unsealer of that (forbidden) tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law: you are she who persuaded him whom the devil was not valiant enough to attack. You destroyed so easily God's image, man. On account of your desert — that is, death — even the Son of God had to die." (On the Apparel of Women, Book I, chapter 1; Ante-Nicene Fathers translation, newadvent.org)

The argument is explicit: Eve's guilt lives on in every woman, and a Christian woman should therefore dress as one mourning and repentant. The reasoning extends the logic found in 1 Timothy 2:12-14 — where Eve's deception grounds a restriction on women teaching — into a claim about inherited, sex-specific guilt that goes beyond anything the New Testament text itself states.

Readers who defend Tertullian's memory add context rather than denial. The treatise belongs to the flamboyant rhetoric of Roman North African moralism; its addressees are women he calls beloved sisters and treats as full members of the church whose conduct can glorify God; and in his treatise To His Wife the same author describes the shared prayer and charity of a Christian couple in warm, admiring terms. Historians also note the irony that Tertullian later attached himself to the New Prophecy movement, which honored the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla. None of that erases the passage; it locates it. Tertullian was never canonized, and no church treats his sentences as doctrine.

sections.title: Jerome: Asceticism, Marriage, and the Purity Question
sections.body:
Jerome (c. 342-420), translator of the Latin Vulgate, was the most formidable biblical scholar of the early Latin church, and his letters and polemics carried immense weight in the medieval West. Two strands of his writing matter here.

The first is his ascetic ranking of women's states of life. In Against Jovinianus (393), answering a monk who taught that marriage and virginity stood equal before God, Jerome pressed Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 7:1 — "it is good for a man not to touch a woman" — to a severe conclusion: "It is good, he says, for a man not to touch a woman. If it is good not to touch a woman, it is bad to touch one: for there is no opposite to goodness but badness." (Against Jovinianus, Book I, section 7; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation, newadvent.org). In the same book he ranks virginity, widowhood, and marriage as hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. His Letter 22 to Eustochium states the hierarchy with famous bluntness: "I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell." (Letter 22, section 20). Contemporaries protested that this effectively disparaged marriage — and Jerome spent years insisting he had not condemned it.

The second strand is purity. A line widely repeated in histories of menstruation — that nothing is so unclean as a menstruating woman, and that what she touches becomes unclean — is commonly attributed to Jerome's commentary on Zechariah. This survey could not verify that wording in an accessible primary text, so it is reported here strictly as an attribution, not as a verified quotation. What is documentable is the framework around it. Leviticus 15:19 declares a menstruating woman ritually impure, and parts of the early church debated whether such purity rules touched Christian worship. Dionysius of Alexandria's canonical letter to Basilides (c. 247) ruled: "Menstruous women ought not to come to the Holy Table, or touch the Holy of Holies, nor to churches, but pray elsewhere." (Canonical Epistle, Canon II; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 14, tertullian.org). Yet the tradition was not uniform: the responsum of Pope Gregory I preserved in Bede's Ecclesiastical History (Book I, chapter 27) ruled the other way, holding that a menstruating woman should not be forbidden church or communion, while praising restraint as devout. Historians of Christian worship, such as Elizabeth Clark, document how purity-based hesitations nonetheless contributed in some times and places to distancing women from the altar and from liturgical roles.

sections.title: Aquinas: "Defective and Misbegotten" and the Biology Behind It
sections.body:
Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225-1274) is the most authoritative theologian of the medieval Latin church, and his Summa Theologiae remains a touchstone of Catholic thought. In the First Part, question 92, article 1, he asks whether woman should have been made in the first production of things. The first objection quotes Aristotle's biology: "the female is a misbegotten male." Aquinas answers that woman's creation was necessary — but his stated reason narrows her purpose: "It was necessary for woman to be made, as the Scripture says, as a 'helper' to man; not, indeed, as a helpmate in other works, as some say, since man can be more efficiently helped by another man in other works; but as a helper in the work of generation." (Summa Theologiae I, q. 92, a. 1; English Dominican translation, newadvent.org). This reads Genesis 2:18's "helper" as a specifically reproductive office.

His reply to the Aristotelian objection concedes its biology at the individual level: "As regards the individual nature, woman is defective and misbegotten, for the active force in the male seed tends to the production of a perfect likeness in the masculine sex; while the production of woman comes from defect in the active force or from some material indisposition, or even from some external influence; such as that of a south wind, which is moist, as the Philosopher observes" — before adding the correction that "as regards human nature in general, woman is not misbegotten, but is included in nature's intention as directed to the work of generation." In the Latin, the operative words are deficiens and occasionatum. The framework is Aristotle's Generation of Animals: the male seed was thought to be the active, form-giving principle aiming to reproduce its like, so that a female birth signaled the seed's aim incompletely realized. Aquinas also holds, in the same question, that "woman is naturally subject to man, because in man the discretion of reason predominates" — a subjection he classes as the benign, "economic or civil" kind that would have existed even before sin. In question 93 he affirms that "the image of God, in its principal signification, namely the intellectual nature, is found both in man and in woman," while adding that "in a secondary sense the image of God is found in man, and not in woman."

Modern Christian assessment spans a spectrum. The egalitarian organization CBE International published a pointed critique by church historian Joe Early ("Thomas Aquinas's 'Misbegotten' Concept of Women," Priscilla Papers 38.4, 2024), arguing that Aquinas's fusion of Aristotelian embryology with theology cast women as defective males suited mainly for childbearing, that this diminished their share in God's image in practice, and that the prestige his system enjoyed after the Council of Trent carried the obsolete biology deep into later tradition. Defenders of Aquinas reply that he explicitly denies woman is a defect in nature's overall intention, that both sexes for him are directly willed by God and equally bear the image of God in its principal sense, and that the "misbegotten" language collapses with the medieval science it depended on — which the Catholic Church has long since abandoned.

sections.title: Basil of Caesarea: Canon 9 and the Double Standard of Custom
sections.body:
Basil of Caesarea (c. 330-379), one of the three Cappadocian fathers and a saint in both Eastern and Western Christianity, wrote a series of canonical letters to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, that were later received into Eastern Orthodox canon law. Letter 188, his First Canonical Letter (c. 374), addresses in its ninth canon the asymmetry between men and women in divorce.

Basil begins by acknowledging that the Gospel standard is symmetrical: "The sentence of the Lord that it is unlawful to withdraw from wedlock, save on account of fornication, applies, according to the argument, to men and women alike. Custom, however, does not so obtain." (Letter 188, canon 9; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation, newadvent.org). The "sentence of the Lord" is Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:32. Basil then records the double standard of his society without overturning it: "Yet custom ordains that men who commit adultery and are in fornication be retained by their wives." A wife's grounds for leaving are examined one by one, and it is here that the canon's hardest sentence appears: "In the case of her being beaten, and refusing to submit, it would be better for her to endure than to be separated from her husband; in the case of her objecting to pecuniary loss, even here she would not have sufficient ground."

Read carefully, the canon does two things at once. It candidly notices that custom contradicts the Lord's even-handed rule — Basil twice contrasts what "custom" ordains with what the Gospel says, and some historians read those remarks as implicit criticism of the custom he was bound to administer. And yet it counsels a beaten wife to endure rather than separate, and penalizes her, not her husband, if she leaves. Eastern canonists later worked within this framework for centuries.

Modern churches of every major tradition have explicitly repudiated the pastoral application of such counsel to abuse. The United States Catholic bishops' pastoral statement When I Call for Help (1992, reaffirmed 2002) condemns the use of the Bible to keep women in abusive relationships and states that separation for safety is morally legitimate; comparable statements exist across Orthodox and Protestant bodies. Defenders of Basil emphasize that a fourth-century bishop regulating Roman-era custom is not a lawgiver for the present, and that his own writings elsewhere show deep pastoral care; critics answer that the canon shaped real women's options for a very long time. Both statements are true to the record.

sections.title: The Mainstream Christian Response, at Full Strength
sections.body:
Christian scholars and churches offer a layered response to this dossier, and fairness requires stating it at its strongest.

First, a category distinction: none of these men wrote scripture. Christian doctrine is normed by the biblical canon; the fathers and doctors are honored witnesses, not oracles, and every major tradition holds them corrigible. The church never defined Aristotle's embryology as dogma, and Tertullian's harshest treatise carries no canonical authority in any communion.

Second, the same men are more complicated than their worst sentences. Tertullian addressed the women he rebuked as "best beloved sisters." Jerome's closest intellectual companions were learned women — Marcella, Paula, and Eustochium — whom he taught Hebrew exegesis and praised extravagantly in his letters, and whose scholarship he defended against male critics. Basil explicitly flagged the tension between the Gospel's symmetry and his society's custom. Aquinas insisted that women fully possess the rational soul and the image of God in its principal sense. A dossier of their generous passages could be assembled with equal documentary rigor.

Third, scripture supplies the internal counter-voice. Galatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus" — has anchored Christian egalitarianism from the abolitionists to the present. The Gospels place women among Jesus' disciples and as the first witnesses of the resurrection, in a culture that discounted women's testimony.

Fourth, modern repudiation is explicit and official. Pope John Paul II's 1995 Letter to Women acknowledged the church's historical share in women's marginalization: "And if objective blame, especially in particular historical contexts, has belonged to not just a few members of the Church, for this I am truly sorry." (Letter to Women, n. 3, vatican.va). His 1988 apostolic letter Mulieris Dignitatem grounded women's equal dignity in creation and in Christ. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that man and woman are created in perfect equality as human persons. Protestant egalitarians (organized in bodies such as CBE International) argue that full equality of authority is the biblical position itself, while complementarians — for example, in the 1987 Danvers Statement — affirm equal worth and dignity with differentiated roles and likewise reject the patristic language of female defectiveness. In short, no living Christian tradition defends "defective and misbegotten" as anthropology; the intra-Christian debate today is about roles, not worth.

Finally, honest Christian scholarship concedes the historical cost. Historians within the church, from Elizabeth Clark onward, document that these texts had real institutional effects — in canon law, in purity-based exclusions, in the medieval reading of women's capacities — and hold that acknowledging this history is part of repairing it.

sections.title: The Same Honesty Applied to the Islamic Tradition
sections.body:
A survey built only from Christian texts would be propaganda, not comparison. The Islamic corpus contains its own hard text, and it sits in Sahih al-Bukhari, the collection Sunni Muslims regard as the most rigorously authenticated book after the Quran.

In Sahih al-Bukhari 304 (Book of Menstrual Periods; Book 6, hadith 9), Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrates that the Prophet, passing the women after a festival prayer, said: "O women! Give alms, as I have seen that the majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire were you (women)." Asked why, he replied: "You curse frequently and are ungrateful to your husbands. I have not seen anyone more deficient in intelligence and religion than you. A cautious sensible man could be led astray by some of you." When the women asked what the deficiency was, he answered: "Is not the evidence of two women equal to the witness of one man?" and "This is the deficiency in her intelligence. Isn't it true that a woman can neither pray nor fast during her menses?" — "This is the deficiency in her religion."

Mainstream Muslim scholarship has never denied this hadith's authenticity; it has argued about its meaning. The classical commentators — Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in Fath al-Bari on Bukhari, and al-Nawawi on the parallel report in Sahih Muslim — make several contextualizing moves. The setting is a festival-day exhortation to charity, a genre of pointed pastoral rhetoric rather than a treatise on female nature. The "deficiency in religion" is defined inside the hadith itself: menstruating women are exempted from prayer and fasting — an exemption legislated by God, for which, commentators stress, a woman bears no blame and loses no standing before God; the wording describes a smaller quantity of ritual acts, not a smaller soul. The "intelligence" remark is tied by the text to a specific evidentiary procedure for documenting debts (treated in detail in the companion article on inheritance and testimony), and classical jurists did not generalize it — in domains such as women's own expertise, a single woman's testimony was accepted. Modern Muslim discussion divides: some scholars read the report as occasion-specific rhetoric that later readers wrongly universalized; others regard it as a normative description tied to those two rulings and nothing more; still others, including some Muslim feminists, argue openly about its implications. Presenting the hadith as either a settled insult or a settled compliment would misrepresent a live debate.

The same corpus carries the tradition's counterweights, with equally strong chains of transmission in their collections. In Jami at-Tirmidhi 3895, Aishah narrates: "The best of you is the best to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives." In Jami at-Tirmidhi 1162: "The most complete of the believers in faith, is the one with the best character among them. And the best of you are those who are best to your women." And the Quran itself supplies the baseline texts quoted earlier: creation from one soul (4:1), mutual guardianship of believing men and women (9:71), and the ten-fold parallel virtues with identical reward (33:35) — alongside 2:228's contested "degree," which Muslims debate much as Christians debate their own hierarchy texts. Note that the bracketed gloss "[in responsibility and authority]" in the Saheeh International rendering of 2:228 is a translator's interpretive addition, not part of the Arabic text — an example of how interpretation enters even at the level of translation.

sections.title: Two Internal Reform Conversations
sections.body:
Both traditions are, right now, arguing with their own archives — and in both cases the argument is conducted from inside, with each side claiming the tradition's deepest sources for itself.

Within Christianity, the spectrum runs from egalitarians, who hold that Galatians 3:28 and the practice of Jesus set the norm and that the patristic and medieval material represents cultural accretion (the case made by historians such as Beth Allison Barr in The Making of Biblical Womanhood), to complementarians, who maintain differentiated roles while repudiating any language of female inferiority. Denominational practice now spans women bishops in the Anglican Communion and women pastors across much of Protestantism, alongside the Catholic and Orthodox retention of a male priesthood justified — in those churches' own words — by sacramental symbolism rather than by any deficiency in women. The Catholic magisterium's twentieth-century reversal of the older anthropology, from Mulieris Dignitatem to the 1995 apology, is itself a documented reform of the tradition surveyed above.

Within Islam, the recovery of women's scholarly history has become a major project. Mohammad Akram Nadwi's al-Muhaddithat, the introduction to his multi-volume biographical dictionary, documents thousands of women hadith scholars across Islamic history — women who taught men, certified transmissions, and issued corrections. The classical scholar al-Zarkashi (d. 1392) devoted an entire work, al-Ijaba, to the instances in which Aishah corrected the Companions' reports — an early, canonical precedent for a woman's scholarly authority over men. Contemporary debates over women's mosque access, female religious authority and iftaa, and family-law reform (Morocco's 2004 family-code revision is a frequently cited legislative example) proceed by contesting interpretations of the same Quranic verses and hadiths quoted in this article, with reformist and traditionalist scholars each claiming fidelity to the sources.

The symmetry is the finding. Each tradition contains foundational texts of equality, historical strata of hierarchy, and living communities deciding how the two relate. Which community is handling that inheritance better is a judgment this article leaves entirely to the reader.

sections.title: Sources and Verification
sections.body:
Every quotation in this article was checked against the following editions, and each is cited in the text by work and section.

Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women, Book I, chapter 1 — Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4, at newadvent.org/fathers/0402.htm. Jerome, Against Jovinianus, Book I, section 7 — Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 6, at newadvent.org/fathers/30091.htm; Letter 22 to Eustochium, section 20, at newadvent.org/fathers/3001022.htm. The menstruation line attributed to Jerome's commentary on Zechariah could not be verified in an accessible primary text and is therefore reported only as an attribution. Dionysius of Alexandria, Canonical Epistle to Basilides, Canon II — Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 14, at tertullian.org. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 92, a. 1 and q. 93, a. 4 — English Dominican Province translation, at newadvent.org/summa/1092.htm and /summa/1093.htm. Basil of Caesarea, Letter 188, canon 9 — Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 8, at newadvent.org/fathers/3202188.htm. Pope John Paul II, Letter to Women, n. 3 (1995), at vatican.va. Joe Early, "Thomas Aquinas's 'Misbegotten' Concept of Women," Priscilla Papers 38.4 (2024), CBE International, at cbeinternational.org.

Hadith citations follow sunnah.com numbering: Sahih al-Bukhari 304 (Book of Menstrual Periods; Book 6, hadith 9); Jami at-Tirmidhi 3895 (Chapters on Virtues) and 1162 (Chapters on Suckling), in the standard English translations. Quran quotations use the Tanzil Uthmani text with the Saheeh International translation via api.alquran.cloud; Bible quotations use the World English Bible via bible-api.com. Classical commentary positions (Ibn Hajar's Fath al-Bari, al-Nawawi's commentary on Sahih Muslim, al-Zarkashi's al-Ijaba) are summarized, not quoted, and are attributed by name so readers can pursue them.

sections.title: Notes on Reading This Material Fairly
sections.body:
Three cautions apply to everything above. First, quotation-mining cuts both ways: a survey of any tradition's harshest sentences will distort unless the counter-texts and the historical settings are kept in view, which is why this article quotes the responses of each tradition at full strength and names its sources throughout. Second, the classical authors wrote inside the science and social order of their eras — Aristotelian embryology, Roman family law, late-antique purity culture — and holding them to knowledge they could not have had explains their errors without excusing the harm those errors did. Third, the Victorian-era translations quoted here (Ante-Nicene and Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers) are the standard accessible English versions but are themselves dated; serious students should consult modern critical editions where wording matters.

This material is offered as information for readers comparing the two traditions honestly — not as ammunition. Behind every text in this article are living communities of women and men who love their faith; both traditions' own scholars, quoted above, model how to face a difficult inheritance without contempt.

title: Five Pillars of Islam
subtitle: The five foundational acts that give Muslim worship its shared shape
summary: The five pillars are the testimony of faith, five daily prayers, obligatory charity, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to Mecca for those able to go. Together they train conviction, remembrance, generosity, self-restraint, and unity before God.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
The five pillars are the shared foundation of Muslim religious practice. They are: testifying that only God deserves worship and that Muhammad is His messenger; performing the five daily prayers; giving the required charity called Zakat; fasting the month of Ramadan; and making pilgrimage to the Kaaba in Mecca once in a lifetime when physically and financially able.

The Prophet Muhammad summarized Islam through these five in Sahih al-Bukhari 8. Calling them pillars does not mean that nothing else matters. Good character, family duties, honest work, justice, learning, and many other obligations remain essential. The image means that these five acts give the life of worship a common supporting structure.

sections.title: 1. Shahada: The Testimony of Faith
sections.body:
The Shahada is the testimony that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah. Its first half is Tawhid: no idol, person, power, desire, or institution has God's right to worship. Quran 47:19 commands knowledge of this truth. Its second half accepts the messenger through whom Muslims received the Quran and learned the religion's practice.

A person enters Islam by sincerely affirming this testimony with understanding and choice. It is not a magical formula detached from life. It commits the believer to direct worship to God alone and to follow His messenger without treating that messenger as divine. Muslims repeat the Shahada in prayer and return to its meaning throughout life.

sections.title: 2. Salah: Five Daily Prayers
sections.body:
Salah is formal prayer at five periods of the day: dawn, noon, afternoon, sunset, and night. After ritual washing when required, a Muslim faces the Kaaba, stands, recites from the Quran, bows, prostrates, and sits in a sequence taught by the Prophet. Quran 2:43 joins the command to establish prayer with giving Zakat and worshipping in community.

Prayer interrupts the claim that work, entertainment, or anxiety should control the whole day. It gathers body, speech, attention, and time into worship. Congregational prayer is especially emphasized for the Friday noon prayer, while homes, schools, workplaces, and clean outdoor spaces can all become places of prayer.

Sunni legal schools agree on the five obligatory prayers and their core form, while differing over some details of hand position, recitation, timing within valid windows, and other movements. These variations should not obscure the unity of the act. Travelers, people who are ill, and others facing genuine hardship have recognized concessions in Islamic law.

sections.title: 3. Zakat: Obligatory Charity
sections.body:
Zakat is a required transfer from qualifying wealth to eligible recipients. The word carries the sense of purification and growth. Wealth is treated as a trust from God, and the poor have a recognized claim rather than being dependent only on occasional generosity.

A commonly encountered rate is two and a half percent on qualifying monetary wealth held above a minimum threshold for a lunar year. That single figure does not describe every asset: agricultural produce, livestock, trade inventory, and other forms of wealth have their own rules, and the legal schools discuss details. A Muslim with assets should learn the ruling that applies to the kind of wealth actually owned.

Zakat is distinct from sadaqah, voluntary charity. A person can give voluntary help at any time, in money, labor, food, counsel, or simple kindness. The pillar establishes a minimum duty while encouraging a much wider culture of generosity.

sections.title: 4. Sawm: Fasting Ramadan
sections.body:
During the lunar month of Ramadan, adult Muslims who are able abstain from food, drink, and sexual relations from true dawn until sunset. Quran 2:183 links fasting with the growth of righteousness and God-consciousness. The fast trains a believer to leave even permitted things for God's sake, making it easier to resist what is forbidden.

Ramadan is also a month of Quran recitation, prayer, charity, family meals, and care for neighbors. Hunger by itself is not the whole purpose. Muslims are taught to guard speech and conduct, reconcile where possible, and become more alert to people who live with hunger without choosing it.

Islamic law includes exemptions and alternatives. Menstruating and postpartum women do not fast those days and make them up later. Travelers and people with a temporary illness may make up missed days. People with a lasting inability may have a different duty, often feeding a person in need, depending on their condition and the applicable ruling. Individual medical questions should be discussed with both a qualified clinician and a knowledgeable scholar.

sections.title: 5. Hajj: Pilgrimage to Mecca
sections.body:
Hajj is the pilgrimage performed on appointed days of the Islamic month of Dhu al-Hijjah. Quran 3:97 makes pilgrimage to the House a duty for those able to find a way. Ability includes genuine physical and financial capacity and safe, lawful access; someone unable to meet those conditions is not failing an immediate obligation.

Pilgrims enter a consecrated state called ihram, gather at the Kaaba, stand in prayer at Arafat, and complete rites connected in Islamic memory with Abraham, Hagar, Ishmael, and Muhammad, peace be upon them. Simple pilgrimage clothing makes differences of status less visible, while the gathering of people from many nations offers a powerful image of equality before God.

Hajj is required once in a lifetime for the able. Umrah is a shorter pilgrimage that can be performed at other times and does not replace Hajj. The rites involve precise timing and practical rules, so prospective pilgrims normally learn them from a reliable guide before traveling.

sections.title: One Pattern of Devotion
sections.body:
Each pillar develops a different dimension of surrender. The Shahada gives worship its direction. Salah orders time around remembrance. Zakat loosens the grip of wealth. Fasting trains desire. Hajj joins personal sacrifice to a worldwide community and the memory of Abraham.

The pillars are not a scorecard for judging other people. Circumstances differ, knowledge grows gradually, and visible practice does not reveal every struggle of the heart. For a new Muslim, learning step by step with trustworthy support is usually healthier than trying to master every detail at once. The shared goal is steady worship of God with sincerity, knowledge, and hope.

title: Six Pillars of Faith
subtitle: The six convictions that form the core of Islamic belief
summary: The six pillars of faith are belief in God, His angels, His revealed books, His messengers, the Last Day, and divine decree. They give Muslims a coherent view of reality: created with purpose, guided by revelation, morally accountable, and always within God's knowledge and power.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
Iman means faith or belief. In the famous Hadith of Gabriel, the Prophet Muhammad defined faith as belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Day of Judgment, and divine decree concerning good and evil (Sahih Muslim 8a). These became known as the six pillars of faith.

They are not six unrelated facts. Together they answer connected questions: Who made us? How does guidance reach us? Who carries divine commands? What revelation has God sent? Who models it? Where is history going? Does anything escape God's knowledge and rule? Islamic faith joins the answers into one view of a purposeful and morally serious world.

sections.title: 1. Allah and 2. His Angels
sections.body:
Belief in Allah comes first. It means affirming the one eternal Creator, His unique names and attributes, His complete knowledge and power, and His sole right to worship. Every other pillar depends on this one: angels are His servants, books are His revelation, messengers are His chosen teachers, the Last Day is His judgment, and decree belongs to His wisdom.

Angels are created beings who obey God. They are not gods, divine children, or independent forces. Islamic sources describe roles that include bringing revelation, recording deeds, taking souls at death, guarding by God's command, and carrying out tasks in the created order. Gabriel is especially known as the angel of revelation.

Belief in angels expands the believer's world beyond what the senses can measure, but it does not authorize fantasy. Muslims affirm what reliable revelation teaches and avoid confident stories about the unseen without evidence.

sections.title: 3. His Books and 4. His Messengers
sections.body:
Quran 2:285 joins belief in God, angels, books, and messengers. Muslims believe God revealed guidance before the Quran, including the Torah given to Moses, the Psalms given to David, and the Gospel given to Jesus. The Quran also mentions pages or scrolls associated with Abraham and Moses. Respect for those original revelations is part of faith.

Islam distinguishes the original revelation from every later manuscript, translation, interpretation, or canon attributed to it. Muslim views about the transmission of earlier scriptures require more careful discussion than the slogan that everything was simply lost or rewritten. The foundational point here is positive: God has guided humanity repeatedly, and Muslims must honor the true revelation He sent.

Messengers deliver and embody that guidance. Muslims believe in Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, and all God's true prophets. They do not worship them or accept some while rejecting others out of prejudice. Muhammad is understood as the final prophet, and the Quran as the final revealed book governing Muslim belief and practice.

sections.title: 5. The Last Day
sections.body:
Belief in the Last Day means that earthly death is not the end of human existence. God will raise creation, expose what was hidden, judge with perfect knowledge and justice, and grant final consequences. The Quran speaks of resurrection, the gathering, the record of deeds, judgment, Paradise, and Hell. Quran 4:136 includes the Last Day among the essential objects of faith.

This belief gives moral weight to choices that human courts never see. An oppressed person is not forgotten, and a powerful wrongdoer does not escape merely by dying with a good reputation. It also prevents ethics from becoming only fear: God's mercy, forgiveness, and acceptance of repentance are central to the believer's hope. Muslims are taught to work, repair harm, and seek forgiveness rather than speculate obsessively about the exact date of the end.

sections.title: 6. Divine Decree
sections.body:
Qadar, or divine decree, means that nothing lies outside God's knowledge, will, and creative power. Quran 54:49 states that all things were created with decree. God knows the whole of reality without learning it in stages, and events do not surprise or overpower Him.

This does not turn human beings into morally meaningless puppets. The Quran addresses people as choosing, intending, obeying, disobeying, repenting, and bearing responsibility. Sunni schools have developed different technical explanations of how divine creation and human agency fit together. Ashari theology is known for the idea that human beings acquire acts God creates, while Maturidi theology often gives a more explicit account of created human capacity; Athari scholars tend to stay closer to the scriptural affirmations without extensive speculation. All reject both an independent human power outside God's rule and a fatalism that erases responsibility.

Practically, belief in decree produces a balance. A Muslim plans, chooses, works, prays, and accepts consequences, because effort is itself part of the created order. After doing what is right and possible, the believer does not imagine that a missed opportunity escaped God's knowledge. Qadar is not an excuse for sin or laziness; it is a source of humility in success and steadiness in loss.

sections.title: Faith That Shapes Action
sections.body:
The six pillars describe convictions of the heart, but Islamic faith is meant to appear in speech and action. Belief in God leads to worship; belief in angels encourages integrity when no person is watching; belief in books creates a duty to learn; belief in messengers invites imitation; belief in judgment strengthens accountability; and belief in decree gives courage without arrogance.

Sunni scholars have used different formulations when explaining the relationship between faith and deeds. They agree that deeds matter deeply and that open disobedience harms the believer. Beginners should avoid using theological vocabulary as a weapon for declaring other Muslims outside the faith. The Hadith of Gabriel itself places Islam, Iman, and excellence within one religion and ends by explaining that Gabriel came to teach the community its way of life.

title: What Are the Prophets?
subtitle: Human messengers who called their peoples to worship God and live by His guidance
summary: Islam teaches that God sent prophets throughout human history with one foundational call: worship Him alone and live responsibly. Muslims believe in Abraham, Moses, Jesus, Muhammad, and all God's true messengers without making any of them divine.

sections.title: In Plain Words
sections.body:
A prophet is a human being chosen by God to receive guidance and lead people toward Him. Prophets do not become divine, share God's power, or deserve worship. Their authority comes from the One who sends them. In Islam, believing in God's messengers is an essential part of faith.

The Quran names figures familiar from the Bible, including Adam, Noah, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, David, Solomon, Jonah, Zechariah, John, and Jesus, peace be upon them. It also names prophets associated especially with Arabian peoples, such as Hud, Salih, and Shuayb. Muslims believe Muhammad is the final prophet, not the only prophet and not the founder of an entirely disconnected message.

sections.title: Guidance for Many Peoples
sections.body:
Islam presents prophethood as a mercy running through human history. Communities differ in language, customs, and circumstances, so particular teachings and laws could differ, but the foundation remained the same: recognize the one God, worship Him, reject false objects of worship, and practice truth and justice. Quran 21:25 states this common call in direct terms.

The Quran names twenty-five prophets, but it does not say that only those twenty-five existed. It teaches that messengers were sent beyond the figures whose stories it relates. A Muslim therefore does not dismiss the possibility that peoples outside the Quran's named settings received genuine guidance, while also avoiding claims about particular individuals without evidence.

Some scholars distinguish nabi, usually translated prophet, from rasul, usually translated messenger, by saying a messenger carries a distinct commission or law while a prophet continues existing revelation. Other explanations focus on the audience or the form of revelation. The exact technical distinction has been discussed, but the beginner-level point is shared: both are chosen human recipients and teachers of divine guidance.

sections.title: Abraham, Moses, and Jesus in One Line
sections.body:
Quran 2:136 teaches Muslims to affirm what was given to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Jesus, and the prophets.
